That both increases your alertness and prevents the residual adenosine from delaying your circadian clock, which would otherwise bias you toward waking up later the next day, then going to sleep later, then waking up even later the following day, and so on (what chronobiologists call a *phase delay*).[^c1-50] Such circadian “drift” brought on by mild sleep deprivation is very common. It is best remedied by viewing morning sunlight to reset your circadian rhythm.[^c1-51]

Third, we need to talk about cortisol. Because it’s often discussed in the context of chronic stress, which is bad, most people think cortisol is “bad” too. But it’s not bad. Cortisol is essential to health and your levels of energy—you just don’t want your cortisol levels to be elevated at the wrong times.[^c1-52]

Your SCN is located in your hypothalamus (H), which is part of a biological circuit that also includes your pituitary gland (P), a small, stalk-like protrusion at the base of your brain that releases hormones into your bloodstream. The circuit also includes your adrenal glands (A), which reside atop your kidneys. This circuit is known as the HPA axis.[^c1-53] The HPA axis is one of the main systems that responds to stress (which is why you’ll hear more about it in chapter 3). Here’s how it works: It starts with signals from the hypothalamus, which then stimulate the release of specific hormones from the pituitary, which in turn stimulate adrenaline and cortisol release from your adrenals.

The HPA axis is also involved in the sleep-wake cycle. When your ipRGCs are activated by low solar angle morning sunlight and your SCN receives the ensuing signal, it alerts your adrenal glands to release adrenaline and cortisol via the HPA axis.[^c1-54] Cortisol and adrenaline dramatically increase levels of alertness, the latter likely by activating receptors on your vagus nerve,[^c1-55] a large portion of which extends from the organs in your body up into your brain and stimulates areas there such as the locus coeruleus to make norepinephrine, which has the net effect of “waking” you up.[^c1-56] Cortisol does a lot of things. It also decreases inflammation and regulates our immune systems to protect against viral and bacterial infections.[^c1-57] And it helps regulate our energy levels. Think about cortisol as a wakefulness-promoting hormone, not a stress hormone, if you want to understand what the cortisol in your body is doing most of the time. It’s also useful to consider how cortisol ebbs and flows across time due to signals from your circadian clock. By measuring cortisol levels every twenty minutes in human subjects, researchers found cortisol reaches its apex at about sixty minutes or so after you wake up and that it is lowest about four to five hours after you fall asleep.[^c1-58] Then it begins to rise sharply across the final two to three hours of your sleep until—boom! You wake up due in large part to what is called the cortisol awakening response (CAR). Yes, reaching a threshold level of cortisol is a major factor in what ultimately rouses you from sleep. As mentioned above, your cortisol continues to rise and peaks about sixty minutes after waking, then slowly drops down as you head into the early and late afternoon. Cortisol levels generally stay low and continue to drop in the evening and at nighttime (assuming it doesn’t spike from stress or intense exercise—more on that below), and then it falls to its nadir in those first four to five hours of sleep before starting to rise again toward morning. We return to this *circadian cortisol curve* in chapter 3, and the role it plays in promoting health in women and men of all ages. For now, the key thing to know is that for cortisol to support our health, it needs to peak in the first hour or so after waking; it then needs to drop precipitously in the evening and night and continue falling to reach its nadir in those initial four to five hours of sleep.[^c1-59]

Viewing morning sunlight doesn’t directly cause the morning peak in cortisol, but it can dramatically amplify its rise by as much as 50 percent.[^c1-60] This also helps ensure that this peak comes early in the day and isn’t shifted to the afternoon. Late-day elevations in cortisol have negative consequences over time such as sleeplessness, anxiety, and metabolic disease.[^c1-61]

A quick note: A morning workout, morning caffeine, and breakfast (provided it isn’t a huge and/or carbohydrate-laden one) will all promote wakefulness, too, and thereby contribute to a well-aligned circadian rhythm. But morning sunlight is the most potent lever for increasing morning cortisol and thus energy during your day, and for improving your sleep at night. Don’t underestimate its power.

Keep your circadian rhythm attuned to the sun, and all of these mechanisms will work as they should.

#### Common Questions

*It’s often dark when I wake up. What do I do if I have no access to morning sunlight but I want to start my day?*

If you wake up before sunrise, and you want to start your day, I suggest turning on as many bright indoor lights in your home—or hotel room, or wherever you may be—as possible. Sunlight cannot be replaced by standard indoor lighting, but turning on indoor lighting first thing won’t hurt. Then get outside to view morning sunlight once the sun is up.

If you wake before sunrise every day, or if you live in a part of the world where it is very dark in winter, you may want to invest in a 10,000 lux light to help ensure you get enough light in the morning (lux is a measure of brightness). Most cost about $100, and some are portable for travel. I often wake up before sunrise, and because the ipRGCs can be activated by very bright artificial lights if those bright lights include sufficient short wavelengths, I keep a 10,000 lux lamp in my kitchen and bathroom.[^c1-62] It lacks long wavelength light, so I also have a red incandescent light next to it and I turn that on too. I use the red incandescent light from SaunaSpace (no affiliation). I turn them both on first thing in the morning and then I get outside to view morning sunlight once the sun is up. I am well aware these lights are not a replacement for sunlight, but they help bridge the gap until the sun is up. Once the sun is up, you can be sure I go outside to view it!

And I will sometimes keep the 10,000 lux lamp and a red incandescent light on and facing me for an hour or so once I’m back working at my desk or getting ready for the day. Chapter 5 further explains the logic and benefits of this extended morning light exposure. There I also mention options that can be of real help for sleep as well as other aspects of health too, such as metabolic health.

But remember, morning sunlight is the best stimulus for your ipRGCs, SCN, and circadian rhythm, and it costs nothing! Figure out how to view it each morning. Again, you don’t need to see it cross the horizon as it rises. If you do, great, but if you wake up after sunrise, that’s fine. Do your best to view sunlight within the first thirty to sixty minutes after waking up. Bring your coffee or tea outside with you. Bring your spouse or kids if they’re awake. Bring your dog if you have one. Remember, dogs, cats, cows, and other animals have ipRGCs and an SCN, too, and they benefit from morning sunlight in many of the same ways and via the same mechanisms as we do.[^c1-63]

*What if it’s cloudy outside?*

To activate your ipRGCs fastest, go outside and face east toward the sun on a nice, clear morning with no clouds in the sky. Obviously, this isn’t possible for everyone every day.

Again, fortunately, sparse clouds do not interfere with the interaction between sunlight and our circadian clock. However, if the sky is densely overcast and gray, a 10,000 lux light can be a real help, but still aim for getting more sunlight in your eyes to compensate for the lower intensity of sunlight and reduced yellow-blue contrast exposure you’re likely to get on very overcast days. In fact, it’s *especially* important that you get sunlight in your eyes on overcast days. This is for three reasons: (1) dense clouds reduce the number of photons reaching your eyes in a given amount of time; (2) they filter out much of the longer (yellow, orange, and red) wavelengths of light, and (3) you are likely to be indoors more on cloudy days, which can cause the SCN to fall out of sync with the solar cycle, which leads to later nights, more artificial light exposure at night, more circadian disruption, and so on.

Aim to extend the sunny, clear day recommendation of a minimum of five to ten minutes, to at least fifteen minutes on cloudy days, and thirty minutes (minimum) on densely overcast days. That may seem like a long time, but remember, you don’t need to stand in one place gazing at the sky. Take a walk. Make a call. Listen to a book or podcast or talk to a friend, partner, or other family member. And even if you can’t be outside for the full time recommended above, some sunlight hitting your eyes in the morning is better than none. If you miss a day completely due to travel or sickness or other reasons, don’t despair—your energy levels that day may be lower because you didn’t get the cortisol spike bright morning light causes, but your circadian rhythm is the reflection of your previous three to four days of sunlight viewing activity.

*Do I need to worry about sunlight damaging my eyes?*

Excessive UV light exposure can cause cataracts and, as we have all heard, skin damage, accelerated skin aging, and some forms of skin cancer, topics I cover in more detail later in the book. But viewing morning sunlight is much safer than viewing overhead midday sunlight—because that Rayleigh scattering of short wavelength light when the sun is low in the sky includes UV and thus reduces your UV exposure significantly. It is when the sun is overhead that the UV index is high. UV light isn’t bad, per se, but you don’t want too much of it reaching your eyes or skin. Chapter 5 goes into the benefits and drawbacks of UV.

NEVER, EVER force yourself to stare at the sun—or any light source for that matter, at any time of day. Your natural blink and “look away” reflex is a built-in circuit (yes, there is a dedicated circuit for this) to protect your eyes. People with macular degeneration or other eye conditions ought to be especially careful about viewing midday sunlight, and if very sensitive to sunlight, they may want to consult with their ophthalmologist before doing any deliberate sunlight viewing.

*What about eyeglasses and contact lenses?*

Eyeglasses and contact lenses are both perfectly fine to wear while viewing morning sunlight. Neither one blocks light from reaching your eyes, even if your eyeglasses or contacts have UV filters.

Sunglasses and transition lenses, however, should be avoided while viewing morning sunlight because they block out a lot of the relevant wavelengths that trigger the valuable mechanisms covered in this protocol. Moreover, they reduce the number of photons reaching your eyes. Of course it’s fine to wear sunglasses as needed for comfort and safety at other times of day.

*What about viewing sunlight through a window or windshield? Is that the same?* People relentlessly ask me this and my response is equally persistent: No, it’s not the same. It’s far less effective, though better than nothing. But if there is any way to get outside, do. Windows and windshields, especially nowadays, filter the intensities and wavelengths you want for this protocol to work. “How come viewing morning sunlight through eyeglasses or contacts is fine but not windows or windshields?” you may wonder. Because windows do something called spectral filtering: They reduce the amount of light—especially short wavelength light—that would otherwise reach your eyes. Corrective lenses don’t; they let far more light through. That’s their job. Well, that and to correct any optical errors in the structure of your eyeballs so you can see things clearly. Windows and windshields do neither.

### Sleep Protocol 2: View Sunlight in the Late Afternoon

#### What to Do

- **Get sunlight in your eyes in the late afternoon or early evening.** Ideally, go outside and spend at least ten to fifteen minutes there before the sun sets. If at all possible, face or walk west toward the sun. You do not need to see the sun drop below the horizon. That’s a wonderful thing if you can—who doesn’t love a sunset? Alas, most of us don’t live or work in the right place to do so. Luckily, just going outside and getting some ambient light in your eyes in the late afternoon or early evening is beneficial. Seeing the sunset is a bonus.
- **A few things to keep in mind.** As with the previous protocol, it is best to face the sun directly, not through a window or windshield, and without wearing sunglasses or a brimmed hat. Perhaps you can get an unobscured view by going up to a rooftop or by walking a few blocks from where you work or live. From a health perspective, that is well worth it. Again it’s especially important to do this protocol on overcast days.

#### How It Works

We’ve already unpacked the basic physiological processes linking your circadian clock, your eyes, and specific qualities of light that drive the sleep-wake cycle. Afternoon sunlight exposure taps into some of the same basic underlying cells, circuits, and mechanisms, but has both distinct and added benefits, including partially protecting you from some of the negative health effects of viewing artificial lights late at night.

Here again we start with the SCN. Earlier I described the SCN as a “cluster of neurons,” but that doesn’t really do it justice. A key feature of the SCN is that it contains two oscillators, each following a roughly twenty-four-hour rhythm of electrical activity, but offset from one another.[^c1-64] It’s as if they are singing in a round, with peaks happening at different yet specific moments within the twenty-four-hour cycle. One peak roughly corresponds to morning and the other to evening, and each can be entrained to sunrise and sunset. And they communicate with one another to be sure neither the morning nor the evening oscillator runs too fast or too slow. That helps generate the SCN’s coherent daily rhythm that all other cells in the body follow. It also allows us to shift our clock forward or back as the lengths of days and nights change across the seasons.

Here’s the best way to think about it: These two oscillators are like bookends buttressing a row of vertically stacked books, making the books less likely to fall over. This is the right analogy given that viewing morning sunlight shifts the phase of our circadian clock forward, making us want to go to sleep earlier and wake up earlier. Viewing late afternoon or early evening sunlight delays the phase of our clock, which, because it shifts the timing of the release of hormones like melatonin, makes us want to go to bed later and wake up later. So viewing both morning and afternoon sunlight thus helps keep us on a regular sleep-wake schedule, because the phase shift effects of morning and evening sunlight offset each other.[^c1-65]

Another great reason to view sunlight in the late afternoon or early evening is that it helps buffer us against the negative effects of viewing bright artificial lights at night.[^c1-66] In the morning, we need to see a lot of bright light to train our SCN with the solar cycle, and to elevate our levels of alertness. Unless it’s a 10,000 lux lamp, most artificial lights and certainly our phone or computer screens just can’t do the job at that time. After sundown, however, it takes extremely little bright light to quash our melatonin levels, and shift our circadian clock. And even if we can still fall asleep at night, that sleep is not going to be as high quality.

In fact, studies show that as little as fifteen seconds of bright light can significantly shift our circadian clock.[^c1-67] And while most screens are not as bright as the lights used in these studies, our ipRGCs and SCN work to sum photons—that is, add up all the light we see from various sources. And let’s face it, most people are looking at their phone and other screens for a lot longer than fifteen seconds after sundown.

To recap: In the morning, you need more bright light in your eyes than a screen or conventional home lighting can provide, and at night you want far less light reaching your eyes than typically comes from a phone or computer screen or conventional home lighting. It all has to do with how our eyes are more sensitive to detecting light at different times of day or night. If that seems inconvenient, you’re right; nowadays it is! But the circuits underlying retinal and circadian sensitivity across the twenty-four-hour cycle evolved long before humans had artificial lighting, much less the bright, short-wavelength-enriched LED screens and LED bulbs that we use today.

I, like most people, often wake up once in the middle of the night to use the bathroom. If I had things my way, our circadian system would be buffered from the phase-shifting effects of light at that time, but I wasn’t consulted at the design phase, and our ipRGCs are *exquisitely* sensitive to bright light in the middle of the night and wee hours of morning. In fact, our ipRGCs and SCN become increasingly responsive to light with every hour after sundown.[^c1-68] If you’re wondering if fireplaces, campfires, candlelight, or moonlight are too bright to view after dark, the answer is no. Firelight sources emit very long wavelengths, and moonlight is low lux. Candlelight is typically just 1 lux. A bright, full moon is *less* than 1 lux! Compare those numbers to a typical table lamp, which is 200 to 400 lux, or commonly used overhead indoor LED lighting, which is 500 to 1,000 lux.

So are we to all avoid artificial lighting and opt for candlelight or moonlight? Maybe, but more on that later. In the meantime, let’s acknowledge that most people just won’t do that, and even if we opt to at home, we can’t control the lighting of most other environments like office cubicles, restaurants, hotels, and the rest.

That is where this protocol can help. Viewing sunlight in the afternoon reduces the sensitivity of neural circuits in your retinas, so that any artificial light you see after dark does not have as strong an effect in disrupting melatonin and other circadian-related molecules and processes in your eyes and brain. This protocol is especially important if your mornings and days are mostly spent under artificial indoor lights, as that will cause any artificial lights you view at night to have an outsized negative effect on your sleep and circadian rhythms.[^c1-69] Think of viewing the sunset as your (partial!) nighttime TV-watching or phone-scrolling inoculation. That said, you should still strive to dim the lights in the evening, and make it as dark as possible while you sleep, as discussed in the next protocol.

#### Common Questions

*What if I can’t get myself to a place where I can see sunlight in the late afternoon or early evening?*

I understand. Most of us are working, driving, or otherwise occupied indoors when the sun is setting—especially in the fall and winter months. And while sunsets are both beautiful and beneficial, telling your boss “I need to leave to go watch the sunset” is not going to go over well. (Although saying “Let’s go watch the sunset together because it’s good for our health” might be a good idea, depending on how you frame the question.) If you can’t watch the sunset, just try to go outside at some point in the afternoon to get some ambient daylight in your eyes before dark, even if it’s just for a stroll around the block, or a few moments on a balcony. Do whatever you can. The ambient light will still serve your SCN, and thus your circadian rhythm, sleep, and health, in numerous beneficial ways.

### Sleep Protocol 3: Avoid Viewing Bright Lights in the Final Hour Before Bedtime

#### What to Do

- **After sundown, limit your nighttime light exposure.** You have a few options for how to do that. Which you use will depend on where you are and what activities you need to carry out.
  - **Option 1: Dim the lights.** After sundown, dim the lights in your home or wherever you are in the hours before sleep.
  - **Option 2: Use red lights at night.** I am a fan of using soft amber or red incandescent (or even amber or red LED lights, which are easier to find nowadays) for indoor lighting after dark as they don’t spike cortisol or suppress melatonin as much as many bright white LED lights do.[^c1-70] Remember, you want to try to keep your cortisol low in the late evening and especially the final few hours before your bedtime at night. You also want your melatonin elevated then. While this protocol might seem extreme, shifting to amber or red lighting in the final hours before sleep can make a marked difference for some people’s ability to fall and stay deeply asleep, which extends to every aspect of next-day energy, mood, and focus.[^c1-71]
    - *Consider buying a few high-quality red light bulbs.* Bon Charge makes great LED bulbs that are just the right level of brightness to see, but not so bright as to disrupt circadian rhythms and Ra Optics has LED bulbs that lack the usual flicker of LEDs and can shift between daytime and “candlelight” mode (I have no affiliation with Bon Charge or Ra Optics, but I use these brands at home, and I travel with one or two of their bulbs when on the road and staying in hotels.) SaunaSpace makes a large, red incandescent bulb that is about the size of a shoebox that can illuminate a medium-sized room. I have one in my living room and another in my bedroom. Incandescent bulbs give off a softer illumination than LED ones, and have some known advantages for mitochondrial health, which I cover in chapter 5.
    - *Consider small, portable side table LED lamps or bulbs that can be flipped from bright white to yellow to red, depending on the time of day or night.* Bon Charge makes these. They are great if you need to navigate to the bathroom at night. They charge off your computer or a wall outlet and (hooray) don’t require Wi-Fi or an app. I know many people who have solved their “I wake up in the middle of the night to go to the bathroom and then can’t fall back asleep” issues by switching to these.

**Note:** *I am not talking about “red light therapy,” and you don’t need a fancy red-light panel for this protocol. In fact, red-light panels tend to be very bright—exactly the opposite of what you want to use at night! They have their place, which I will discuss later in this book.*

- **Option 3: Use combination UV, blue, and green light blocking glasses after sundown.** This is the most versatile and cost-effective option. Consider buying a pair of blue and green light blocking glasses if you need to be on a computer, look at a phone, or watch TV at night. They are also helpful when you can’t control the lighting because you’re out at a restaurant, in an airport, et cetera, at night.

  I helped design ROKA Wind Down glasses, which block the full range of blue and green light, are lightweight, and come in a variety of frames. They are excellent quality.

- **Option 4: Use good ol’ candlelight.** Just make sure to blow it out before you go to sleep!

#### How It Works

Humans are not the strongest or fastest creatures on earth, but we are the best at building technologies. Every technology—the automobile, the smartphone, airplanes, antibiotics—brings the potential for unprecedented power over nature in our daily lives. Artificial lights have vanquished darkness. But in the case of LED lights, in particular, this technology also carries a risk to our circadian cycle, our mitochondria, and thus, our health.

Until about ten years ago, most artificial lighting used incandescent bulbs, which contain more long-wavelength light and a more even distribution of different wavelengths than LED bulbs. Incandescent bulbs have been largely phased out because they are less energy efficient than LED bulbs. Nowadays, most indoor lighting comes from LEDs, which emit a disproportionate amount of short-wavelength light that can potently reduce melatonin levels.[^c1-72] Emerging evidence also points to negative effects of LEDs on mitochondrial health (which we’ll go into later, in chapter 5).[^c1-73]

Those are some of the risks. Now let me explain why bright artificial light at night may also be affecting our mood. Each of us has a brain structure called the habenula that sits at the middle and top part of an egg-shaped brain structure called the thalamus.[^c1-74] Your thalamus is a station for routing different types of sensory and motor information to the correct parts of your brain so you can detect and integrate that information into your thoughts and actions. When I was an undergraduate and graduate student taking neuroanatomy, the habenula was listed as having an “unknown function.” Recent studies in rodents, fish, and humans finally revealed what it does.[^c1-75]

We now know the habenula is part of a network that controls depressive feelings and disappointment.[^c1-76] Habenula activation creates those states by altering dopamine and serotonin dynamics in brain areas associated with reward.[^c1-77] Why would we harbor such a structure and circuit? The answer is that not all behaviors are meant to be rewarded. Some need to be punished so we are less likely to repeat them. And it turns out that viewing bright light in the “you really should be asleep now” phase of your circadian cycle is one of them. Animal studies and emerging evidence in humans show that viewing bright lights at night causes your ipRGCs to activate a specific region called the perihabenula.[^c1-78] That leads to elevated levels of cortisol, reductions in dopamine, next-day anxiety, and deficits in learning—all consequences that appear to be separate from any reductions in total sleep time.[^c1-79]

For most people, the “you really should be asleep now” time is somewhere between the hours of 11:00 p.m. and 4:00 a.m. But of course, neither your SCN nor your habenula knows clock time; they only know circadian time, which follows the circadian body temperature, cortisol, and other twenty-four-hour rhythms I described briefly earlier in this chapter. Your body temperature starts to rise in the final two hours before waking, and continues to rise throughout your morning and day until you reach the mid to late afternoon.[^c1-80] At that point, it starts to decline. That decline continues as we sleep, reaching its lowest point, called, unimaginatively, your *temperature minimum time* about two to three hours prior to waking.[^c1-81] So when I say avoid viewing bright lights from LEDs or other sources at night, I am referring to the time about six to eight hours before your temperature minimum time. This may seem overly technical, but knowing your temperature minimum time can be very valuable. And no, you don’t have to measure your body temperature; your temperature minimum is the approximate time in your twenty-four-hour circadian cycle that roughly corresponds to two hours before you typically wake up, alarm clock or no. The exact clock time of course will vary depending on whether you are a morning lark or a night owl, or somewhere in between (more on how to determine that soon). But since most people wake up between 6:00 and 8:00 a.m., their temperature minimum time is between 4:00 and 6:00 a.m. If that’s you, assuming you’d like to fall asleep anytime between 10:00 p.m. and midnight, it means you should avoid viewing bright artificial lights between 11:00 p.m. and 4:00 a.m. You would do even better to dim the lights starting around 8:00 or 9:00 p.m. Put simply, to avoid habenula activation and shifting your circadian clock, avoid bright artificial lights in the four to six hours prior to your temperature minimum time.

If you want to figure out your exact temperature minimum time, simply take the average of your wake-up times over the course of three to four days and subtract two hours. Then strive to avoid viewing bright artificial light in the full six-hour period prior to that. I generally wake up at about 6:30 a.m., which means my temperature minimum time is 4:30 a.m., so I avoid viewing bright artificial light between 10:30 p.m. and 4:30 a.m.

I know this all sounds technical, but it’s very simple. By doing it, you’ll likely enjoy improvements in your sleep and thus daytime mood, focus, and alertness. I acknowledge that many people can fall asleep after being under bright artificial lights in the hours before bedtime, but knowing several such folks, I can assure you even they benefit by adopting this simple (and incidentally cost-saving) change. Bonus: your home feels cozier at night too.

A bit more on those mood improvements: In 2018, a team of researchers, including noted UCLA psychiatrist Peter Whybrow, reviewed the data on the potential link between LED lighting and mental health. They concluded that exposure to blue light, in particular, posed a risk to sleep and other processes governed by the circadian system.[^c1-82] There is also evidence suggesting that the way in which artificial lighting at night interferes with this system may lead to depression.[^c1-83]

These findings do not mean we should all throw away our LED lights. However, if you can find incandescent lights for your home, they are preferable because they’re less disruptive to the circadian system. In a study from 2020, researchers found that incandescent lighting interfered with the production of melatonin far less often than LED or fluorescent lights.[^c1-84] (I cover why this is in chapter 5.) If you can’t find incandescent bulbs, consider the Bon Charge or Ra Optics bulbs or ROKA Wind Down or other short wavelength (not just “blue”) blocking glasses.

Experiment with the options in this protocol to see what works best for you. And no matter what bulbs you choose for your home, still dim them before bed, and keep it dark in the six to eight hours prior to your temperature minimum time. If a light is bright enough, it doesn’t matter if it is an LED or incandescent, it will still alter your circadian cycle.[^c1-85]

#### Common Questions

*What if I want to go to a game, concert, party, or movie and view bright lights? Will that destroy my sleep that night?*

This is an important question, as we need to live a life that is not just focused on health. From a circadian perspective, no, it will not destroy your sleep. Your natural wake-up and to-sleep times are determined by your genetics, your social activity, your exercise routine, your stress levels, and the average timing and amount of your morning and evening light viewing—especially morning sunlight—in the prior days. As I mentioned earlier, the idea is to strive to get great sleep about 90 percent of the nights of your life, and reserve the remaining about 10 percent for when challenges or fun keep you up late, or even until dawn. Yes, wearing glasses that block UV, blue, AND green wavelength light can help keep your sleep on target, even when you’re going out a lot, but who wants to wear those lenses on a first date or on your wedding night? They can be fun to wear to concerts and dinner, but I hate to think that anyone would miss out on the joys of life to avoid bright light exposure to their eyes. That said, if you’re getting a lot of screen LED light in your eyes at night because you’re scrolling on your phone or computer or watching a big flat-screen monitor, that will take a negative toll on your health. Please adjust this protocol so that it works for you. Also, you shouldn’t wear these glasses while driving, for obvious reasons; there are a lot of road signs and lights that you would not be able to see accurately—or at all depending on their color, and you could get into an accident.

What I describe here is what to strive for. Everyone diverges from that now and again. Enjoy your life and meet its moments by prioritizing your health most of the time and not stressing about the occasional night out.

*What about kids? Do the same rules about lighting apply?*

Yes. They need great sleep even more than we do, given the stage of brain and bodily development they are in. Teens, though, tend to stay up late to socialize online or otherwise. Keep in mind that kids and teens often need eight to ten hours of sleep.[^c1-86] But their socialization is vital, too, so you’ll have to strike a balance between encouraging a healthy relationship to artificial light, screens, and their social life. That said, if your teen or child is depressed or anxious, it’s important to assess their sleep patterns and relationship to light, especially the amount and timing of screen use. I have heard from many parents whose kids had a significant improvement in their mental health with the protocols listed here. Some were only able to convince their teens to use their phones outside in the yard instead of in their rooms in the morning. Others have told me their kids love the morning and evening sunlight viewing for the immediate mental and physical benefits it provides. I won’t make this a parenting protocol, but the phrase “be a channel, not a dam” comes to mind as possibly useful in this context.

*My infant wakes up frequently throughout the night. Can dim lighting help me cope with interrupted sleep?*

Yes. Even if your infant is waking frequently through the night, try to keep the lights as dim as possible during those stretches, and/or use red light bulbs (again, not the same as red light therapy panels). Dimming lights will help you fall back asleep with your infant and will also help your baby’s circadian system start to become attuned to the solar cycle. Babies have very different REM and other sleep cycles compared to adults—they naturally get much more REM, but the general effects of light and darkness on their cortisol and melatonin levels are very similar to those of healthy adults. That is one reason why the practice of dividing breastmilk refrigerated for later use into “collected in morning” and “collected at night” is becoming more commonly discussed in health circles. The former contains relatively more cortisol and the latter relatively more melatonin.[^c1-87]

### Sleep Protocol 4: Find Your Ideal To-Sleep and Wake-Up Times and Strive to Adhere to Them

#### What to Do

- **Find your chronotype to set your schedule.** Some people sleep better when they stay up late and sleep in late; others feel best when they go to bed early and wake up early; and most people fall somewhere in between, preferring to go to sleep somewhere between 10:00 p.m. and midnight and to wake up between 6:00 and 8:00 a.m.
- **Try to stick to your schedule.** As long as you sleep for at least six to eight hours a night, pick a sleep-wake schedule that works for you. Even shifting slightly closer to your chronotype will afford you much more restorative sleep.

> **A systematic approach to figuring out your ideal sleep-wake schedule:**
>
> Let’s get something out of the way. If you’ve been reading this chapter and thinking, “Hmm, my circadian rhythm is nothing like the one you describe,” then maybe you are a night owl. Or maybe you just think you are. Kenneth Wright, whose lab at the University of Colorado Boulder studies circadian rhythms, wanted to figure out how much of people’s preference to go to bed long after sundown and sleep in many hours past sunrise was due to a natural inclination, and how much was due to the influence of artificial indoor lighting.[^c1-88] He and several colleagues gave participants wrist monitors that measured the intensity and timing of their light exposure throughout the day, as well as their activity patterns, so that they could know when the participants were sleeping. Next, they measured their melatonin levels every hour to see whether the participants’ bedtimes matched up with their circadian-driven increases in melatonin—which is a reliable measure of circadian clock output. Finally, the participants were sent packing. They went camping for a week, with only the sun and campfires as their light sources; no flashlights, screens, or other electronic devices permitted.
>
> That one week was all it took for participants to sync sleep-wake cycles to the rising and setting of the sun. Before the outing, some of the participants were convinced they were morning people and others were convinced they were night owls. After a week in the wilderness, those differences faded. They all went to sleep around sunset. The researchers noted that the intensity of the light the participants experienced while camping was four times greater than the intensity of light in their normal lives—a testament to how much time they normally spent indoors. Interestingly, just one weekend spent camping had a similar effect of shifting people’s circadian rhythm toward being early risers and people who prefer to go to sleep early. Mind you, those shifts were not just while camping. They persisted *after* they came back. This study was small and in no way does it mean there is no such thing as a night owl. But the rapidity and degree of the change suggest that artificial lighting masks the preference of many people to have a solar-cycle-aligned rhythm.
>
> There are potential health implications tied to shifting toward (or away) from your innate sleep-wake timing. And they suggest that except for bona fide night owls, a more solar-cycle-aligned rhythm is beneficial. A large-scale 2019 study of nearly 700,000 subjects showed a causal link between being a morning person and better mental health—that’s right: a causal link.[^c1-89] A different study found a higher risk for cardiovascular disease among people who went to sleep later and slept for a long time.[^c1-90] Another analysis using data from 6,258 people in Finland found a link between routine late nights and type 2 diabetes.[^c1-91] The patterns a night owl keeps have also been linked to depression.[^c1-92]
>
> And there are new data showing that even if you prefer to go to bed and sleep late, shifting to becoming an early riser can improve your health.[^c1-93] But telling a night owl to become a morning person can be dangerous—people cling to their natural sleep cycles like a pit bull on a rope toy.
>
> Whether you think you’re a night owl or not, by systematically experimenting with your to-sleep and wake-up times a bit and by limiting bright artificial light exposure in the final hour or two before sleep, you can determine the ideal sleep-wake schedule for you. Few people can do genetic testing or sleep lab analysis to determine their true chronotype, but there is a simpler way and it’s worth exploring.
>
> - **Here’s how:**
>
>   Unless you are perfectly happy with your sleep, for one week, try getting into bed by 8:30 to 9:00 p.m. If you’re not ready for bed at that time, read a book or do another non-screen activity, but turn all the lights out by 9:00 to 9:30… maybe 10:00 p.m. at the latest.
>
>   Many people who do this wake up at 6:00 a.m. or even 5:00 a.m. the next day feeling more refreshed than ever before. Those who had previously been going to sleep at 11:00 p.m. or 12:00 a.m. and assumed they needed eight or more hours of sleep to feel rested often find they can feel great with just six or seven hours of sleep if they just get to sleep a bit earlier.
>
>   This process aligns your sleep more accurately with your genetically driven cortisol and melatonin rhythms. The genes that determine chronotype impact what are called clock genes, which are located in your SCN, and in almost every other cell of your body too. Your SCN entrains every cell in your body by changing its patterns of clock gene expression, either directly or indirectly, by altering the timing and type of peptides, hormones, and neural signals those cells receive. It’s a multipronged and highly distributed network that allows your SCN to do that. That is one reason why once people find their correct sleep schedule, they often notice their digestion and immune systems improve, as well as key biomarkers of metabolism, not just their sleep and mood. It’s not unusual to get more deep and REM sleep and awaken feeling substantially more refreshed when you obey your chronotype. Nocturnal growth hormone release[^c1-94] is strongly regulated by your circadian clock,[^c1-95] and is released in the first hours of sleep. If you are meant to go to sleep between 8:30 and 10:00 p.m. and you stay up late, you miss out on getting some of that growth hormone. And growth hormone is vital for bodily and brain repair, metabolism, and myriad other health functions.[^c1-96]
>
>   A few things to keep in mind as you try this protocol. If you typically have been going to sleep after 10:30 p.m., dim the lights as described in Sleep Protocol 3. Also, remember that it is perfectly normal to wake up once to go to the bathroom in the middle of the night. If you do, I highly recommend that you do not look at a clock or turn on bright lights. Chances are you’ll fall back asleep within thirty minutes or less. No matter when you typically have been going to sleep, eating too close to bedtime and/or drinking caffeine late in the day will mess up this whole experiment—both lead to more frequent nighttime wakings, so don’t do either.[^c1-97] In general, eating your last bite of food at least two to three hours before bedtime is best, provided you are not experiencing gnawing hunger near bedtime, in which case a small snack one hour before is helpful. Yes, eating too close to bedtime may disrupt sleep, but gnawing hunger will keep you awake, so we need to be practical about this whole “don’t eat too close to bedtime” thing.[^c1-98] And try not to drink caffeine after 1:00 or 2:00 p.m. (more on the reasons why in Sleep Protocol 11).
>
>   If you are not used to going to sleep this early, and you find yourself unable to fall asleep even after several nights, you may just be genetically wired to go to sleep between 10:30 p.m. and midnight. True night owls do exist! There is nothing wrong with that, provided your schedule lets you sleep long enough for you to feel rested the next day. Again, this assumes you are not drinking caffeine after 1:00 or 2:00 p.m., stressed out, or otherwise generating elevated levels of arousal late in the day, all things that can affect your sleep-wake schedule.
>
>   Indeed, people prefer different sleep schedules. Approximately 33 percent of people feel great going to sleep between 10:30 p.m. and midnight and waking up between 6:30 and 7:30 a.m.[^c1-99] The other 33 percent do best going to sleep between 8:30 and 10:00 p.m. and waking up between 4:30 and 6:30 a.m. The remaining third are bona fide night owls—in the absence of caffeine or work demands, their genetically driven melatonin rhythms and circadian rhythms cause them to be wide awake until 12:30 a.m., 1:00 a.m., or even 2:00 to 3:00 a.m., and they do best waking up between 9:00 and noon.[^c1-100] The point is to determine which group you are in, and to do so while not letting other variables screw up your experiment.
>
>   It is oh-so-valuable to know what your body and brain need, and thrive on. If you’re truly an early or late chronotype, perhaps you can delegate tasks to family members or roommates to meet life’s demands. You can select courses and workout times that better match your rhythms. I will even go so far as to say that, because of the way that getting your sleep-wake times right generates outsized positive effects on your health and cognition, you might even be wise to try to build your life around it. Tell your boss you’ll have fewer sick days (you will), tell your partner you’ll be a better partner (you will), and if you have kids, a better parent (you will). Feel free to cite me during the negotiations. There are aspects of our biology that we can neglect for a while before it causes issues. Chronotype is not one of them. Of course, we can shift our circadian clock for child-rearing, work, or travel, and this book teaches you how to do that more effectively, but we can’t disobey our chronotype for more than a few years before it catches up with us, and often it only takes a few weeks of disobeying it before we start to notice mild to severe malaise, irritability, or poor digestion. Fortunately, the reverse is also true. Align better with your chronotype—even by just an hour or two and you’ll often feel much better within days.
>
>   That said, our ideal sleep timing and total sleep needs do change as we age. Some of that is socially driven, but other aspects are related to changes in our pineal gland—the gland that makes melatonin and other hormones and neurotransmitters.[^c1-101]
>
>   Also, when we are sick or recovering from an injury or bout of chronic stress, we need more sleep. The point here is to figure out the best sleep schedule for you, this year, and know that it may drift a bit over time, or in specific circumstances.

> **Key point 1:**
>
> Keep in mind that regardless of your ideal sleep-wake schedule, you benefit from being consistent with any sleep-wake schedule. That means going to bed and waking up at the same time, plus or minus thirty minutes, six to seven nights out of the week. Consistent does not mean neurotic. Strive, don’t strain, to get things right. Nothing is worse than trying to force yourself to sleep.

> **Key point 2:**
>
> It is very normal to feel very awake about one to three hours before your bedtime. That increase in arousal, sometimes referred to as the “wake maintenance zone,” is thought to be an adaptive mechanism for allowing us to secure our physical surroundings and safety prior to sleep, but that is just speculation. A transient increase in alertness—that for some occurs around sunset and for others around one to three hours before their typical bedtime—also may happen; it’s well documented in sleep studies, although to my knowledge its physiological basis has not yet been explored in detail.[^c1-102] Remember, this is a transient increase, so don’t sweat it. Let it pass and embrace the drop in body temperature, the rise in melatonin, and sleepiness that follows.

#### How It Works

The intricacies of what happens when we sleep—the so-called architecture of sleep—deserves a book of its own, and indeed many have been written about it.

Rarely discussed, however, is how the architecture of each sleep-wake cycle influences our sleeping *and our waking* states. We touched on this topic a bit earlier in this chapter. But now, by exploring the architecture of sleep itself, we can start to understand how the placement of six to eight hours of sleep in each twenty-four-hour cycle, and the consistency of that placement from one day to the next, has a profound effect on exactly what happens while we sleep, and how that impacts whether our sleep is maximally restorative.

##### The Stages of Sleep

Many people are familiar with the two major types of sleep: rapid eye movement, or REM, sleep, and non-REM sleep. Non-REM sleep is often referred to as deep or slow-wave sleep, but that’s oversimplified. Non-REM sleep consists of three distinct phases that we enter, one after the other. These are referred to as N1, N2, and N3 sleep, and only in the N3 stage does actual deep or slow-wave sleep occur. Cycling through N1, to N2, to N3, to REM sleep takes, on average, about ninety minutes. So a person who sleeps for three hours might make it through two cycles, a person who sleeps for six hours experiences four cycles, and a person who sleeps 7.5 hours gets five cycles, and so on.

We enter N1, or *light sleep*, first and it typically lasts five to ten minutes. It is easy to rouse us from N1 sleep. But N1 is not merely a transition stage; during N1, our body starts to generate additional adenosine triphosphate, or ATP, the chemical that fuels all our biological processes. What’s more, proteins that have become misshapen or broken during our waking hours get repaired during N1, and proteins that help build memories by reconfiguring our neural circuits are created.[^c1-103]

Next we enter N2 sleep, which lasts about twenty minutes. During N2 our body temperature drops, our heart rate slows down, and our brain produces sleep spindles—surges of transient brain activity that help consolidate information we have learned in the days prior.[^c1-104] Sleep spindles are vital for learning new cognitive information and motor skills, which both represent types of neuroplasticity.[^c1-105] We explore this in greater detail in chapter 6.

N2 has another intriguing feature: PGO waves, which are surges of large-scale brain activity that travel from the pons (P) of the brainstem, to the geniculate (G), a structure in our thalamus (the sensory waystation we discussed earlier), and then to our occipital (O) cortex, which resides in the back of our brain and is involved in, among other things, visual processing. PGO waves trigger the release of massive amounts of glutamate, an excitatory neurotransmitter that is a requisite component of the multistage process of learning, such as in the formation and elimination of synapses.[^c1-106]

After N1 and N2 we enter deep sleep, what sleep researchers call *slow-wave sleep*, or N3. This is an extremely restorative stage of sleep. During N3, our brain waves shift to very high amplitude and low frequency, aka *slow*; our heart rate slows way down, and growth hormone is released from our pituitary gland into our bloodstream.[^c1-107] What’s more, the active repair of our muscle, brain, and other bodily tissues occurs—including our tendons, skin, heart, et cetera.[^c1-108] That process involves a lot of protein synthesis, or the repair and regeneration of cells and tissues by use of specific amino acids.[^c1-109] Some of that repair and regeneration occurs in response to tissue damage from exercise, but most of it is simple “housekeeping”-based cellular turnover and repair, which is also vital to our health and longevity. N3 is also when *glymphatic washout* of our brain occurs.[^c1-110] This process was discovered just in the past fifteen years or so and involves the pulsing of lymph-like fluid through our brain, thereby removing the waste products caused by normal brain metabolism and any cellular debris that accumulated the previous day.[^c1-111] This glymphatic clearance is actively governed by multiple brain regions—including the locus coeruleus—that we will talk about more below and in later chapters.

REM sleep, or rapid eye movement sleep, follows N3, but often we cycle from N3 back to N2 for a few minutes or more before advancing into REM sleep. REM sleep is crucial for sorting through all that waking life brings our way by eliminating or strengthening specific neural connections in accordance with what information we need to keep and what we should discard.[^c1-112] Thus, think of REM sleep as an experience audit, with only the meaningful experiences surviving the cut.

One more interesting thing about REM: Our body becomes mostly paralyzed during this stage, a phenomenon known as sleep atonia.[^c1-113] The most prevalent hypothesis to explain sleep atonia is that it keeps us from acting out our dreams during REM sleep.[^c1-114] Our brains are extremely active during REM and the dreams we experience during this stage tend to be vivid and emotionally laden—often marked by flying, swimming, being filled with anxiety or awe, and highly dynamic in how we move through time and space (in the dream of course).[^c1-115] The idea is that REM-associated atonia prevents us from acting in accordance with what are essentially in-sleep hallucinations, which would put us in danger.

The relative amount of time we spend in REM sleep increases, and the amount spent in deep N3 sleep decreases, as we complete more sleep cycles across a night of sleep. This means our most vivid dreams tend to occur as we approach morning. A baby’s sleep is largely REM sleep, and the amount of REM we experience decreases with age starting in adolescence.[^c1-116] If we are sleep-deprived, or we do something that reduces the amount of REM sleep we get on a given night—using cannabis, for instance—the next night we experience REM rebound by entering REM sleep sooner in the sleep cycle, and experiencing more REM overall. Chronic cannabis users who stop using cannabis often report vivid dreams in the first weeks and months after quitting.[^c1-117]

Alcohol and many prescription drugs reduce the fraction of our sleep that is REM as well. Once someone stops using these, they also experience an REM rebound.[^c1-118]

REM sleep is fascinating. As stated before, it is characterized by more brain activity than we ever experience in our waking life, and yet we are paralyzed while our brain is in that hyperactive state. And there’s more. REM sleep is also the only time in our lives when our locus coeruleus—the brainstem region that releases norepinephrine and increases our focus and alertness—goes largely dormant. Also, we don’t readily release adrenaline from our adrenals during REM.

Researchers believe that this paradoxical state, during which our brain is highly active but our body is paralyzed, our locus coeruleus is almost silent, and our body can’t easily release adrenaline, serves as a sort of naturally occurring therapy, unloading the emotional burdens from our daytime experiences. Indeed, this general set of conditions parallels many established trauma therapies, in which patients recount a traumatic event while in an intentionally or progressively lowered state of anxiety, so as to detach the body’s and brain’s emotional responses from the details of the memory. People selectively deprived of REM sleep have a harder time unloading emotional burdens from past experiences, including traumas.[^c1-119]

REM, like some of the other sleep stages, is also a key time for the consolidation of new skills and information that are of a nonemotional nature. We will cover more on that in chapter 6.

##### Health risks of sleep deprivation

Given all this, it becomes clearer and clearer how lack of sleep, but also altered sleep architecture, affects our mind and body in a variety of ways. Sleep deprivation is associated with diminished response time, alertness, attention, memory, and executive functioning.[^c1-120]

Additionally, as described at the chapter outset, lack of sleep can bring about longer-term problems as well. Insufficient REM sleep may increase the risk of dementia. In 2017, a group of researchers published their investigation of links between dementia and sleep architecture.[^c1-121] They looked at three years of data on thirty-two adults over age sixty with dementia and found that the likelihood of cognitive decline fell in line with a reduction in REM sleep. In fact, with every 1 percent reduction in REM sleep, the risk of dementia rose by about 9 percent. (Non-REM sleep deprivation did not share this connection.) The role of REM in building and consolidating neural connections, thereby protecting against cognitive decline, may also explain why truncating this stage would raise the risk of dementia, but direct evidence for this mechanism in humans is still lacking.

Getting sufficient REM sleep is also connected to overall longevity. In 2020, a group of researchers from multiple institutions reported that less REM sleep is associated with an increased mortality risk. Using data from 4,050 people, they found that for every 5 percent decrease in REM sleep, the mortality rate increased by 13 percent.[^c1-122] That held true for most causes of death, including cardiovascular disease.

Ask any sleep researcher “How can I get more REM sleep?” and they will tell you “Sleep in an extra hour or two.” But most people can’t afford to sleep in an extra hour or two past their usual wake-up time. The good news is that *when* we sleep is almost as important as getting enough of it. If we get to bed and wake up at a time that is in sync with our chronotype, we end up getting more growth hormone release, and we spend less time in light sleep and more time in deep sleep and REM sleep. As a consequence, we tend to need less sleep overall. Our sleep can become more efficient and restorative.[^c1-123]

Studies of shift workers tell us what happens if we sleep enough, but at the wrong times of the twenty-four-hour cycle. The short answer is: Bad things happen. Working at nighttime and sleeping in the daytime is associated with greatly elevated risk of type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease, depression, and suicide.[^c1-124] Shift workers are also susceptible to neurocognitive impairment and at greater risk for substance abuse.[^c1-125] One large survey from Canada found that executive function is significantly worse among people whose jobs take place outside normal work hours.[^c1-126] One study found the level of performance impairment to be equal to a blood alcohol concentration of 0.10, which exceeds the legal limit for driving in many places.[^c1-127]

To be clear: Being a night owl is not the same thing as forcing yourself to be nocturnal, so if that’s your chronotype, don’t worry. The health detriments of shift work are likely to be multifactorial—the lack of sunlight, the altered social interactions associated with an inverted schedule, and more. We know that one of the worst types of shift work for one’s health is the swing shift, where people switch back and forth from daytime to nighttime work each week or even within the same week.

How long we sleep, when we sleep, and how consistent we are with our sleep-wake schedule affect our physical and mental health. That’s why I hope you try the approach outlined here. Figure out what is best for you and then stick with it.

#### Common Questions

*Does changing time zones for travel or moving the clock for daylight saving time affect our sleep-wake cycle?*

Yes. When we turn the clocks forward an hour to move from standard time to daylight saving time, or back an hour to return to standard time, or when we change time zones during travel, our circadian clock has to shift.

Changing our clocks forward or back means we have collectively decided that 7:00 a.m. is now 8:00 a.m., or 8:00 a.m. is now 7:00 a.m., but our SCN really doesn’t care about clock time, it only knows time according to the entrainment cues it receives. You already know the most powerful entrainment cue and that’s viewing morning sunlight. Even if we move the clocks just by one hour, the SCN needs a few days to shift its patterns of gene expression and communication with all the cells of the body to get them on schedule. In the meantime, we are groggy at times in the morning when we were perfectly chipper the day before. And a whole host of other systems in our body and brain have to shift before we feel like ourselves again. The dangers of such shifts extend beyond mere irritability. Traffic accidents increase in the days immediately following seasonal clock changes.[^c1-128] So do heart attacks.[^c1-129] It also makes people more susceptible to depression.[^c1-130]

Jet lag occurs when our sleep-wake cycle no longer matches the solar cycle of our location. Our internal timekeeper may be telling us it’s time for bed when the locals are just eating dinner. Many people find that traveling east, into a later time, is harder than traveling west, into an earlier time, because we have to move our circadian clocks forward. It’s often easier to stay up a few hours longer, or even take a brief nap, than to force ourselves to go to bed before we’re ready.

Some people don’t suffer much from jet lag. Others suffer tremendously. For those of you in the latter group, Sleep Protocol 15 offers a technique that can help avoid jet lag or at least dampen its impact.

*Is it bad to sleep in on weekends or to stay up late now and again?*

We should all strive to keep a consistent sleep-wake schedule, for the reasons discussed above. That means we should try to get to bed at the same time, plus or minus thirty minutes, on most nights. Same goes for waking up; try to wake up at roughly the same time each day, plus or minus thirty minutes. Larger changes in sleep or wake times every once in a while won’t be too disruptive, because the entrainment of your SCN reflects the weighted average of inputs from multiple factors, as discussed. So by all means, enjoy that birthday or wedding or New Year’s celebration and don’t despair about arriving home late. One late night is not something to worry about.

Many people wonder whether wake times should be later after that occasional late night. If you usually go to sleep somewhere between 8:30 and 11:00 p.m. and have a night where you’re up until 1:00 or 2:00 a.m., should you sleep late or wake up at your usual time? In general, it’s best to get enough sleep to feel rested but not to sleep more than one or two hours past your usual wake time. So on those “I stayed up too late last night” mornings, get an extra hour in bed asleep if you can, and try to take a twenty-minute nap, or practice non-sleep deep rest (NSDR) in the afternoon (more on that soon), and then get to bed around your usual time that night. Your SCN—and thus you—thrive on consistency. If you go to bed much later than usual and sleep in much later, too, be sure not to shift your whole schedule forward. It’s still fine (and encouraged) to view sunlight, exercise, and so on, but be especially mindful not to drink caffeine much later in the day than usual, or you will soon find yourself off your usual rhythm and it will take three to four or more days to get back to it.

*What about children and teenagers?*

The advice is a little different for young children and teenagers. Babies need to sleep A LOT and enter REM far more frequently and for longer than any other age group. Toddlers and young children should also sleep as much or as often as necessary, or desired, to support their extraordinarily fast brain and bodily growth rates. The amount of neuroplasticity in infants and children, all the way up to adolescence and beyond, is incredible—and sleep is a key part of that process. Limiting their sleep is never recommended but of course once kids are in school, setting a regular schedule (and keeping devices out of their rooms near bedtime and throughout the night) becomes important.

Sleep needs are somewhat different for teenagers. Bedtimes shift during puberty for at least two known reasons. First is what researchers call the homeostatic sleep drive. This term refers to a brain and bodily pressure to sleep that builds up gradually throughout the day, mainly due to adenosine accumulation.[^c1-131] The longer we are awake, the more adenosine in our bodies, and the greater the pressure to sleep. Adenosine levels drop while we sleep and begin to mount again when we wake up for the new day. This pressure to sleep is separate from the circadian clock mechanisms we have discussed a lot thus far. Teenagers (good rebels that they are) resist this pressure and force themselves to stay up late, building up more adenosine and, therefore, the desire to sleep in the next morning.[^c1-132]

And they often don’t need to force themselves to stay up late; it just happens naturally, as the hormonal testosterone, estrogen, and progesterone surges of puberty shift their circadian clock to a later phase.[^c1-133] Melatonin production begins later in the teenage brain than in the brains of either adults or younger children.

All of these changes leave the typical sixteen-year-old awake until about 11:00 p.m.[^c1-134] And this age group should be sleeping about nine hours per night, making 8:00 a.m. the preferred wake-up time. Studies have found that moving school start times to 8:30 a.m. or later leads to better grades and other measures of academic performance. There is even evidence suggesting that this shift also reduces car crashes among teen drivers.[^c1-135] It’s beneficial for teenagers to have days when they can sleep as long as they want, even if that means staying in bed until noon. That doesn’t mean they should never be woken up earlier on a Saturday or Sunday, but parents and caregivers do not need to worry about prolonged sleeping on the weekends. Teenagers, yes, reference this book if you need leverage to sleep in and parents, yes, you still want to encourage them to get sunlight in their eyes once they get up, even though it is midday, and not low-solar-angle sun.

Current data indicate that teenagers in the US are in the midst of an epidemic of sleep deprivation that is likely having serious consequences for their health. Ideally, young people between the ages of six and twelve years should sleep at least nine hours per night, and thirteen-to-eighteen-year-olds should sleep at least eight hours per night. More than 70 percent of young people do not sleep enough, according to one large survey from the CDC.[^c1-136] Anxiety, mood disorders, obesity, high-risk behavior, poor academic performance, and substance use have all been tied to sleep deprivation among adolescents.[^c1-137] Good practices for teenagers include shutting off screens at least an hour before bedtime, keeping the phone (and the laptop, the tablet, etc.) out of the bedroom at night and the room cool and dark, having a consistent bedtime, and, ideally, sleeping for those eight to nine hours per night.

*Do sleep patterns change for older adults?*

Parsing the changes in sleep that arise in older adults is tricky. Ailments and medications of various kinds impact sleep in many ways. Absent any such interferences, sleep can vary in our later years, but not to a great extent. Older adults sleep a bit less than middle-aged adults by about an hour or so, on average.[^c1-138] It can take longer to fall asleep as we move past age fifty, but again, not in a dramatic way. And older adults are able to doze back off to sleep after a middle of the night waking, just as well as teenagers and younger adults can.

The stages of sleep also shift a bit as we age. The percentage of time we spend in deep sleep and REM decreases, although studies have shown a surge in REM in people between the ages of seventy-five and eighty-five years.[^c1-139] Older people also tend to nap more.

*Does counting sheep help with falling asleep?*

Counting sheep has long been recommended for calming a busy brain before bed. The idea is that by giving ourselves a task, we stop ruminating on the day and going over our to-do lists for tomorrow. It turns out that counting sheep isn’t such a great nighttime activity. Allison Harvey, a psychologist at UC Berkeley, found that counting sheep actually made it more difficult for people to fall asleep.[^c1-140] She concluded that this basic mental imagery was not engaging enough to hold the attention of people lying in bed trying to keep anxieties at bay. Without that focus to help calm our brain, we’re back to ruminating and reviewing to-do lists. A subsequent study in which Harvey instructed participants to deliberately suppress whatever thought was most likely to intrude into their mind before sleep found this didn’t help—predictably, the thought they were supposed to be suppressing just became more preoccupying.[^c1-141] *Instead, try these somewhat weird tricks:*

*Take a mental walk:* **Imagine walking from your bed to your mailbox and then down**

**the street and to a nearby location, then home again by the same or different**

**familiar route.** Occupying a busy brain with an easy and engaging task can help stop ruminating thoughts. Mental walks like these are occupying but not stimulating. And they have the tendency to lull people off to sleep.

*Move your eyes following the pattern described below:* **Warning: This is going to**

**sound a bit out there, but it works well for many people, and studies are indirectly**

**starting to suggest why.**

Lie down in bed and close your eyes. Keep your eyes closed and move your eyes slowly to the right then to the left, then up, then down, then counterclockwise and then clockwise. Then cross them somewhat by directing them gently toward your nose. Finally, do a big inhale and long exhale. Repeat one to three times as needed.

Told you this would sound a bit out there! This trick often helps people fall asleep, because to do so we need to stop thinking about our limb position, or proprioception. Our visual and vestibular systems, or balance, and proprioception systems interact, and the eye movements just described “confuse” those systems. A similar mechanism partially explains why gentle slow rocking and pacing can help babies, and slow rocking of a bed (yes, such beds exist) can help adults improve their sleep metrics.[^c1-142] We need more data to understand the mechanism behind this pattern, which is why it’s not its own protocol, but it is reasonable to assume it is related to the eye-to-vestibular circuits involved in, among other things, proprioception and sleep. New eye mask and rocking-bed technologies that trigger this eye movement pattern are designed to cause similar eye movements. I have tried a few of these nascent technologies and confess I fell asleep in less than two minutes! Meanwhile, this technique is free and easy to try. “Next thing I knew it was morning!” is not an uncommon refrain from people with whom I have shared this trick.

### Sleep Protocol 5: Lower Your Core Body Temperature at Night

#### What to Do

- **Lower the temperature of the room you sleep in at night.** Cooler ambient temperatures facilitate sleep. Keep your bedroom between 65 and 68 degrees Fahrenheit, and a maximum of 70 degrees.
- **Warm your extremities before bed.** A hot shower, hot bath, sauna, or even washing your face with very warm water can help induce drowsiness by warming hands and feet and by triggering a drop in core body temperature in compensation for this heating.
- **Make sure your feet and hands can be easily exposed from underneath your covers.** The skin of these areas is a primary way we shed heat from our body. Exposing them to cool air is one of the most effective ways to decrease core body temperature. So untuck your sheets at the foot and sides of the bed.
- **Avoid wearing socks while you sleep, especially if you tend to wake in the middle of the night.** Socks can stop the natural cooling process that happens through the feet. (People who tend to run very cold at night may want to skip this recommendation.)

#### How It Works

Socks or no socks? Window open or closed? Blanket or just sheets? Feet exposed? We all have our sleep habits and a lot of them revolve around temperature. That makes sense. Thermoregulation—the maintenance of our core body temperature—and the management of our sleep environment to control our body temperature is crucial for a great night’s sleep, both falling and staying asleep. Indeed, changes in our core body temperature both reflect and influence our circadian rhythm, how much melatonin and other hormones we release, and even the amount of deep and REM sleep we get in a given night.

As I mentioned earlier in this chapter, our core body temperature declines as the day goes on, eventually reaching its lowest point at a specific time—we call this temperature minimum time.[^c1-143] A decline in body temperature precedes us falling asleep. The rate of temperature reduction, and not just the absolute core temperature value, seems to matter. In one experiment, researchers made the case that people tended to head off to bed at exactly the time that their temperature was declining fastest.[^c1-144] Body temperature starts to increase shortly before we wake up. The relationship between core body temperature and our level of autonomic arousal—which is what sleepiness and alertness reflect—is causal but is best thought of as “necessary but not sufficient,” meaning we need the change in temperature, but other factors are key too.[^c1-145]

Research has found that the ideal ambient temperature while we sleep is between approximately 66 and 70 degrees Fahrenheit, which typically brings the microclimate immediately around our skin down to somewhere between 88 and 95 degrees Fahrenheit.[^c1-146] To fall asleep our core body temperature needs to decrease by about 1 to 2 degrees.

A lower core body temperature facilitates various sleep-related biological processes you are now familiar with. First, research indicates that this reduction may help initiate non-REM sleep,[^c1-147] and our lowest body temperature is associated with deep sleep. Melatonin, a hormone that facilitates falling asleep, is released in sync with the nightly drop in body temperature. In one small study of twelve women who were entrained to the solar cycle, the secretion of natural melatonin at night occurred with a simultaneous decline in core body temperature.[^c1-148] Other studies have observed a similar coupling.[^c1-149]

The stillness of our body during early sleep also plays a role in further dropping our core body temperature. In sleep, our autonomic nervous system shifts from more sympathetic activity (or tone, as it’s often referred to), which is related to being alert and able to generate movement, to a far more parasympathetic tone, which is associated with calmness, lower heart rate, and less or no bodily movement.[^c1-150] All that combined causes our blood to flow more to our periphery, to our hands and feet, where it “dumps heat,” which in turn leads to a lower core body temperature.

This means that warming up our hands and feet a bit before getting into bed could facilitate falling asleep. That may seem paradoxical: Why would warming up your periphery help at a time when cooling down your core body temperature is the goal? Because heating your periphery acts as a trigger. A hot shower or bath, or a sauna, warms the surface of your body. That causes the preoptic area of your hypothalamus—a brain area that works sort of like a thermostat—to trigger a compensatory response, lowering the core temperature in your body.[^c1-151] This process makes it easier to fall asleep, a phenomenon known colloquially as the *warm bath effect*.[^c1-152]

Once you get in bed, having your sleeping environment cool is also helpful. Many people sleep best in a cool room but with their whole body under loads of warm blankets. Other people run hot and like to sleep under just a sheet or a light blanket. Try out a few of these recommendations and pick what suits you best.

##### In My Experience

I prefer a comforter and a weighted blanket, but stick my bare feet out from underneath them, which we know helps cool core body temperature. And I keep the room about 68 degrees Fahrenheit. Closer to morning, I find that I often bring my feet under the blankets (in my sleep!), which we know can increase the amount of time spent in REM in the final few hours before waking.[^c1-153] Temperature-controlled mattress covers like Eight Sleep make controlling your bed temperature across the night easy, and I use one. (They are a podcast sponsor, and I am a scientific advisor to Eight Sleep). But with or without Eight Sleep, it is a good idea to use programmable room temperature controls to help create that cooler-at-start and warmer-toward-morning sleep environment. Experiment and find what works for you.

#### Common Questions

*Do daytime temperature changes affect nighttime sleep?*

Some data from animal studies suggest that a slightly elevated body temperature for a few hours in the afternoon may lead to more time spent in N3 sleep at night, when waste products from the brain and spinal cord are cleared away (among other processes).[^c1-154] That’s one reason why many people find that doing some moderate to intense exercise in the early or midafternoon improves their sleep, provided they don’t consume a lot of caffeine before their workout.

*So should I avoid exercising at night?*

It’s best to avoid intense exercise late at night, within three to four hours of sleep. High-intensity exercise raises our core body temperature, which is counterproductive to falling asleep. That said, some people can only exercise at this time, and many learn how to down-shift afterward with a hot bath or shower, and by using some of the tools covered in chapter 3, like deliberate long-exhale breathing.

If you consistently find it difficult to fall and stay asleep after exercising hard at night, consider moving your more intense workouts to mornings and doing something lighter in the evening. A review of several randomized clinical trials found that meditative movement like tai chi and qigong improved sleep quality.[^c1-155]

However, if night is the only time of day you can exercise, then it’s more important to get the workout in than to skip it just because it’s late in the day (more on that in chapter 2). In this case, it may help to take some additional steps for ensuring a solid night of sleep: no caffeine after 1:00 or 2:00 p.m., a nighttime wind-down routine, a hot shower, some breathing exercises to reduce stress, no screens, and dim lighting will all help counteract the energizing effects of late evening exercise.

### Sleep Protocol 6: Increase Your Core Body Temperature in the Final One to Two Hours of Sleep Before You Wake Up

#### What to Do

- **Program your heating system for the room you sleep in at night.** If you have one that can be set to different times, program it to rise one to three degrees above your room temperature, starting one to two hours before your wake-up time.
- **Keep clothing by your bed.** If you wake up one to two hours before your preferred wake-up time or in the middle of the night to use the bathroom, try putting on some socks, sweats, or even a knit cap and go back to sleep until your preferred wake-up time. This can increase your core body temperature, which increases the amount of REM sleep you get and will help you wake up feeling energized.

#### How It Works

We touched on this in the previous protocol but given the importance of getting sufficient REM sleep for mental and physical health, and for performance, it’s worth delving into this topic as its own protocol. So here it goes: Just as cooling our core body temperature facilitates falling and staying asleep, warming our core body temperature starting about one to two hours before we wake up can lead us to feel far more refreshed and ready to lean into the day.

Hot temperatures are disruptive to falling and staying asleep.[^c1-156] Interestingly the body tends not to adapt; even after several days of trying to sleep well in hot temperatures, sleep remains disrupted.[^c1-157] One theory holds that wakefulness itself is triggered by the need for thermoregulation; in other words, waking up is a way to bring our body temperature back to normal.[^c1-158]

We have less data on the use of temperature in this part of the sleep cycle than we do for the previous protocol. However, we know that our lowest body temperature, or temperature minimum time, occurs at about two hours before we wake up and begins to rise after that.[^c1-159] A return to our normal core body temperature accompanies our return to wakefulness, so it stands to reason that supporting the general process of warming up after we reach our temperature minimum helps us wake up feeling energized.[^c1-160] (It likely reflects having had at least two REM-enriched sleep cycles.)

Admittedly, there’s a small problem here. It’s hard to get out of a warm bed into a cold room. Heating the room you sleep in on a timer that increases the temperature one to two hours prior to waking solves that problem. Otherwise you just have to get up and get to the thermostat.
