There is a lot of debate (of course) as to whether animal-based proteins are superior to plant-based proteins, but the debate is often misleading because it neglects a key feature of any protein. And that is what I will refer to as the complete-protein-to-calorie ratio (CP:C ratio). Even when comparing animal-based complete proteins to one another, it is important to consider their relative CP:C ratios. I’ll illustrate this concept by comparing some examples of different foods: 150 calories of chicken versus 150 calories of lean beef versus 150 calories of whole eggs versus 150 calories of tofu versus 150 calories of beans and rice. All are considered complete proteins.

Now, importantly, while you would need to eat beans and rice (or nearly any legume and any grain combination) to get all nine essential amino acids, these do not need to be eaten in the same meal to be utilized effectively. As long as you get sufficient essential amino acids across your meals over the course of a day, it works.

150 calories of chicken has about 28 grams of complete protein

150 calories of lean beef has about 25 grams of complete protein

150 calories of whole eggs contains about 13 grams of complete protein

150 calories of tofu has about 15 grams of complete protein

150 calories of beans and rice has about 6 grams of complete protein

150 calories of peanut butter on a slice of wheat bread has about 6.5 grams of complete protein

And let’s throw in 150 calories of scallops, which has about 29 grams of complete protein.

The reason different foods and food combinations yield different amounts of complete protein at the same caloric level is because none of these foods are 100 percent protein. They also contain some fat, or in the case of plant foods, carbohydrates and fats.

Most animal-based foods like meat, eggs, and shellfish contain zero (or close to zero) carbohydrates, and varying amounts of fat. Dairy products contain protein and fat (unless defatted, like skim milk, for example), and dairy includes carbohydrates to varying degrees.

So we need to ask: Does a given “protein” contain all nine essential amino acids? And: What is its CP:C ratio?

In other words: How many calories of a given “protein” food do we need to eat in order to get enough of those nine essential amino acids?

The answer to that question matters for body composition, health, and the pleasure you experience from eating, because getting those nine essential amino acids is crucial for satiety. That’s because how much you eat at a meal is driven in part by your brain’s and body’s hunger for complete proteins. When you get enough complete protein, you tend to feel satisfied during, and for a long while after, the meal. When you don’t, you tend to feel hungry again soon after eating.

The nine amino acids are not the only reason we eat, but they are a big part of it. Below I’ll explain how, if we don’t get enough complete protein per calorie, we start to run into problems. Luckily, those problems are easy to fix. I’ll explain how to do that too.

I often hear: “But I eat protein! I eat beans, I eat peanut butter…” Well, neither of those are complete proteins, but if the beans are served with rice or if the peanut butter is spread on wheat bread, then they become complete proteins. Problem solved? Usually not. In fact, often it’s problem *created*. Remember, beans and rice together provide 6 grams of protein for every 150 calories. That means you would need to eat more than four times as many calories of beans and rice (700 calories) to hit the same amount of protein (28 grams) found in 150 calories of chicken. Peanut butter on wheat bread is a similar story, given that in those 150 calories, you’re only getting 6.5 grams of protein. That brings us back to CP:C ratio. Chicken has a high ratio; beans and rice or peanut butter on wheat bread has a low ratio.

To be fair, some animal-based foods also have a low CP:C ratio. Take most pork for instance. One hundred fifty calories of lean pork will give you about the same amount of protein as 150 calories of chicken or beef (about 25 grams). But most commercially sold pork products, such as bacon, ham, and pork chops, are not lean. Most contain a high percentage of fat, and often have sugar added to them too. One hundred fifty calories of low-sugar bacon has only about 10 grams of protein. Typical store-bought bacon with sugar added? About half that, at 5 grams. You would need to eat about 400 to 500 calories of bacon to get the protein found in 150 calories of chicken.

The takeaway here is that we need to prioritize eating complete protein foods, and we need to consider the CP:C ratio when selecting which to eat. While protein is not the whole story, the best nutrition plan typically places proteins with a high CP:C ratio at the center of the plate.

**WHAT PROTEINS ARE BEST?**

If you eat animal products, I suggest you prioritize lean cuts of beef, elk, venison, or bison, as well as fish and chicken. They have a high CP:C ratio. Many dairy products do, too, such as Greek and Bulgarian yogurt, and cottage cheese. Eggs are great as well, even though they do not technically meet the benchmark, given their ratio of protein to fat. That said, I still incorporate eggs into my diet most days. After years of public debate on whether eggs are healthy or unhealthy, the FDA consensus as of 2025 is that, yes, eggs are healthy. They appear on a list right next to salmon, 100 percent olive oil, fruits, and vegetables.[^c4-12] Our grandparents were right (again!).

Powdered proteins such as whey protein have a very high CP:C ratio and are a convenient way to get enough protein for perhaps a meal or snack per day, maybe two if you’re on the go. But they should not be your only complete protein source because they lack a number of important vitamins and minerals and other micronutrients found in whole foods. You want to prioritize whole foods for that.

Plant-based sources of proteins, by contrast, tend to have a low CP:C ratio. So much so that it is best not to think of most plant-based foods as proteins at all. It’s more accurate to think of grains, like rice and quinoa, and legumes, like beans, simply as carbohydrates, because that’s mainly what they are. And think of the lipid-rich plant-based sources of proteins, like nuts, as fats, because that’s mainly what they are. There are exceptions, but by and large the CP:C ratio of these foods is just too low to consider them otherwise. Unless you’re burning significant calories through long-duration exercise or physical labor, relying on low CP:C ratio foods to try to get enough complete protein often leads to eating excess calories and putting on body fat. And for those trying to gain weight—yes, such people are out there—devote your additional calories to high CP:C ratio proteins, carbohydrates, and healthy fats.

And before you say “He’s an anti-vegan, ketogenic carnivore!” I assure you that is not the case. None of this is leading up to me suggesting a purely animal-based diet. I think vegetables and fruits are fantastic. I eat them daily and some grains too. Vegans who are willing to put in the work to seek out or prepare dishes with a variety of ingredients—such as beans and other legumes, rice and other grains, and tofu and tempeh—can get adequate amounts of the nine essential amino acids across the day without eating animal products. They just need to be mindful not to eat too many calories relative to their overall energy needs. I have seen a vegan diet work great for some people, but admittedly they tend to be very diligent about the sourcing and combining of their plant-based foods to achieve complete proteins. Or they do a lot of cardiovascular exercise—they run marathons, triathlons, and distance races of that sort—which comes with very high caloric needs compared to that of most people.

One more consideration as you select a protein source is the bioavailability of that protein source—how much protein you can absorb as you digest it, and then how much your cells can make use of it. There is ongoing debate about this amount. Classic studies concluded that we can only absorb about 30 grams of protein per meal.[^c4-13] That amount became a sort of “law” of nutrition, especially in resistance training fitness circles that prioritize muscle protein synthesis—a process that is stimulated by weight lifting, but that is also involved in muscle maintenance for everyone, lifters and non-lifters alike. Later studies showed, however, that our bodies can use pretty much any amount of protein we ingest.[^c4-14] What changed? Mostly the conversation around protein absorption.

A portion of the protein that we consume at any given meal is used by our muscles. But there’s a limit to the “dose” of protein our muscles can synthesize; that dose is around 30 to 50 grams at one time.[^c4-15] Whatever amount we consume beyond that will be absorbed by the gut and the liver, and used for things like neurotransmitter production, hair and collagen growth, immune system function, and much more. (Note that for kids still growing, and for those who resistance train regularly, the amount directed for protein synthesis is probably closer to 40 to 50 grams per meal, with the excess available for other tasks.)

Does this mean that you must consume 30 to 50 grams of protein at every meal if you want to maintain your current muscle mass? Nope. Research on intermittent fasting (a good setting to investigate this question because daily calories are consumed in a small window rather than as three meals spread across a day) found that lean muscle mass is preserved as long as enough total protein is consumed in a day.[^c4-16]

All of this explains why people versed in nutrition don’t just talk about how much protein we can absorb, but the metabolic fate of the proteins we eat. In fact, there are times when assimilating 100 grams (!) per meal is possible.[^c4-17] Does that mean you should eat 100 grams of protein per meal? Not necessarily. First off, how many meals are you eating? And how much protein do you need? Again, we return to the data.

**HOW MUCH PROTEIN DO YOU NEED?**

Most people should aim to consume 1 gram of protein, ideally from high CP:C ratio protein sources, per pound of body weight each day. It’s not crucial that you eat exactly that much every day. I suggest it as a target from which you experiment a bit to find your protein needs. If you find yourself too full or otherwise unable to hit it, that’s okay. You should never feel like you’re force-feeding yourself just to hit a protein goal. Strive to hit the 1 gram of protein per pound of body weight (or close to it) most days. And if you prefer to divide your protein into multiple meals and snacks per day, do that. If, however, you prefer to eat twice a day and ingest more protein at those meals, do that, even if you’re resistance training specifically to gain muscle. While it’s true that spreading out your protein across four to five meals and snacks per day can provide a marginal increase in muscle protein synthesis if you’re resistance training and aiming to gain the maximum amount of new muscle, the difference it makes won’t be meaningful for the majority of people. So figure out the timing of your meals and snacks that works best for your hunger, energy levels, sleep, and schedule. Be mindful of, but don’t obsess about, that 1 gram of protein per pound of body weight target.

Some people worry that eating too much protein can cause kidney problems or gout, but the data show that only becomes an issue if people consume something in the vicinity of more than 3 grams of protein per pound of body weight—an absurdly high amount that most people would struggle to reach.[^c4-18] So don’t fear eating high CP:C ratio foods. That’s one more debate that’s easy to settle.

Another debate: There is also talk that deliberately eating far less protein than we need can help us live longer. The theory is that eating protein stimulates a rise in the level of mTOR (which stands for mammalian target of rapamycin), a protein related to cell growth that, when suppressed, has been shown to extend lifespan in animals.[^c4-19] So far, however, the data point to “NOPE” on whether a low-protein-to-suppress-mTOR diet helps humans live longer.[^c4-20]

Entire books could be devoted to any of the topics above but for now, let’s just keep the CP:C ratio in the back of our minds as an important metric to consider when making food choices. Prioritizing eating enough foods with a high CP:C ratio to reach that 1 gram per pound of body weight removes a lot of confusion in the “what to eat” debate.

##### How to Think About Carbohydrates

Carbohydrates, or carbs, as we often call them, have become appropriately controversial in the last few decades. I say that because carbs include both healthy and very unhealthy varieties. And no, that’s not determined by just whether a carb is complex versus simple, a term that refers to their molecular structure (more on that later). Some carbs quell hunger. Others can make you eat with abandon. Sometimes it depends what those carbs are combined with. Carbs combined with fat and with sugar, for example, can make people with a sweet tooth feel like an addict who just scored: focused on getting more. It becomes very easy to overeat.

Should you just cut out all carbs? Well, cutting out carbs completely will make you lose weight fast, but mostly you lose water weight as carbs cause you to “hold” water.[^c4-21] For most people, I don’t suggest suddenly cutting out carbs completely, though cutting back on certain types of carbs can be beneficial for many people. I’ve seen folks with autoimmune issues resolve them by moving to a carnivore (meat, salt only) or ketogenic (very low carb) diet. Then, most gradually reintroduce carbs over time, learning which carbs are problematic for them and which are not. I have also seen people who could not lose body fat do so on very low carb diets. Ketogenic diets have also been shown to be an effective treatment for some forms of drug-resistant epilepsy[^c4-22] and in some cases for schizophrenia[^c4-23] and depression.[^c4-24] Also, some people just “feel better,” both mentally and physically, on a zero or near-zero carbohydrate diet. Incidentally, I am not one of those people. I love fruits and vegetables and I eat starches, but I am thoughtful about which and, to some extent, when.

I also know people who have done well on an “animal-based” diet, which recommends people eat only meat, fish, eggs, and dairy. It’s actually a misnomer because the actual animal-based diet made popular by Paul Saladino, MD, includes not just meat, eggs, fish, and dairy, but also fruits such as dates, bananas, cucumbers, and tomatoes (yes, those last two are fruits).[^c4-25] This diet is much easier to adhere to, and arguably much healthier in the long run than a pure-meat carnivore diet. The controversial part is that it is ostensibly “anti-vegetables.” In the last year, I have seen public messaging from Paul that asparagus now gets the green light. (No pun intended.)

The low starch, minimal-to-zero vegetables thing can be a real challenge. The vast majority of us are—and want to continue to be—omnivores, meaning we would like to eat meat but also fruits, vegetables, and, yes, other carbohydrates. So with that in mind, let’s parse this category of macronutrients.

First, there is no such thing as an essential carbohydrate—you can survive by eating only proteins and fats. But all our cells run on glucose and, assuming we eat them, carbs readily get converted to glucose. That glucose is absorbed into our bloodstream—which leads to a rise in blood sugar, which in turn triggers the release of hormones like insulin that help manage this fuel. Typically, the breakdown of carbs into glucose is what our bodies prioritize for energy, then fats, and finally protein. That’s an oversimplification, but all things being equal, that’s the sequence.

To fully understand how carbs work, you need to know a bit more about how carbs are processed alone and in combination with other foods, and how they impact appetite. Carbohydrates can be broadly divided into complex carbohydrates and simple carbohydrates. Complex carbohydrates can be further (and still broadly) divided into starchy complex carbs and fibrous complex carbs. As a general rule, starchy complex carbohydrates, aka starches, are complex carbohydrates that completely or mostly dissolve in your mouth (after they are cooked or manufactured). Examples include rice, potatoes, beans, yams, pasta, lentils, bread, chips and crackers, and so on. When consumed with little or no added fats or sugars, non-processed starchy carbs are what some call clean starches. So if you’re wondering—chips and crackers, while mostly starch, are not clean. Although fairly calorie dense, clean starches like oatmeal, potatoes, rice, beans, and lentils are terrific sources of energy because they are more slowly converted to glucose by the body. Breads made without excess sugar or preservatives such as rye bread, sourdough, and unbleached wheat bread can also be considered clean(ish) starches.

That being said, you can overconsume starchy carbs.[^c4-26] Four things tend to lead you there:

- If you don’t eat enough high CP:C ratio protein along with them.
- If you add sugar to them including jams, honey, syrup, and more.
- If you add fat to them like butter, oil, or cheese.
- If you add both sugars and fats.

Starchy carbs are easy to overconsume, in no small part because they literally melt in your mouth. They are flavorful especially when combined with fat and salt (think bread alone versus bread and butter with salt or bread dipped in olive oil with salt, or french fries, or macaroni and cheese). And when starches are combined with fat and sugar and just enough salt to bring out the sweet taste (think cheesecake, doughnuts, chocolate cake, pie, ice cream, and most breakfast cereals nowadays) most people find them super tasty, and hard to not overeat. Processed starchy carbs, like chips, crackers, store-bought cookies, frozen pizza, burritos, et cetera, are basically starches with fats and/or sugar blended evenly throughout, so every bite tastes identical—identically scrumptious that is. Chips and crackers are especially easy to overconsume because they activate the “eat more of this!” circuit in your brain and body, without any of the usual satiety promoting features of whole foods. They tend to have a very low CP:C ratio, and they are incredibly calorie dense for their size. You can easily eat 800 calories of chips without feeling full… and in many cases doing that will tend to increase your appetite. By comparison, you would have to eat about 16 ounces (a pound!) of cooked steak to get to the same 800 calories. I’m betting by the tenth ounce of steak, you’re going to feel very satiated, and would stay that way for many hours.

I don’t want to demonize starches. I eat them. I love them. Rice and pasta dishes and a great thick-crusted rye, or sourdough bread with olive oil or butter and salt are some of my favorite foods. I also think most people can enjoy a slice of cake or pie, a scoop of ice cream, a hot dog, a slice or two of pizza, and other carb-fat-sugar combinations now and again without any issue. But even if they are homemade, or from a bakery or restaurant that uses quality ingredients, they should not be a staple of anyone’s diet. And the packaged, processed versions are certainly damaging to our health. This is true for a variety of reasons, but their low micronutrient value and their tendency to make people overeat are just two.[^c4-27]

**SO WHICH CARBS SHOULD WE EAT?**

Most people, unless following a ketogenic, carnivore, or animal-based diet, should consume some clean carbs one to three times per day. How much? A simple solution is to scale your starchy carb intake with the amount and type of physical activity you’re doing. Unless you are still growing, are very lean (less than 10 percent body fat for a man and less than 15 percent for a woman), or are doing a lot of cardio (1.5 hours or more per day on average) or hard manual labor (3-plus days a week), it is probably best to limit your starch intake to a third or less of your daily calories. Strive to make that from clean starches, and don’t add more than one to two tablespoons of fat (butter or olive oil, etc.) to any one starch serving. And don’t add sugar.

If you do intense cardio or hard resistance training three or more times a week (meaning you are doing compound multi-joint exercises and take your work sets to failure; see chapter 2 for details), then consider also consuming some clean starches in the meals that follow your training session. Ideally, eat some fruit too. Long, intense cardio and resistance training of the sort described in chapter 2 can deplete your glycogen reserves.[^c4-28] You would be wise to consume 30 to 75 grams of high CP:C ratio protein in that same meal. By the way, unless it’s very intense, a yoga class or bodyweight workout won’t meaningfully deplete your glycogen reserves. Nor will half an hour of Zone 2 running or easy laps in the swimming pool. That is not what I’m talking about. But if you push yourself running, swimming, or cycling or training with heavy (for you) weights for forty-five to seventy-five minutes, or do a truly hard Pilates workout, then you likely need to replenish your glycogen reserves. Eating some clean starches (and fruit and some high CP:C ratio protein) is a great way to do that. In fact, unless you’re in ketosis and familiar with that state, failure to replenish your glycogen, or dropping your starches to zero for one to two days in a row, can lead to sleep challenges, headaches, and brain fog. Resistance training with any real intensity when you haven’t eaten any starches in the preceding days can be extremely difficult. Most need those clean starches, just not in excess. And if you resistance train with intensity—taking sets to failure or close to it (as described in chapter 2)—you’ll want to eat those clean starches to have the glycogen your muscles need to continue your workouts.

On that note, if you follow a ketogenic, animal-based, or carnivore diet, you’ll have to make up for the lack of starch with calories from fat and/or protein, and be mindful of replenishing your glycogen in other ways after hard workouts. Protein can be converted to glucose by your liver through a process called gluconeogenesis. I know very few people who consistently follow a pure ketogenic or pure carnivore diet who also consistently resistance train with intensity, but they exist. Shawn Baker, MD, a popular public educator and proponent of the carnivore diet, is a good example of someone for whom this approach works. I’ve seen a fair number of low/no-carb folks who do pull-ups and push-ups and other body weight exercises as well as cardio. But for most people, if you train with weights in a manner similar to how I described in Exercise Protocol 2, you’re going to want to eat starches, especially in the meal following training.

There’s another type of carbohydrate to discuss: fibrous carbohydrates, which as their name suggests, are high-fiber-containing carbohydrates like broccoli, cucumbers, lettuce, kale, chard, asparagus, and so on. These tend not to dissolve in your mouth, even if they are cooked first. It’s hard to overstate how great complex fibrous carbs are for us. Indeed, most of us should be trying to eat more of them. They are rich with vitamins, minerals, and other micronutrients and, as their name suggests, they contain a lot of fiber. We’re told all the time that we need to eat more fiber, but trying to get fiber mainly from starches is a mistake. That tends to make people gain body fat, and I’m hearing from more and more people about allergy and gut issues due to eating too many grains. Look to get most of your fiber from vegetables. Though be mindful to chew your fibrous carbs well or they can be hard on your digestive tract. And it’s good to note if any specific fibrous carbs do not agree with you (you’ll know!). But as a general rule, ingesting more fiber from vegetables and from low-sugar fruits is associated with better health outcomes and longevity.[^c4-29] Fibrous carbs also slow the absorption of glucose into your bloodstream for a steadier rise in your glucose levels, and they make you feel full.[^c4-30] Our sense of satiety comes from a combination of having eaten enough essential amino acids and fatty acids, and from our glucose levels having risen (but not too high), but also from the mechano-sensation of the stretch sensors in our gut… which is nerd-speak for “feeling full.”

There are even more benefits. As I mentioned, vegetables contain remarkably high levels of micronutrients, like vitamins, minerals, and more, and deliver those with very few calories. Whether they taste “yum,” “yuck,” or “meh” to you tends to be a function of age (know many kids under eight that love chard?), and how these foods are prepared. It should be obvious that adding a lot of oil or butter or sugary sauces can quickly make fibrous vegetables easy to overeat, and very calorie dense—especially if the vegetables are cooked—so add those sparingly.

And we should all avoid fried vegetables, fried starches, and fried meats. Fried foods are terrible for your cardiovascular health and longevity and even have been linked to poorer mental health.[^c4-31] They are high in calories, often high in sodium, and can contain trans fat, which has been linked to heart disease and other bad outcomes. If you’re serious about your health, ditch them. If you indulge occasionally with a doughnut or French fries, no big deal. But if eating fried foods is a daily, or even a weekly habit, it will likely catch up to you.

There’s one last carbohydrate relevant to this conversation. Simple carbohydrates are what are often referred to as sugars—although that can lead to a lot of confusion.

Unfortunately, when most people hear the word *sugar* they immediately think of white table sugar, or sucrose, but simple sugars exist in many forms. Naturally occurring simple sugars in foods that have fiber and fairly high water content, like fruits or vegetables, are absorbed more slowly. The simple sugars found in honey or maple syrup, which have very little fiber, and no fat, are absorbed very quickly. Lactose, the simple sugar found in full-fat milk, is absorbed slowly because of the presence of fat. The point is that sugars vary in type, and how fast they are absorbed depends on the other macronutrients (proteins, fats, and carbs) you eat with them.

Maybe you’ve heard that “sugar is poison.” This is not true of the sugar in fruit and vegetables, or in many full-fat milk products. If your goal is to have stable blood sugar and energy levels, those sources of sugar should account for about 95 percent of your sugar intake. And while you must be careful not to overconsume maple syrup or honey and other natural liquid sweeteners—they are very dense with sugar and calories—they are not poison. So adding a small bit of pure honey or pure maple syrup to your food or drinks every so often is no big deal.

Refined sugars are another story. Refined sugars are simple sugars that have been stripped of their fiber or fat content and are often chemically modified to taste extremely sweet. Some are so sweet that consuming them may change your sweet taste threshold and make otherwise savory or sweet tasting foods taste more bland.[^c4-32] Luckily that effect is reversible if you cut out refined sugars even just for a few days.

Sucrose, which is refined from sugarcane, is the most basic example of a refined sugar. A bit of it here or there, like table sugar in dessert, is generally not a problem for most people. Keeping refined sugars to 5 percent or less of your sugar intake is a good idea. Or, if you loathe tracking that sort of thing, simply limit yourself to one serving—a scoop of ice cream or piece of cake—per week. To some of you that may seem spartan. To others, that may seem indulgent. Later we will discuss sugar cravings, and how to beat them. In the meantime, I can assure you that it is possible to stop craving sugar, and cutting out refined sugars entirely, or close to it, is the first step in that process.

Alas, these days, sucrose or high-fructose corn syrup are put into all sorts of foods that we think of as savory (e.g., soups, cereals, sauces, and salad dressings) in order to make them taste sweeter than they would otherwise. So be a bit more vigilant and read food labels if your goal is to avoid added sugars of any kind.

Sugar is immensely reinforcing—ingesting it makes you want to eat more. So while people debate if sugar is truly “addicting,” most everyone agrees that consuming refined sugars is highly reinforcing, and is not healthy—or at least offers little, if any, nutritional benefit.[^c4-33]

So while I don’t think that sugar is “poison,” nor do I feel it meets the classic definition of addictive, which would mean its use is progressive and destructive to multiple areas of life, I do, however, think eating too many sugars, and especially refined sugars, is bad for us. It can lead to gaining body fat due to the overconsumption of calories with little nutritional value, as well as insulin sensitivity problems that, at the extreme, can cause diabetes and other metabolic issues.[^c4-34] It can even lead to mental health challenges, such as depression.[^c4-35]

And sugar is everywhere. Consider that complex starchy carbohydrates—like wheat, rice, potatoes—if refined to remove their fiber content become more like simple carbohydrates. Foods containing refined flours, such as bread, pasta, cereals, crackers, and most packaged snack foods, are good examples. And they often contain added sugar as well. Even if the packages show some amount of fiber, these foods almost always act more like sugars in the body—they get absorbed fast, and almost always lead to an overconsumption of calories with little nutritional value. While eating something fibrous (like a salad) or fatty (like almond butter) with these refined complex carbs will typically slow their absorption, the outcome is almost always the same: an overconsumption of calories with little nutritional value. I’m not out to demonize the packaged food industry but their goal is simple: to get you to buy and consume more of what they sell. And it’s clear they’ve been successful in reaching that goal given the prevalence of these foods and the declining health of those who consume them. We have plenty of evidence now linking ultra-processed foods with serious health issues, including heart disease, type 2 diabetes, obesity, depression, and impaired sleep.[^c4-36] The more cryptically problematic foods, in my opinion, are refined carbohydrates with added sugars. We don’t think of them as highly processed compared to, say, chips or microwave meals, but they are nearly as bad in terms of our propensity to overeat them. Luckily there is an easier and much more satisfying way to eat. One that is affordable too. But first, we have to understand fats.

##### How to Think About Fats

First off, it’s a real shame this category of macronutrients is called *fats* because that immediately makes people think about body fat, which almost no one wants. But you do want fats in your diet. *Lipids* would have been a better choice in my opinion but alas, here we are.

Fats are lipids, and they are calorically dense: 9 calories per gram compared to 4 calories per gram for carbs or protein. And fats are vitally important. We can’t live without them. In fact, a large part of each of our cells is made of fats, and thus consuming enough fats is crucial for cellular function and repair throughout the body. You need to eat fats, but the right kinds and the right amounts. So get it out of your mind that fats are bad. Remember, there are no essential carbohydrates, but you absolutely must eat protein and fat to survive.

Fats can be broadly divided into saturated fats and unsaturated fats.

The simplest way to recognize a saturated fat is that these are generally solid at room temperature. The saturated fat in cheeses and meats are good examples of this. While some non-animal sources such as coconuts and Brazil nuts contain saturated fat, most saturated fats come from meat, dairy, and eggs. People love to debate if saturated fats raise your cholesterol, and it’s become a circular argument because yes, they do, but then the discussion turns to if cholesterol levels, HDL and LDL (classically referred to as the good and bad cholesterols, respectively), are truly meaningful in predicting heart disease and longevity, or if there are more important metrics. The whole thing can get rather confusing.[^c4-37] Some people who eat low saturated fat diets have high LDL, due to genetics or other factors like age; some people who eat high saturated fat diets don’t have high LDL, but they also tend to eat a lot of fiber, and not much starch and sugar. Pretty soon, talk turns to how insulin from carbs and not just fats impacts LDL… and the debate rages on.

**SO HOW MUCH FAT DO I NEED IN MY DIET?**

If you are eating animal-based proteins daily, and that includes eggs, red meat, or full-fat dairy, chances are good that you are getting enough saturated fat. If you are vegetarian or entirely plant-based, you might consider incorporating eggs and dairy (if vegetarian), along with coconut or coconut oil, macadamia nuts, cashews, or other foods and oils that have saturated fat.

Although debated, the data show that you want only moderate amounts of saturated fats in your diet because high levels of saturated fat consumption can increase systemic inflammation—an effect that is only made worse if you also ingest sugar.[^c4-38] Some might argue that is a consequence of eating saturated fats and carbs, not the fats per se. Yet, even if you’re following a strictly ketogenic diet, excess saturated fat consumption is not good for your immediate or long-term health.[^c4-39] So regardless of whether you are an omnivore, keto, or vegetarian, consuming leaner cuts of meat and emphasizing proteins with high CP:C ratios will help keep your saturated fat intake relatively low. It’s worth noting that I regularly do blood work to keep an eye on my cholesterol levels and other blood biomarkers. I think this is a good practice to truly understand how diet is affecting your blood lipids. Function Health, a company I’m an advisor to, makes this type of testing quite affordable. There are other companies entering the space as well and helping to drive the cost of blood tests down.

**WHAT ABOUT UNSATURATED FATS?**

Unsaturated fats tend to be liquid at room temperature. There are two types: monounsaturated and polyunsaturated fats, both of which come mainly from fish, seeds, olives, and avocados. (More on the benefits of unsaturated fats in Nutrition Protocol 5.)

And for those of you following the ongoing debate about seed oils—canola, grapeseed, corn oils, et cetera—I give my take on them in Nutrition Protocol 5. Some evidence points to the idea that if seed oils are used to replace someone’s saturated fat intake, their health improves.[^c4-40] Though that overlooks the fact that consuming seed oils often tends to correlate with eating more processed foods, and carb-fat combination foods. And some argue excessive heat during seed oil processing makes them potentially hazardous, which is why this topic is contentious. (Nutrition Protocol 5 gives you a fuller picture.)

My recommendation is to save yourself a giant headache and when given the choice between cooking with seed oils or other fats, go with pure olive oil or avocado oil, or perhaps some small amount of butter, tallow, or ghee. If you need to cook at high temperatures, avocado oil is your best bet given that it has a high smoke point. Smoke point is the temperature at which an oil starts to smoke under high heat—which can lead to it degrading as the fats oxidize, and that produces harmful compounds linked to inflammation. When it comes to seed oils, I personally avoid them, opting to cook and make salad dressing from olive oil and using small amounts of butter here and there. No one debates olive oil’s health benefits.[^c4-41] And it’s delicious.

#### The Best Diet for You

We have covered a lot here. But if you’re realizing that the use of words like proteins, carbs, sugars, and fats requires distinguishing the different types of each and how they interact, then you’re on track to devise the best diet for you. The good news: There are several different diet frameworks that allow for that, so you have options. Here they are:

##### Low Carb/Keto

Technically speaking, as discussed, we can get all we need to survive from consuming only proteins and fats, and can skip carbohydrates entirely. Done right, the ketogenic diet tends to raise energy levels and assist weight loss, because you excrete a lot of water that starches normally cause you to retain. Ketogenic diets have also been shown to help resolve symptoms of epilepsy, as mentioned already, as well as major depression, bipolar depression, even schizophrenia, in some people, and there is growing evidence it may help for people with gut and autoimmune issues.[^c4-42] But to do it right means eating mostly fat, some protein, and very, very little carbohydrates, along with all the vitamins and minerals you need—which takes a lot of discipline and attention to detail. Most people just won’t do that for long because they can’t imagine saying goodbye to bread, fruit, pasta, salads, et cetera, forever. Still, it might be the right choice for you. Ask yourself this: Are you willing to give up starches and fruit?

##### Pure Vegan

By pure vegan, I mean no animal products whatsoever. That’s possible. A vegan friend of mine (yes, I have some vegan friends) is a “platinum star” vegan, meaning he’s never knowingly eaten any animal products. The real challenge with this diet is getting enough high CP:C ratio proteins without eating too many calories, and to make sure you don’t overconsume processed foods, just because many of them—such as French fries or coconut ice cream—are vegan (and convenient and delicious). I know people who have been vegans for many years and thrive. One thing all vegans must be careful of is muscle loss, especially as they age. Resistance training can help offset that, but getting those high CP:C ratio proteins is key, of course, too.

##### Animal-Based

This diet has a very misleading name, as, yes, it includes meat, eggs, and fish, but also fruit, honey, dates, tomatoes, avocados, coconut, hard cheeses, and other full-fat dairy. Sounds decadent, no? It is. But it also takes some discipline to follow because it’s an omnivorous diet minus any starches or vegetables. That means no rice, no oatmeal, no bread, no broccoli, no lettuce, and on and on. Yes, it intentionally lacks vegetables. And the only processed food you’ll eat on this diet is hard cheese like Parmesan. This diet is possible for pescatarians who want to eat fatty ocean fish such as salmon and sardines. It’s also fine for people who don’t like red meat but eat poultry. I have heard from many people who have achieved impressive body composition results and improved their health outcomes by following an animal-based diet. That said, because it includes a lot of calorie-dense foods, you still need to watch your total caloric and saturated fat intake. In my view, any dramatic effectiveness of this diet is likely to be multifactorial, including that it limits starch-fat and starch-sugar combinations, and that it makes no room for processed foods or refined sugars of any kind. It tends to quell hunger fairly well and contribute to stable blood sugar. That said, it can tend to lead to very high LDL levels in some individuals, which can be correlated with increased risk of heart disease and stroke, a result of fatty plaque building up in arteries.[^c4-43] If you opt to follow an animal based diet, I suggest getting a calcium CT scan of your heart before starting and again a year later to see if it causes you to add plaque to your arteries. I know people for whom it has made plaque worsen, and those for whom (independent of their LDL levels) it has not caused increased blockages. We still have a lot to learn about the relationship between LDL, markers like ApoB, diet, and cardiovascular diseases. Meanwhile, assess your current cardiovascular risk profile and how your diet—animal-based or otherwise—is impacting it.

##### Clean Omnivore

My diet of choice is what I call the Clean Omnivore Diet because it checks off all, not just a few, of the key pillars of effective, health-promoting, delicious, cost-effective, and practical nutrition, which makes it easy to stick to. If we take a step back from the debates, and ask what we need and want from a great overall diet, the answer that emerges is this:

- **Plenty of protein from high CP:C ratio sources:**
  - Aim for 1 gram per pound of body weight of high CP:C ratio proteins. Some days a bit more, some a bit less. If that feels excessive, and you find yourself dreading eating these foods, scale it back a bit.
- **Plenty of fiber, vitamins, and minerals and micronutrients, from vegetables:**
  - 35 grams of fiber recommended for men each day.
  - 25 grams of fiber for women each day.
- **Healthy fats:**
  - Like olive oil, avocados, and maybe a bit from dairy like Greek or (my favorite) Bulgarian yogurt or nuts. Small amounts of butter are fine. Nuts and nut butters are calorically dense, and most people tend to overeat them, but assuming they contain no added oils or sugars (including cane sugar) they are also fine. (Read the packaging; manufacturers seem to sneak those into everything nowadays!)
- **Fruit:**
  - Two to four pieces or servings per day depending on activity levels and caloric needs. Berries are a great choice, but expensive. Look for citrus, apples, peaches, and on and on. If you want to look up the sugar and fiber content of different fruit, do; opt for the lower sugar, higher fiber varieties if you can.
- **Clean starches:**
  - Think rice, oatmeal, potatoes, yams, sourdough or rye bread, beans, lentils. The goal is to eat enough of these to fuel your brain and bodily activities, including regular moderate to intense exercise four to six days per week.

  That’s what to seek out.

  And not to sound like a broken record, but most people are best off limiting starch-fat combination foods and starch-fat-sugar combination foods. That means very little, if any, highly processed food like candy or cookies, boxed or frozen meals, or sugary drinks. Just cut them out. You’ll feel so much better in every way—not just in appearance, but your cravings for sugar will be greatly reduced.

If you want a decadent homemade or real bakery-made dessert, homemade pasta, or a couple of slices of pizza or ice cream now and again—as in up to once a week—no big deal (especially if you’re exercising as described in chapter 2).

Alas, there is no official name for this diet. While it’s pretty straightforward, it’s certainly not the Standard American Diet. Nor is it paleo or Mediterranean or animal-based. That’s why I called it the Clean Omnivore Diet. It’s clean, it’s healthy, and it’s satiating. It’s also flexible, meaning it works both for your preferences and your goals. For instance, at the end of this section I offer a suggestion that explains how one slight modification of this diet can allow for meaningful fat loss that you can maintain over time.

So aim for 30 to 50 grams of high-quality protein at each meal. That’s about one large chicken breast, a 6- to 8-ounce piece of salmon or other fish, or a 5- to 7-ounce steak. This will fill about a third of a standard dinner plate.

Fill another third of that plate with vegetables.

If you’re having starch with that meal, the starch can fill the remaining third of the plate. This is approximate. Don’t obsess. If you completed an intense resistance training session or a hard cardio training session lasting longer than forty-five minutes that day, feel free to increase the starch portion a bit. Otherwise, keep your starch intake moderate.[^c4-44]

#### How Much to Eat: Calories In, Calories Out

Whatever diet you decide is best for you, you’ll need to pay attention to how many calories you consume. Calorie is the unit we use to measure how much energy is in what we eat and drink. And the number of calories you consume versus the number of calories you burn determines whether you will gain weight, lose weight, or stay at your current weight. “Calories in, calories out” is the phrase to remember. Or, if you prefer acronyms, CICO. This is not a matter for debate; it’s a matter of thermodynamics.

If you want to lose weight, then you must consume (and absorb) fewer calories than you burn. I say “absorb” because not every calorie you consume is absorbed. Complete proteins are 4 calories per gram as they head into your mouth, but the metabolic requirement of processing those proteins ends up making them closer to 3 calories per gram when all is said and done. And while it’s not a dinner-table-appropriate topic, some of the calories in food pass through your digestive tract without being absorbed. For example, humans have engineered fats that improve the taste of a food, but that get eliminated from your digestive tract with no absorption of calories. Other calories fail to be absorbed because they have a rapid rate of passage through your digestive tract, or bind to fiber. But for the most part, calories eaten equals calories absorbed.

Which takes us to the calories-out part of CICO.

As covered in chapter 2, your basal metabolism is the number of calories you burn if you were to just lie in bed all day and night and do literally nothing. Contrary to what many people once believed, your basal, or resting, metabolism doesn’t change a whole lot with age, at least not after age twenty-five or so.[^c4-45] Unless your muscle mass changes. If you lose muscle, your resting metabolic rate decreases. If you gain muscle, your resting metabolic rate will increase. This suggests that one reason people put on weight as they age is they lose muscle mass. Another is that as people get older in age, they tend to walk less and just generally move around less (even while seated!) and thus burn fewer calories each day. This kind of non-exercise movement, or non-exercise activity thermogenesis (NEAT) in nerd-speak, may not seem important, but it is. It can burn greater than 1,000 calories a day in some people… so knee bouncers and fidgeters rejoice.[^c4-46]

While NEAT is (amazingly) a key aspect to your daily caloric expenditure, you of course can’t get away with just fidgeting and walking. As explained in detail in chapter 2, exercise—specifically resistance training and cardiovascular training—is critical to maintaining healthy body composition over time. Also, if you are choosing to be in a calorie deficit to lose weight, and you resistance train, more of the weight you lose will come from body fat and less will come from muscle. If you don’t resistance train, you’ll lose roughly equal amounts of body fat and muscle.

The reverse is also true. If you’re in a calorie excess, you’ll gain weight that is a mix of muscle and body fat, but probably more body fat. That is, unless you resistance train, in which case you’ll gain more weight that is muscle, especially if many of the additional calories are from high CP:C ratio proteins.[^c4-47] And if you resistance train while eating at maintenance levels, you’ll likely add muscle and reduce your overall body fat percentage.[^c4-48]

So viewed purely through the lens of thermodynamics, does it matter what you eat? If you are thinking about total weight on the scale, then technically no, it doesn’t matter. A calorie is a calorie. But as you can see from everything we’ve discussed so far in the chapter, there’s more to it than that.

Physiologically speaking, we eat for four main reasons:

- To provide our cells with the raw materials like amino acids and fatty acids that they need to rebuild themselves
- To provide our cells with glucose to fuel their activities, that is, to give them energy
- To get micronutrients (such as vitamins and minerals) for our cells
- To provide sustenance for the beneficial bacteria that live in our gut

(We also eat for psychological reasons, but those reasons are countless in number: because it’s social, or it reminds us of home, or it reduces our anxiety, or it just tastes good, and on and on.)

That’s why I believe, given most people are (and want to remain) omnivores, that the healthiest possible way to eat is to get enough high CP:C ratio proteins, plenty of fibrous vegetables and some fruit, healthy monounsaturated and polyunsaturated fats, and a bit of saturated fat, too, and enough clean starch to fuel our brains and bodies. And to do all that without eating more calories than we need. It hits each of these four reasons, while helping us stick to the requirements of CICO.

> **A Word About Weight Loss, or the Clean and Lean Omnivore Diet**
>
> One of the best ways to avoid eating too many calories is to avoid processed foods entirely, while also restricting starch-fat and starch-fat-sugar combinations, even if the ingredients are not processed.
>
> There is even a case for dropping starches entirely—at least for a while. I know it seems crazy, but I have a dozen or more close friends who really struggled with their weight for years who switched to a diet consisting of meat, fish, eggs, vegetables, fruit, olive oil, coffee, tea, and water (there’s an argument to be made that diet soda is fine to include too) and only used salt, pepper, and cinnamon for added flavoring.[^c4-49] Without any calorie counting, they have lost anywhere from twenty-five to sixty pounds in four to six months, and kept it off. These friends also made sure to consume some low-sugar fermented foods each day, too, such as sauerkraut or kimchi, which promote microbiome health. All of them exercised but no more than they were doing prior to eating this way. Each reported “cheating” two to three times a year, usually for a holiday meal or birthday. They simply got right back to the plan the next day. And after a year or so of eating this way, the ones exercising regularly and intensely were able to start adding moderate amounts of clean starches, like potatoes, beans, and rice, back into their regimen with no detriment.
>
> Their results were remarkable, but not atypical. Again, since the laws of thermodynamics are immutable, we have to conclude this diet naturally puts active people into a caloric deficit. What is wild is how fast it works, and how easy it is to stick to, and how it stands in bold contrast to their many other failed attempts to lose body fat in a sustainable way. You might say “No bread?! No ice cream?! No pasta?!” All I know is that the people who elected to eat this way report feeling very sated, which I attribute to the fact that they were getting everything their body needed physiologically and psychologically, without counting calories. And their improved body composition and other indicators of health, including sleep, just further reinforced their decision. I guess if we had to name this diet we would call it the Clean Omnivore No Starch Diet but that’s a mouthful so I’ve defaulted to calling it the Clean and Lean Omnivore Diet instead.

##### Calculating Your CICO

After you’ve decided on what to eat, you’ll want to dial in to how much. That’s where calculating your CICO comes in.

I actually think it’s a good idea for people to calculate their CICO for a few days or so, at least one to two times a year, and update their food intake accordingly, the same way that I think it’s a good idea to get your blood pressure checked one to two times a year, and update your stress control tools accordingly.

Luckily there is an easy, no-cost way to determine your caloric needs. It’s called the Katch-McArdle formula. I discussed it in chapter 2, so please refer to page 174 to refresh your memory on how your daily caloric needs are calculated.

If you want additional support for body fat loss, muscle gain, et cetera, as I mentioned I highly recommend the Carbon App, created by Layne Norton, one of the world’s foremost experts on nutrition, especially for health and body composition. (Note: Carbon is a sponsor of my podcast.) It allows you to determine what you need to eat and how much of each macronutrient and it makes it easy to enter your calorie and specific food intake. It also learns your nutrition patterns over time, and makes valuable suggestions. So it’s not just a calorie and macronutrient counter; it’s a nutrition coach. I have used it for years now and everyone I have recommended it to thanks me for the ease and results it’s brought them around nutrition and body composition.

#### Straight Talk About Highly Processed Foods

It is true that eating 3,000 calories of highly or “ultra” processed food will not cause any more or less weight gain than eating 3,000 calories of non-processed food, but the damage the former does is real. Let’s acknowledge the one thing everyone in the nutrition field seems to agree on—the vegans, the carnivores, the keto enthusiasts, the vegetarians, and the omnivores: Highly processed foods are genuinely bad for us.

When we talk about highly processed foods, we’re referring to multi-ingredient, packaged products that are either ready-to-eat or only need to be heated up to eat. We’re not referring to single ingredient starches that just need to be baked or cooked in boiling water, like rice or potatoes or beans. That’s not “processing”; it’s “preparation”: And those are healthy, non-processed foods. Highly processed foods are problematic for many reasons related to our short-and long-term health. These products—even the ones labeled “Heart Healthy”—are often high in sugar, as well as various preservatives and artificial dyes that, while perhaps not deadly on their own, seem to pose a risk to health.[^c4-50]

And recent studies suggest that eating a lot of processed foods can increase your risk of psychiatric illnesses, likely due to changes in brain metabolism.[^c4-51] In fact, that is one reason why, as mentioned above, ketogenic diets (which are very low in carbohydrates) are increasingly being prescribed as a tool to improve mental health. Whether that is due to the absence of carbohydrates, the reduced intake of processed foods, or a direct effect of improved insulin sensitivity remains unclear, but the results are nonetheless compelling. We also have reliable evidence that diets low in fiber and high in processed foods, or even simply just high in refined carbohydrates, such as white rice and white wheat flour, increase the risk of cancer[^c4-52] and cardiovascular disease.[^c4-53] As do deli meats, which are effectively highly processed meats.[^c4-54]

It’s hard to tack the health-degrading effects of processed foods to one aspect of their makeup. A study published in 2017 reported that nearly half of all deaths due to cardiac or metabolic issues are rooted in poor diet.[^c4-55] The Center for Science in the Public Interest, a nonprofit organization, estimates that 678,000 US deaths each year are due to diseases stemming from an inadequate or otherwise poor diet.[^c4-56] Half! Personally, I view highly processed foods as destructive to health mostly because of the other actually healthy foods you could be eating in their place. You still have to obey CICO according to your goals, and make sure you get the right macro- and micronutrients, but avoiding processed foods will likely add years to your life.

#### When to Eat

Then there is the question of when we eat. Here again, people debate. In the 1990s it became popular to eat four to six small meals per day, following a 1989 study published in the *New England Journal of Medicine* on the subject of “nibbling versus gorging.”[^c4-57] The idea was that grazing throughout the day would prevent overeating in any one sitting and stimulate metabolism. It fell out of favor because it’s impractical. It also turned out to have a trivial impact on metabolism.[^c4-58]

Most people default to eating three to four times a day, with one to two of those instances as snacks and the others as meals. Job, school, and social constraints usually dictate when, exactly, people eat.

The practice of time-restricted eating, also called intermittent fasting, as discussed earlier in this chapter, became popular a few years back, and many people follow this practice either deliberately or by default because they are not hungry in the morning. They end up restricting their eating to a window of four to ten hours each day, and most typically seven to eight hours.[^c4-59] Some people limit themselves to one meal a day, which means their window is only one to two hours a day. There is now a fair bit of science—including clinical trials—on time-restricted eating. Intermittent fasting was made popular first as a way to lose weight and improve insulin sensitivity, meaning the extent to which our cells use glucose for energy (the more efficiently this happens, the less insulin we need to produce in order to regulate blood sugar levels). Soon it was studied and touted as a tool to live longer, to avoid cancer, and on and on.[^c4-60]

When it comes to losing weight, the data show that intermittent fasting does indeed help when compared to “unrestricted eating.” However, it likely helps because people end up eating fewer calories when they limit their eating to a specific time window. So ultimately, it all comes back to CICO. When you put intermittent fasting head-to-head with a diet where people can eat whenever they want, but the two diets are matched for total calories consumed, the results end up being the same. A yearlong randomized study found that people with obesity who followed a calorie-restricted diet and ate only within an eight-hour window did not lose more weight or body fat compared to those who followed calorie restriction without the accompanying time-restriction plan.[^c4-61] That being said, many people find it easier to control the hours in which they eat than to control the portion of what they eat, and thus find intermittent fasting a very effective tool for eating fewer calories than they would otherwise.

Many people opt for intermittent fasting because they incorrectly think that means you don’t have to think about the types or amount of food you eat, but if you care about your health you still do. Fasting doesn’t change our need for micronutrients.

Debate continues about what it can do. Intermittent fasting has generated interest for its potential to extend life.[^c4-62] However, the only strong link between fasting and extended lifespan appears to be restricting calories, not meal timing.[^c4-63] That said, Satchin Panda’s lab at the Salk Institute has shown that mice who eat across a twenty-four-hour window of time compared to an eight-to-twelve-hour window, even when calories are held constant, suffer negative health outcomes such as obesity, elevated glucose levels, insulin resistance, and fatty liver.[^c4-64] Studies from Satchin’s lab have also shown similar adverse effects for humans.[^c4-65] Further studies show that not eating within two to three hours of bedtime does seem to improve sleep quality,[^c4-66] growth hormone release[^c4-67] in sleep, and next-morning glucose regulation,[^c4-68] all of which may indirectly impact lifespan. While restricting eating within two to three hours of bedtime does seem to be a best practice, there are some exceptions based on the type of meal. For instance, if you’re hungry and need a snack, consuming 30 grams of casein, the protein found in dairy, can help reduce blood pressure and perhaps even aid in exercise recovery, especially for those doing resistance training.[^c4-69]

Some research suggests that time-restricted eating extends life because it increases autophagy, a process that removes damaged or used cells and cellular material from our bodies.[^c4-70] We also know that extended fasting, such as consuming only water and electrolytes for one to three days, is linked to increased autophagy.[^c4-71] But again here, it’s not the timing that increases autophagy; it’s the overall daily calorie deficit.[^c4-72] And whether autophagy truly extends human lifespan is still unclear.[^c4-73] Most evidence we have linking caloric restriction or intermittent fasting to lifespan is still largely from animal studies.[^c4-74] Prolonged fasting in humans will no doubt improve certain health metrics, like insulin sensitivity, but it risks reducing lean mass. Exercise—both resistance and cardio training—stimulate autophagy but improve lean mass with the added benefit of improving fitness.[^c4-75]

I reflexively do something similar to intermittent fasting. My first meal is typically around 11:00 a.m. or noon. I wake up at about 6:00 a.m. most days and I find it easy to wait to eat my first meal because I tend not to get hungry until 10:30 or so. Around 3:30 p.m. I usually get hungry again and I’ll have a snack. I prefer to eat my last meal of the day around 7:00 p.m., but I stay somewhat flexible on that depending on my schedule.

Since I’m typically done eating around 8:00 p.m., my eating window is usually eight to nine hours, maybe a bit longer. I’ve found that this slightly restricted window allows me to feel at my best while also helping me to manage my daily caloric intake.

From a health standpoint, it’s best to eat at fairly consistent times each day,[^c4-76] but you don’t have to be neurotic about it. If someone sets a dinner time for an hour earlier or later than usual, or a bit outside your eating window, it’s not a huge deal.

#### What’s Ahead

The following protocols are not yet another trend to follow. When I said I hoped you’d find the best diet for you, what I meant is one that you can stick to.

These protocols are not complicated, they are not expensive, and they do not involve searching out obscure ingredients or creating an elaborate schedule of meal prep. They follow directly from the ideas discussed in this introduction to the chapter. Each explores a key point here, then offers one simple tool. My hope is that they will provide you with the inspiration and rationale to make easy yet meaningful shifts in your nutrition, and therefore immediate and long-term health. Adopting any of these into your daily routine can improve your digestion, your energy levels, and your ability to focus and concentrate. For those of you seeking dramatic positive transformations in body composition, I offer a sustainable way to do that too. Of course, exercise—per the recommendations in chapter 2—is critical for getting sustainable and healthy body composition changes, and exercise has its own benefits altogether. Some of the suggestions that follow will be familiar. Others may sound a bit heretical. But I assure you they work.

### Nutrition Protocol 1: 90 Percent or More of the Food You Eat Should Be Unprocessed or Minimally Processed

#### What to Do

- **Eat and cook with single-ingredient, non-processed foods.** These include meat, fish, eggs, poultry, fruit, vegetables, rice, lentils, beans, oatmeal, pasta, olive oil, avocado oil, and even butter (albeit in small portions). They can be consumed alone or combined in recipes, and of course you can use spices, seasonings, and salt as well.
- **Avoid ready-to-eat packed foods or packaged multi-ingredient foods.** Most pre-packaged sauces and condiments should be avoided; these typically contain a fair amount of added sugar. Read nutrition labels to check.
- **Consume nut butters in moderation.** These can be healthy, but some contain processed oils and even added sugar. Even when nuts and salt are the only ingredients, all have a very high calorie-to-protein ratio. If you’re trying to lose body fat, then it’s best to abstain from nut butters entirely.
- **Consume full-fat yogurt and cottage cheese and other forms of dairy, but in plain flavors only.** Here too added sugars should be avoided. Add fruit, a drizzle of honey, or a pinch of cinnamon for taste if you don’t like these foods plain.

#### How It Works

Food is amazing. Despite the debates, I think we can all agree on that. We eat for the building blocks food supplies our brain and body, as described in the introduction to this chapter, and of course for the pleasure of it. For many people, food is one of their biggest joys. I count myself among people who love to eat.

But the type of food we eat is probably second only to sleep and exercise for its importance to our long-term health. Centering our meal and snack choices on whole (that is minimally or non-processed) foods has so many benefits—disease prevention, longevity, cognition, mood, energy, reduced inflammation, healthy weight management, and more. The increasing concerns about processed foods stem from the plethora of data linking them to obesity, high blood pressure, heart disease, gastrointestinal disorders, cancer, and other serious ailments.[^c4-77] Chemical additives used to color, preserve, texturize, and flavor these products have been linked to potential health hazards.[^c4-78] Processed foods also tend to contain high amounts of sugar, even in products that would seem to not require it. And excessive sugar consumption is tied to diabetes, heart disease, cancer, and an increased risk of early death.[^c4-79] All of which is to say, we need to make it a point to eliminate, or at least vastly reduce, processed foods.

The good news is that eating healthily is not complicated or expensive. We can all make incredible tasting meals and snacks using whole foods, if we learn just a bit about how to prepare them. Think: a perfectly cooked steak and carrots roasted with olive oil, salt, and some spices. In some cases, these foods need no preparation at all. Like a juicy orange or fresh berries. If these sound bland or overly simple, chances are your taste circuits in your brain and body need some recalibration.

If you have grown accustomed to eating processed foods, this recalibration can seem difficult. Processed foods alter our brain and gut to make us perceive other, more nutritious foods as less appetizing. It’s because of how sugar, certain starch-sugar, and starch-sugar-fat combinations are metabolized in our gut, and how they change our brain’s reward pathways. You’ll be happy to know, however, that the cells in your gut and brain are perfectly happy to rewire to make healthy, unprocessed foods literally taste better. It doesn’t take long, and it will make eating healthy most of the time reflexive.

This protocol looks at the gut-brain axis, the connection between the cells in our digestive tract and specific areas of our brain. That connection is the key to understanding how processed foods affect us.

Our gut talks to our brain via two main parallel pathways. The first involves the cells in our gut communicating with our brain using a neural pathway called the vagus nerve, a bidirectional superhighway linking the organs of our body and our brain. You may remember the vagus from chapter 3.

Our body and our brain are connected by a second pathway, through secreted hormones and small proteins called peptides (in general, the vagus pathway is the faster of the two). The hunger sensation arises, in part, because our stomach produces a hormone called ghrelin[^c4-80] in amounts proportional to how much time has elapsed since our last meal. Ghrelin travels to our hypothalamus, a marble-sized brain region located over the roof of our mouth, where it activates our drive to seek food.[^c4-81] Other hormones and peptides made by both our gut and our brain make us want to eat less; for example, the peptide GLP-1 gives us a feeling of fullness, which is why GLP-1 analogs are used as drugs to treat obesity. (The gut microbiome, the trillions of bacteria living in our digestive system, also influences hunger—more on that in Nutrition Protocol 6.)[^c4-82]

At the same time, specific nutrients in the foods we eat—most notably sugars, but also fatty acids and amino acids—activate cells in our gut called neuropod cells that communicate with the brain via the vagus nerve, leading to the release of dopamine.[^c4-83] And while dopamine does many different things in the brain and body, when it is stimulated in this context, it can drive the urge to consume more of that food. It’s an elegant mechanism if you think about it, because the taste of food in our mouth is not a great indication of the actual nutrients in a given food. Taste is more of a guess, a correlate. The cells in our gut, on the other hand, are poised to respond to the broken-down components of food, letting the rest of our body and brain know what we ate and what to eat more (or less) of. Amazingly, all this happens below our conscious awareness.

Given how sugar drives the urge to consume more, it’s no mystery why it’s in so many foods. Processed food manufacturers add sugar to foods so we buy and consume more of these foods. That’s why sugar can be found in everything from packaged mac-and-cheese to frozen pizza, and most everything else on the supermarket shelves. Even tortilla and potato chips can have added sugar. So does most store-bought pasta sauce. And salad dressings. And condiments. Which is why so many people crave sugary food all the time.

You get the idea. It’s a clever, albeit diabolical, tactic.

As mentioned in the introduction to this chapter, sugar that gets added to food is considered a simple carbohydrate. Typically it is added as sucrose, but sometimes as high-fructose corn syrup, or something similar. The exact form doesn’t really matter however. Our brains are hardwired to detect simple carbohydrates. Studies in both mice and humans show that even when we are unable to taste sweetness, we still show a strong preference for sugary foods and beverages, indicating that the brain can detect sugar by a pathway other than conscious taste.[^c4-84]

Here’s a simple and fun experiment you can try; it’s something that Anna Lembke, MD, a world expert in dopamine and its role in craving and addiction, taught me. Eat one small piece of chocolate or one spoonful of your favorite ice cream. Both have sugar and fat, a combination known to trigger a lot of dopamine compared to eating either one alone. Pay attention to how it tastes, but then also notice your thoughts as you swallow. You’ll notice how quickly they move from “mmm, yum” to “I want more.” The immediate sense of craving that overlaps with pleasure is the power of dopamine in action. Sugar, in particular, amplifies that response, even after the flavor experience has passed, by activating the gut-to-brain pathway.[^c4-85] It even works for sugary foods that don’t taste that good! And it’s why processed foods that we don’t even think of as sweet often contain added sugar.

Again, I want to be clear that I do not subscribe to the view that all sugar is inherently bad. A homemade dessert, chocolate, or ice cream once in a while… all can definitely fit within a healthy diet. But I do think we should limit these foods and avoid, as much as possible, consuming non-dessert foods that have added sugar, as well as any highly processed foods, except on rare occasions or out of true necessity.

Maybe you’re wondering about fruit, which as I mentioned contains a sugar called fructose. Fruit contains a lot of water, fiber, valuable nutrients, and polyphenols, compounds found in plants that have various beneficial properties. All these components contribute to the prevention of heart disease, cancer, and other serious health issues.[^c4-86] And the high fiber content of most fruits slows down the absorption of sugar, which makes them less stimulating than desserts, sweets, or highly processed foods. But there are a few fruits that contain more fructose than others—like grapes. Note, too, that dried fruits, without their water content, now contain concentrated amounts of sugar. Fruit juices, like orange juice, are generally best avoided. They are high in sugar and calories, too, and the absence of fiber means that the sugar contained there is easily absorbed into the body, which means it spikes blood sugar quickly. Because that spike leads to a subsequent crash in blood sugar,[^c4-87] consuming it often can lead, in the short run, to fatigue, sugar cravings,[^c4-88] and, in the long term, an increased risk of diabetes[^c4-89] and heart disease.[^c4-90]

Then there are artificial and low-calorie sweeteners. The data show that artificial and low-calorie sweeteners do not drive the same craving typical simple sugars do. Stevia for instance, is safe, and may even have some health benefits.[^c4-91] Aspartame appears to be safe too.[^c4-92] Saccharin and sucralose, though, may negatively impact the gut microbiome.[^c4-93] And there’s interesting data on diet sodas. In a randomized controlled trial from 2024, people who consumed diet sodas lost more weight than people who drank equivalent amounts of water.[^c4-94] The underlying reasons include less hunger among soda drinkers and more cravings for sweetness among the water drinkers. At the same time, people who consume a lot of artificial sweeteners often experience increased overall appetite, perhaps due to glucose and insulin disruption.[^c4-95] There isn’t a broad rule that applies to all artificial and low-calorie sweeteners. For some people, they seem to help with weight loss, whereas for other people, they stimulate hunger in ways that may make it harder to keep from overeating. You have to figure out which group you are in.

If a few diet sodas a day help quell your sugar cravings at a time when you’re trying to lose weight, then great. If you don’t like diet sodas, there is no reason to consume them. I drink beverages containing stevia and occasionally enjoy an aspartame-sweetened diet soda. When developing the zero-sugar cold brew yerba maté for Mateina (as noted, a company I partially own), I chose to include a small amount of stevia. I drink that for much of the early part of the day. I avoid sucralose and saccharin.

#### Common Questions

*Do you have any suggestions for beating sugar cravings?*

Yes. Some are conventional; one is not (more on that in the last protocol of this chapter). As with many cravings, sugar can be hard to quit. If you think you’re overdoing it with sugar, then try committing to having no sugar for a certain period. I suggest one week. I promise that soon you will stop craving it so much, though it takes a few days to “get over the bump” (the heightened cravings) as they say.

Focus on consuming high CP:C ratio proteins, at least three times per day. And dietary fiber, mostly from vegetables and lower sugar fruits like apples and berries. If you crave chocolate, try and slowly develop a taste for raw cacao beans (five or six per day), which are rich in polyphenols, which again have various beneficial properties. Similarly, you can try 100 percent chocolate (not baking chocolate!). You read right. That’s no sugar, and no stevia either. It’s an acquired taste, but once people develop a taste for it, they generally like it. If you really struggle with sugar cravings, cut sugar out entirely but consider drinking a half tablespoon (about 3–5 g) of l-glutamine powder dissolved in water two to three times a day; this powder may reduce cravings by regulating blood sugar levels and thereby quelling the need for sugar.[^c4-96] This is a somewhat unconventional tool—one for which we need more studies—but anecdotally speaking (about my own experience), it works.

### Nutrition Protocol 2: Stay Hydrated

#### What to Do

Regardless of what and when you choose to eat:

- **Consume 18 to 24 ounces of water upon waking.** Try to do this first thing in the morning before drinking or eating anything else, including coffee or other forms of caffeine.
- **Aim to consume about 80 ounces of water across the first ten hours of the day.** That’s about 2.4 liters. It is not necessary to consume 8 ounces each hour, but try to spread it out in a way that works for you. The earlier in the day you drink it the better. It’s typically best to avoid a lot of water in the hours before bedtime, since you want to wake as infrequently as possible to use the bathroom.
- **For optimal performance during exercise, consume water according to this equation: Your body weight in pounds divided by 30 equals the number of ounces to drink for every 15 to 20 minutes of your workout time.** This calculation originates with the work of human performance expert Andy Galpin, director of the Human Performance Center at Parker University, and is referred to below as the “Galpin Equation.”

> Example: Total body weight of 150 pounds ÷ 30 = 5 ounces every 15 to 20 minutes, which means 15 to 20 ounces consumed during an hour-long workout. You can sip water throughout, drink at regular or non-regular intervals. Your pattern of consumption during exercise will of course be dictated by the type of exercise you’re doing: running, cycling, swimming, et cetera.

#### How It Works

Your body is made mostly of water. By one estimate, obtained by sending a weak electric current through the body, an adult human is about 62 percent water, with that percentage starting to decrease around sixty years of age.[^c4-97] Water is essential for every biological process that we need in order to live and function.[^c4-98] If there is one protocol that is most overlooked and that can immediately and significantly improve your energy levels, focus, and general feeling of well-being, it is this: Hydrate properly. It is rarely discussed. When we do hear about hydration, the message is typically a warning against dehydration, not the great benefits of hydration.

So let’s talk about what hydration is, and why it’s so powerful.

Hydration is the process of providing the cells of our body with the water they need for all those biological processes. Some hydration is achieved by breathing, some is produced through metabolism, and some comes through the foods we eat. Most hydration comes from the liquids we consume. The water we take in through eating and drinking enters our gut and is absorbed into our bloodstream and finally our cells.

Proper hydration is crucial to both the body and the brain. Hydration helps prevent injuries, improves recovery, and is also important for maintaining body temperature during and following exercise.[^c4-99] It reduces the risk of kidney stones.[^c4-100] Drinking water stimulates the sympathetic branch of your autonomic nervous system, the circuitry that increases your alertness and focus. (See chapter 3 for more on this.) Research indicates that drinking water can trigger the release of norepinephrine, the hormone that helps keep us focused and alert.[^c4-101] In a study of fifteen children, proper hydration was tied to improved performance on tasks involving motor skills and memory.[^c4-102] Similar findings have been observed in adults.

Dehydration, on the other hand, quickly becomes problematic. It’s also common.
