This is unfortunate because even slightly insufficient amounts of water in your body can diminish your concentration, alertness, short-term memory, visual perception, and other cognitive functions.[^c4-103] Mild dehydration can cause low-level confusion, fatigue, depression, and irritability.[^c4-104] One review found that a 2-percent decrease in body mass due to dehydration was enough to diminish mood, increase fatigue, and reduce alertness. That is remarkable because most people do not consume enough water to maintain hydration, and spend much of their day suffering the ill effects of mild dehydration… without even realizing it.

A mildly dehydrated state can reduce brain volume and alter the activity of neural pathways associated with motor output and cognition.[^c4-105] It also reduces blood flow, which in turn diminishes the supply of oxygen to the brain. What’s more, it can cause headaches and lethargy, and of course a dry mouth and thirst.[^c4-106] It’s important to note amidst all this that we can be dehydrated without registering thirst.

People engaging in intense exercise need to be especially vigilant about hydration, and not just in hot and/or dry environments either. In one study, eight trained cyclists rode for two hours on a stationary bike, consuming either 2.4 liters of an energy drink or 0.4 liters of water plus sports gel to equal the carbohydrates in the energy drink. The low-hydration riders became exhausted sooner and exerted less energy as they rode.[^c4-107] In a study of seven experienced resistance trainers (all male), insufficient hydration decreased performance during exercise.[^c4-108] These studies are small but are representative of what happens when we exercise.

The quantities provided in this protocol do not need to be followed to the precise ounce or milliliter. They are general guidelines to help ensure sufficient hydration.

One reason to focus on getting about 80 ounces of fluid in the first ten hours of the day is that this time is when our kidneys function at their best. Our kidneys filter fluid and produce hormones to regulate water and salt balance, among other things, and their efficiency at doing so is strongly governed by our circadian clock[^c4-109] (see Sleep Protocol 1 for more on the circadian clock). Our kidneys are simply much better at filtering water and other fluids we drink in the morning and daytime than at night; their function tends to peak in midafternoon and is slowest around midnight.[^c4-110] Focusing most of your water intake to the time of day when fluid filtration by the kidneys is at its most efficient will also help prevent, or at least reduce, having to get up in the middle of the night to use the bathroom, which is among the more common causes of sleep disturbance.

The quantity of 80 ounces across the first ten hours of the day gives us a solid metric to aim for. Simply make sure to drink 8 to 16 ounces of water (one to two glasses) upon waking, and again approximately every waking hour during the day. That will get you in the ballpark of 80 ounces in the first ten hours. Individuals living in hot environments tend to need more water. So do people who move around a lot, even if that’s in a temperature-controlled office or home.

But if you’re exercising, that’s where the Galpin Equation enters the picture. If you want to improve your exercise performance, hydrate according to this calculation. You’ll be amazed by the difference it makes. Again, anyone living in hot environments will tend to need a bit more water here too; so increase the amount from the equation by a few extra ounces every fifteen to twenty minutes.

Beyond these three points, just remember: Stay hydrated. Hydration sounds boring but it’s actually really powerful when it comes to improving health and performance and again, it’s one of the more overlooked tools out there. It’s important for your brain, for your skin and appearance, for your digestion, and for your mood. You will notice the difference in all these areas after starting to follow this protocol.

#### Common Questions

*How do I know if I’m dehydrated?*

There are so many myths around this. Among the more popular ones is that clear urine indicates sufficient hydration. Wrong. Many factors impact urine color besides hydration status. Your urine can be yellow and you can still be plenty hydrated. Another: If you pinch the skin on your hand, it should retract in less than two seconds. Wrong again. This response depends on age, skin thickness, and other factors. It’s true that if you pinch the skin on the top of your hand and it does not return to its original state within three to five seconds, then there’s a decent chance you’re dehydrated. Same goes if your urine is *much* darker than usual. But that’s not the best way to guide your hydration, nor is whether your ankles are swollen… all of these are myths.

The best way to be certain that you are hydrated is… to not wait for some less-than-reliable marker to tell you so. Simply drink enough water.

*Do I follow both protocols at once when exercising? In other words, do I drink the recommended amount during general waking hours plus the amount recommended for hydration during exercise?*

Yes. Drink the amount recommended for ten hours of waking, and add more using the Galpin Equation. If you don’t want to bother with the calculation, then just aim to ingest 80 ounces of water across the first ten hours of the day and add an extra 15 to 20 ounces of water for every hour spent exercising—and drink it while exercising.

*Should I drink more if I’m someone who sweats a lot?*

People who tend to sweat a lot can increase the Galpin Equation by 50 to 100 percent during exercise. The same holds true if you are doing some kind of heat exposure that promotes sweating. For example, it would be appropriate to drink 8 to 16 ounces of fluid for every twenty to thirty minutes you spend in a hot sauna.

Electrolytes (particularly sodium, magnesium, and potassium) are also beneficial, especially if you are sweating. If you’re working or you’re exercising in a warm environment, or you’re spending time in a hot sauna, add a pinch of sea salt to water (and add a little lemon juice to offset the salty taste). Or use a commercial source of electrolytes to help replace those lost through sweat. I’m a fan of LMNT, a sponsor of my podcast, which has more sodium than most electrolyte formulas. (It also has zero sugar, which is good since many hydration formulas have added sugar.) Many people worry about salt intake but if you eat clean—meaning limited or no processed foods—there is a good chance you need more, not less sodium.

*Even if I slow down my water intake after the first ten hours of the day, I’m still concerned about frequent nighttime waking. Is there a way to reduce this?*

It’s normal to wake up once during the night to urinate. To avoid waking more than once, try this:

1. Hydrate sufficiently during the day to ensure you are not excessively thirsty in the evening.
2. Reduce fluid intake in the evening (obviously).
3. If you do drink fluids (of any kind) later in the day or in the evening, sip them slowly. The rate at which fluid moves from the gut to the bladder is determined partly by the rate at which we drink. Gulping water quickly leads to sooner urination; sipping slowly leads to more time between urination.[^c4-111]

   That said, if you are still waking up often, that could reflect a bladder or prostate issue. Talk to your doctor.

*I drink coffee, tea, diet soda, et cetera. Does that count toward my daily hydration needs?*

Technically, yes, but drinking good ol’ plain water is still important. Beverages containing caffeine act as diuretics; they stimulate urine production and therefore do not contribute to hydration to the same extent as non-caffeinated drinks. The amount of caffeine most people consume is usually not enough to cause significant dehydration, but anyone who drinks more than two cups of strong coffee per day—meaning more than 200 to 400 milligrams of caffeine—should make sure to drink at least those 80 ounces of water in addition, and perhaps as much as 100 ounces.

Keep in mind that many commercial coffee vendors brew their coffee strong, as in 300 milligrams or more of caffeine per serving. If you tend to feel shaky or lightheaded after drinking that coffee, you may be low on electrolytes, as caffeine causes excretion of sodium, a key electrolyte. I’ve known a lot of people who were able to eliminate caffeine-induced lightheadedness and shakes, and even the caffeine crash, by drinking a glass of water with a small pinch of salt dissolved in it, or by drinking water with a serving of electrolytes (sodium, magnesium, and potassium) alongside their coffee or other caffeine-containing drink. In fact, people who drink a lot of caffeinated beverages report that they feel much more energetic, and avoid the caffeine crash, when they are careful to also ingest some electrolytes before, alongside, or after their caffeine.

### Nutrition Protocol 3: Eat High CP:C Ratio Protein at Each Full Meal

#### What to Do

- **Aim to include 30 to 50 grams of high complete-protein-to-calorie ratio foods at each meal or snack.** Your daily goal should be around 1 gram per pound of body weight. This is the cornerstone of your diet.
- **The number of calories from those foods will depend on what you select.** Poultry, lean red meat, fish, and shellfish are the best high CP:C ratio sources of protein for those who eat animal-based products. Eggs are great as well, but they do have a relatively high calorie-to-protein ratio. Whey protein and plain full-fat Greek yogurt and cottage cheese too. Plant-based complete protein sources include beans and rice (together), lentils, soy, seitan, and some grains, such as quinoa. Just be aware that these have a less-than-favorable protein-to-calorie ratio.
- **Nuts, nut butters, and most cheeses are not high-quality protein sources.** And all of them are very calorie dense. Peanut, almond, and other nut butters are mostly fat, and most nut butters on the grocery shelf often also contain added sugar and/or seed oils. If you’re going to eat nut butters, limit them to a few tablespoons a week and be sure they contain only nuts and salt. No sugar or added oils. It would be better to avoid nut butters and eat whole seeds and actual whole nuts. But these are mostly fats; they are not high CP:C ratio proteins.
- **If you are someone who tends to overeat, whichever foods you choose, eat your high CP:C ratio proteins first.** Then any starches, then your fibrous vegetables. You’ll enjoy more satiety, better appetite regulation, and better digestion because apparently the French have it right about “salad last.”

#### How It Works

I know it’s not much fun to see a delicious steak and think “amino acids,” but that’s what your body does. If you took apart any protein, you would find an array of amino acids.

As I explained in the introduction to this chapter, all living things need amino acids to make protein. The human body needs twenty different amino acids. Nine of these are impossible for our body to make on its own. We get them through the proteins we eat. The proteins that have all nine are considered complete proteins, and we want to consume these proteins, because the body uses them to maintain a healthy immune system, produce certain hormones, and maintain and increase muscle mass, among other functions.[^c4-112] You might be amazed to learn that most of your organs, not just your muscles, are made of proteins that are remade every few weeks to months. And it’s these nine essential amino acids that allow for this to occur. Your spleen, your heart, your liver, your muscles—the protein we consume allows them to keep working as they should.

Your body is smart. While you might think you eat for pleasure, it’s actually how your body keeps you seeking the food it needs to maintain these processes—that is, seeking those nine essential amino acids.

Whole grains, vegetables, seeds, and legumes do not contain all nine amino acids, but it is entirely possible to obtain all nine by consuming a variety of these plant-based proteins. Whether you eat meat or not, you are foraging for amino acids as you choose your proteins each day. That’s why we feel so satisfied after we eat complete protein; it’s because the feeling of satiety is strongly linked to obtaining enough essential amino acids.[^c4-113]

And there is one particular amino acid we prioritize in that foraging, even if we are not consciously aware of it. An expanding body of evidence indicates that leucine, one of those nine essential amino acids, is especially impactful.[^c4-114] Rising leucine levels in a cell launch a signaling pathway associated with the protein mTOR (I mentioned it in the introduction to this chapter), which in turn triggers the body to make muscle.[^c4-115] This amino acid also has several other known effects. Research has found links to improved immune function, for example,[^c4-116] as well as increased muscle mass among older individuals.[^c4-117]

As discussed earlier, mTOR has been linked with aging and cancer. One mutant strain of mice lived three times longer than usual after treatment with the drug that lowers mTOR, called rapamycin.[^c4-118] But again, those results don’t appear to translate to humans, and in fact they have translated to far less dramatic results in normal mice. There is currently no evidence that stimulating mTOR has a life-shortening effect on humans. Rather, eating complete protein foods, and especially those rich in leucine such as lean meat, fish, and eggs, should be the cornerstone of your diet.

And not to belabor the point, but once again, we are less likely to overeat when we consume sufficient protein because it leaves us feeling full and satisfied.[^c4-119]

#### Common Questions

*Eating 1 gram of protein per pound of body weight leads me to gain weight and/or I don’t feel good. What should I do?*

Most people who strive to eat 1 gram of protein per pound of body weight do feel better than they did before adopting that habit. From time to time, though, someone will tell me they just don’t feel “right” eating so much protein, and that they feel that they must force themselves to do so, even if their overall caloric intake is in proper range for them. We don’t have the exact knowledge to know why that might be. I notice my protein hunger follows the intensity and amount of exercise I do, and while that makes sense based on how protein synthesis works, we don’t have any formal studies on training and protein hunger, so take my experience as what it is: anecdotal.

For those of you who struggle to eat 1 gram of quality protein per pound of body weight, there are a few things to consider: Make sure you’re eating high-protein foods without excess fat or preservatives. If that does not eliminate the discomfort, then try replacing about a fourth of your protein calories with clean starches, like rice, and with fibrous foods, like salad, broccoli, or apples, while keeping your overall calories approximately the same. Starches are calorie dense, so it won’t take much to offset the slightly lower protein intake. Then, make adjustments until you arrive at a way of eating that is sustainable, and makes you feel good.

CICO—calories in, calories out—is a universal law of nutrition. Well, that and we all do need adequate protein and essential fatty acids to survive (which is what this protocol is all about). Other than that, figure out what works for you. And what works best for you may even change over time. I have long made it a point to eat enough protein daily, but I need to eat more vegetables now than I did when I was younger to feel my best.

### Nutrition Protocol 4: Choose Fibrous Vegetables and (Some) Fruit as Your Major Sources of Carbohydrates

#### What to Do

- **Vegetables should form the second major brick in the foundation of your diet and fruit, the third.** If protein is the cornerstone, these foods build on it by helping to ensure enough vitamin, mineral, and other micronutrient intake.
- **These foods are also essential for our fiber intake.** Men should aim for at least 35 grams per day, and women at least 25 grams per day.

#### How It Works

Many readers know already why vegetables and fruits are so important: They contain vitamins, minerals, and other micronutrients like flavonoids, all of which our bodies need to function optimally.[^c4-120] Once you understand how nutrient-rich vegetables and fruits are, you won’t think about them the same way again. Eating vegetables isn’t a chore; it’s a gift.

The fiber in vegetables and fruits is also important.[^c4-121] A bit about fiber: It provides support structure for the plants that produce it, be that in the roots, the stems, or the leaves. And it’s the part we can’t digest when we consume them. Fiber can be insoluble (will not dissolve in water), soluble (will dissolve in water), or prebiotic (feeds bacteria).

We need all three. Insoluble fiber, present in root vegetables and fruits with edible seeds, helps with stool formation. Soluble fiber, present in foods such as avocados, carrots, and Brussels sprouts, collects waste products as it travels through the body, helping to eliminate them. Prebiotic fiber, present in apples, asparagus, onions, and garlic, provides sustenance for the beneficial bacteria in our gut microbiome, which promote intestinal health and also healthy brain functioning via the gut-brain axis.[^c4-122] (The foods noted above are just a few examples from each category.)

And they do a lot more. Studies also indicate that dietary fiber reduces the risk of metabolic syndrome, a cluster of symptoms that increase the risk of heart disease and diabetes. The heart-protecting benefits of fiber are widely known. A study that followed 9,776 US men and women for an average of nineteen years found that those who ate the least dietary fiber had a significantly higher risk of coronary heart disease compared to those who ate the most dietary fiber.[^c4-123] A review of eleven meta-analyses, which each included several studies, confirmed the link between high fiber consumption and a reduced risk of several cancers, including ovarian, prostate, colon, breast, and pancreatic.[^c4-124]

Consuming fiber can also leave us feeling full, simply from the physical bulk of the food in our gut and the slowed gastric emptying that results.[^c4-125] It also leaves us less fatigued. That’s because consuming adequate fiber helps adjust what’s called the postprandial glucose response, the entry of sugar (and fat) into the bloodstream, which can otherwise cause “brain fog” and tiredness. Fiber also blunts post-meal inflammation that often follows eating a dish high in fat and carbs. That inflammation, in which levels of some proteins and hormones rise in the body, can contribute to the risk of heart disease if it occurs with any regularity.

How much fiber should we get? Men should get at least 35 grams per day and women 25 grams per day. Very few people actually do that. In fact, an estimated 95 percent of Americans do not consume recommended amounts of fiber.[^c4-126]

Some people fear adding more fiber to their diet because it can cause gas and/or bloating. It’s true that a sudden increase in daily fiber intake may temporarily result in both. But once you’re eating enough fiber on a regular basis, this usually becomes a non-issue. In one study on the link between bloating, sodium, and a high-fiber diet, the researchers found that while this diet did increase bloating to some extent, an accompanying decrease in sodium lessened that side effect, pointing to the idea that it’s often what we add to vegetables that becomes the problem, not the vegetables themselves.[^c4-127]

And at risk of sounding like your mother, vegetables require more chewing. You need to slow down and chew them well for them to digest properly, and for you to reap their full benefits.

A few notes on fruit: Some people find that eating fruit at the end of a meal causes some digestive discomfort. Others have no such issue. If you experience this problem, try eating fruit alone, before a meal, or as a snack rather than to cap off a full meal. It may help.

Beyond fiber, these foods contain, as I mentioned, essential vitamins, minerals, and other micronutrients. The words *vitamins and minerals* are thrown around a lot (I did it above). But knowing which ones tend to be lacking in most people’s diets, and knowing how to get more of these from food, can make a real difference to our health. Magnesium is largely an under-discussed, beneficial component of many foods. This mineral, the eighth most abundant element on earth,[^c4-128] is used by the body for energy production, bone development, making DNA, muscle contraction, nerve impulses, and even for regulating our heartbeat.[^c4-129] In fact, it’s involved in more than three hundred systems in our body and thousands of crucial biological processes. Yet most people don’t get enough of it. It’s easy to rectify, and I’m sure you can guess how: by eating enough fruits and especially enough vegetables.

Studies of the so-called Paleo diet, which focuses on fruits, vegetables, lean meat, fish, eggs, and nuts (in other words, foods that likely reflect the diet of a hunter-gatherer living in the Paleolithic era) indicate that we once had a magnesium intake of about 600 milligrams per day, leading researchers to theorize that human metabolism is adjusted to this high level.[^c4-130] Health authorities currently recommend 420 milligrams of magnesium daily for adult males and 320 milligrams daily for adult females. Available data indicate that most people consume less than that already low recommended amount. For Americans, the average is about 323 milligrams per day for males and 228 milligrams per day for females. This level is due, in part, to not eating enough foods containing magnesium, but likely also because many foods that would be high in magnesium are grown in soil depleted of this mineral due to modern farming methods.[^c4-131] Major or persistent magnesium deficiency can cause heart problems, neurological problems, and also dangerous reductions in calcium and potassium.[^c4-132] And we don’t know how moderate deficiencies over time may more subtly diminish our health and vitality.

Vegetables and some fish, such as salmon and mackerel, are excellent sources of magnesium. Avocados (technically a fruit) and certain dairy products, such as milk and cheese, also contain magnesium. Among the foods with the highest amount of magnesium are pumpkin seeds, almonds, black beans, and soybeans. And I know it can be hard to feel excited about kale, spinach, and chard, but a few minutes spent enlightening yourself about magnesium will likely change that. Dark, leafy greens are an excellent source of it and very low in calories; one cup of cooked spinach contains more than a third of the recommended daily intake and fewer than 50 calories.

And there are more vitamins and minerals that vegetables offer. Potassium (beets, tomatoes, butternut squash) is integral to muscle contraction and nerve impulses.[^c4-133] Calcium (broccoli, kale, edamame, leafy greens) is crucial for our bones and our teeth.[^c4-134] Flavonoids, a category that includes a wide number of compounds present in the plant world, can reduce inflammation; the risk of diabetes, heart disease, and breast cancer; antibiotic resistance; the formation of free radicals (atoms that can damage cells and can contribute to cancer formation); oxidative stress, which can contribute to various diseases and conditions including neurodegenerative disorders; and the risk of viral, bacterial, and fungal infections.[^c4-135]

We could continue talking about the benefits of high-quality protein, vegetables, and fruits until the cows (and cauliflower) come home. In fact, cruciferous vegetables such as cauliflower and broccoli offer numerous additional benefits such as sulforaphane, which can help scavenge and detoxify endocrine disruptors and generally supports healthy reproductive hormones in women and men,[^c4-136] and on and on. I hope that all we’ve covered in this protocol has inspired you to fill half your lunch or dinner plate with vegetables. Perhaps even add some spinach and tomatoes (though, again, technically a fruit) to your breakfast too.

Though one last note on fruit: Most people, unless they are very lean (less than 10 percent body fat for men and less than 15 percent for women) should probably not be eating more than three servings of fruit per day, especially if they are trying to lose body fat. Too much fruit, despite its fiber and water content, can stimulate hunger. Don’t get me wrong, fruit is amazing, and is always a part of a healthy diet. Enjoy it, but don’t overdo it.

#### Common Questions

*Should I take magnesium supplements?*

I suggest turning to magnesium supplements such as magnesium bisglycinate or L-threonate before bed only as an if-needed sleep aid, as described in Sleep Protocol 9, and then only if you’ve tried all the other protocols in chapter 1. For the benefit described here, stick primarily with foods that contain magnesium as a source.

That being said, magnesium supplements can help us get our daily recommended amount of this mineral. Magnesium L-threonate and bisglycinate seem to avoid the issue of gastrointestinal distress that some people experience with this supplement. By contrast, magnesium citrate can cause gastric distress and can sometimes even act as a laxative.

For adults, a 135-milligram magnesium L-threonate or bisglycinate supplement daily before sleep may also help ensure you are obtaining the recommended daily amount. Or you can take it with dinner. Be sure to consult with a physician before adding any supplement into your routine.

### Nutrition Protocol 5: Consume Healthy Fats as Part of Most Meals and Snacks

#### What to Do

- **Most of your fat intake should come from unsaturated fats.** These are present in olives, avocados, olive oil, and avocado oil, among other foods. Cook with olive oil, and use it for your salad dressing. If you need an oil with a higher smoke point for certain recipes, avocado oil is a good choice.
- **Consume omega-3 polyunsaturated fats.** These are present in fatty ocean fish, like salmon with the skin, and in various fish oil and krill supplements. (More on the benefits of omega-3 in Nutrition Protocol 7 of this chapter.)

#### How It Works

Perhaps no category of food is as feared, misunderstood, and maligned as fat. Part of the problem is terminology: The fact that we call dietary lipids fats brings to mind body fat. The two are not the same but they are easy to conflate.

I want you to create a healthy relationship with fat. The purpose of this protocol is to do that, based on science.

We all need some fat in our diet. The question is not if, but which and how much. Which? It turns out there are quite a few to choose from. And how much? As you learned earlier in this chapter, it depends on the other macronutrients you are eating, or avoiding, according to your overall diet (keto, clean omnivore, vegan, and so on).

And yet we have become wary of this macronutrient. This fear is based less on science than on history. Concerns about a link between fat and heart disease date back to the 1940s and grew in the ensuing decades.[^c4-137] In 1990, the USDA Dietary Guidelines recommended that Americans limit fat to 30 percent or less of their total calories and saturated fat to just 10 percent of their total calories, a recommendation that led to a proliferation of low-fat and nonfat products.[^c4-138] It soon became clear that these foods, often ultra-processed, were much worse for us than the fat we were now avoiding. These guidelines scared many people away from highly nutritious, high-quality protein foods that also contain some fat, like red meat and eggs. Moreover, we were then living without two crucial benefits that consuming fat provides: the way it slows the rise of glucose in the bloodstream and the way it increases satiety between meals. And Americans, on average, gained weight and suffered from rising rates of heart disease in the following years.

More recently, the pendulum swung the other way with rising interest in ketogenic diets, which involve eating mostly fat, some protein, and extremely few carbohydrates.[^c4-139] Interestingly, this diet first originated as a treatment for some forms of epilepsy in the 1920s. It’s also been studied as a treatment for schizophrenia[^c4-140] and bipolar disorder.[^c4-141] As a daily routine, the ketogenic diet is hard to stick with. But this and similar trends helped spread the awareness that many fats, such as monounsaturated and polyunsaturated fats, are good for us.

How can we move forward? Again, by looking at the science. Though a comprehensive review of all types of fat is beyond the scope of this book, a few things are helpful to this discussion. Above we established that fats are made from fatty acids. The body breaks down the fat we eat into these component parts, which are then absorbed into the blood. Once inside the body, fatty acids contribute to the structure and function of cell membranes, help regulate metabolism, and influence hormone production, among other roles.[^c4-142] Yes, dietary fat can be more readily converted into body fat, and it’s higher in calories per gram than carbs or protein—but at the end of the day, if we are burning as much or more of the calories we eat for energy to meet our metabolic needs, then it doesn’t matter if the calories we eat come from fat, carbs, or proteins.

We covered the main types of dietary fat in the introduction to this chapter: monounsaturated, polyunsaturated, saturated. There is also trans fat. A bit more detail on all is warranted. The terms *saturated* and *unsaturated*, and the reason the former are solid at room temp and the latter are not, have to do with their different chemical bonds inside the chains of fatty acids.

The lack of double bonds in saturated fats makes the molecules stack on each other more easily, which makes the fat more stable; this is why products like butter stay solid at room temperature. These fats are hard to digest, which can leave us feeling tired. They can also increase certain forms of cholesterol.

Unsaturated fats are kinked in their structure. When you want to consume fat, these are the ones to prioritize. They contain fatty acids, which trigger circuitries involved with many bodily processes mentioned above.[^c4-143] Some fatty acids are directly involved in neuroplasticity, which we can loosely define as the continued ability to learn and form new memories and skills.[^c4-144] Fatty acids are also integral to regulating appetite. The presence of fat triggers communication along the gut-brain axis, which prompts the brain to release chemicals that deliver a sense of satiety. In addition, fat in our body releases a hormone called leptin, which activates neural circuitries primarily in the hypothalamus that also result in the feeling of fullness.[^c4-145] Leptin is also involved in the signaling pathways related to the menstrual cycle and sperm production.[^c4-146] It is one reason why having enough body fat, but not too much, is needed for libido and fertility. It’s the signal from the body to the brain that food resources exist in sufficient abundance to potentially bring another member of our species into the world.

The fourth kind of fats, trans fats, are unsaturated, but the type of chemical bond is different from those in the other unsaturated fats. Although trans fats that occur naturally in some foods like meat and some dairy are relatively neutral or even beneficial to our health, when we hear about trans fats it usually refers to industrial-made versions.[^c4-147] These types of trans fats negatively impact cardiometabolic health, and were banned from the US food supply in 2018.[^c4-148] When you hear about partially hydrogenated vegetable oil, that is an industrial trans fat. Prior to 2018, many commercial products, such as margarine, processed meat, microwave popcorn, and packaged baked goods, made in the US contained trans fat, but no more. Health authorities recommend restricting industrial trans fats to 1 percent of total calories consumed—20 calories of a 2,000-calories-per-day diet, which is less than even one tablespoon. If you travel or live outside the US you’ll need to see if industrial trans fats are still used in foods there.

As I note in this protocol, ideally choose monounsaturated fats. Also include some amount of saturated fat.[^c4-149] Although some studies have found that switching from saturated fats to polyunsaturated fats reduces the risk of heart disease somewhat,[^c4-150] other studies have not confirmed this connection.[^c4-151] And a common challenge that can arise when eliminating saturated fat from the diet is that it can lead to an increased consumption of ultra-processed carbohydrates and added sugar (we reach for a processed snack instead of, say, some cheese or full-fat yogurt), which is also detrimental to health.[^c4-152] This often happens when someone decides to eliminate meat, and ends up eating more packaged foods to reduce the effort required to prepare high-protein meals. Ultra-processed foods often contain a lot of calories and little to no fiber. I believe it is better to have a little bit of satisfying saturated fat than to replace it with foods that do not trigger a satiety response from the brain, that the body cannot digest effectively, or that lead to overconsumption.

If you’re at this part of the protocol still wondering exactly how much fat to incorporate into your diet: Aim for 10 percent or less of your diet to consist of saturated fat. Keeping your overall fat intake to about 30 to 35 percent of your diet will help enable you to receive the benefits of this macronutrient without weight gain. Learn to love the right fats and your hormones, connective tissues, heart, and palate will all thank you.

#### Common Questions

*Should I consume more fat on certain days or post exercise?*

No. Assuming you’re eating 30 percent or so of your calories from fat, and that fat is a mix of saturated fats from high CP:C ratio proteins, and otherwise unsaturated fats such as avocados, olive oil or avocado oil, and some nuts and seeds, there is no reason to spike or drop your fat intake. If anything, we need to increase our clean starch intake, not our fat intake, on days we exercise. That’s because intense exercise depletes us of glycogen, a sugar that the body makes as a way to store energy, which eating clean starch can replace.

### Nutrition Protocol 6: Consume Low-Sugar Fermented Foods

#### What to Do

- **Consume two to four servings of low-sugar fermented foods per day.** Eating foods like sauerkraut, kimchi, pickles in brine (that require refrigeration), kefir, low-sugar kombucha, miso, and natto supports a healthy gut microbiome, which in turn supports all your bodily functions.

#### How It Works

The human microbiome—the bacteria that colonize our skin, mouth, digestive system, and the rest of our body—has become a focal point of both health research and health trends in recent years. Data from the Whitehall II study,[^c4-153] which has been tracking the health of thousands of British civil servants between the ages of thirty-five and fifty-five since 1985, found that eating fermented dairy foods like yogurt and kefir reduced the risk of death,[^c4-154] as long as coronary heart disease and diabetes were not present. In one surprising study of 710 people, consumption of fermented foods was linked to less social anxiety among those who were prone to it.[^c4-155] That finding was correlation, not causation, and it’s impossible to know whether eating something like sauerkraut made people less anxious. But connections like these start to make mechanistic sense as we learn more about the microbiome.

Recent research suggests that our microbiome starts forming before we are even born.[^c4-156] Bacteria we are exposed to during the birth process and in the early months of life continue to build this internal environment, which is then added to by microbes we take in through what we eat, what we drink, the people we come into contact with, the air we breathe, even the pets around us, and the soils we come into contact with. The specific makeup of our microbiome, including how diverse it is, changes according to our diet and our environment.[^c4-157] Even exercise affects our microbiome. A review of twenty-eight studies found that moderate-to-high-intensity exercise done for thirty to ninety minutes at least three times per week, for at least two months, “is likely to produce changes in the gut microbiota.”[^c4-158] The reason for this benefit is not fully understood, but may be connected to the changes our body goes through when we exercise, suggesting that temporarily being pushed out of our comfort zone is good for our gut diversity.[^c4-159] Then again, we update our gut microbiome from all sorts of sources around us. The mere act of lacing up our muddy running shoes helps build our microbiome. I know that sounds crazy but that’s how the microbiome works: It’s an internal reflection of our interactions with the outside world.

Not all bacteria that enter our bodies take up residence in our gut.[^c4-160] Some cannot survive the acidic environment, for example. Other bacteria cannot survive in areas with high oxygen concentration. And antibiotics tend to wipe out both the beneficial and detrimental bacteria from our gut.

And it’s important to have that beneficial bacteria present there. Studies have found connections between the content of our gut microbiome and many digestive disorders, such as irritable bowel disease and colorectal cancer.

The gut microbiome also appears to influence mood and mental health through the gut-brain axis (introduced in Nutrition Protocol 1).[^c4-161] A 2022 review of twenty-four observational studies and nineteen experimental trials, totaling about four thousand participants, identified differences in the beta diversity—which measures how dissimilar the various bacteria types present are to one another—between individuals who had been diagnosed with major depressive disorder and those who had not.[^c4-162] Researchers theorize that disruptions to the gut microbiome alter the release of serotonin and dopamine, setting off a cascade that ultimately ends with the release of cytokines, proteins that trigger the immune system into action and heighten inflammation.[^c4-163] Specific inflammatory cytokines have been linked to depression.[^c4-164]

On the positive side, we know that when our gut bacteria are provided with sufficient L-tryptophan (the amino acid precursor to serotonin) and short-chain fatty acids, they can readily help synthesize serotonin and signal for our brain to do the same, via our vagus nerve.

The Human Microbiome Project, the American Gut Project, the British Gut Project, and other ongoing large collaborative studies are continuing to uncover the function of the gut microbiome—both its role in healthy biological processes and its influence on chronic and acute ailments. Studies also seek to figure out which specific species of microbiota are beneficial and which are not. As a general rule, diversity is the most important feature of a healthy gut microbiome.[^c4-165] Diet plays a huge role in ensuring that our gut hosts a wide range of healthy bacteria.[^c4-166] Fiber has long been a focus in this endeavor to ensure a healthy microbiome (more about how to prioritize fiber in Nutrition Protocol 4).[^c4-167] But fermented foods appear to play an equally if not more significant role as well. Hence this protocol.

Take the study led by Stanford University biologist Justin Sonnenburg comparing how dietary fiber and fermented foods affected the microbiome of thirty-six participants.[^c4-168] Half of the individuals consumed a high-fiber diet for ten weeks, increasing their intake of soluble and insoluble fiber by eating more fruits, vegetables, legumes, grains, nuts, and seeds. They also consumed more vegetable protein and decreased the quantity of animal protein and salt. The other half upped their intake of fermented low-sugar foods like yogurt and kefir and also consumed fermented vegetables (sauerkraut, kimchi) and beverages (kombucha and vegetable brine). The researchers collected blood and stool samples before the ten weeks began, at four weeks into the intervention, and at the end of the following six weeks. The participants then began following a diet of their choice—maintaining their study diet or something else—and samples were collected after another four weeks.

Analyses of the blood and stool samples revealed that the group focused on fermented foods experienced a significant decrease in nineteen markers of inflammation, including the cytokines interleukin-6, interleukin-10, and interleukin-12b. The researchers also observed beneficial increases in the diversity of the gut microbiomes, as well as decreases in markers of immune system disruption in the low-sugar fermented food condition. The increase in microbial diversity was notably greater among the fermented foods group compared to the high-fiber group. This diversity lasted through the final four weeks of the study, after participants returned to the diet of their choice, indicating that the change was not due to a temporary passing-through of microbes but rather an “ecosystem remodeling,” as the researchers call it in their 2022 report in *Cell*.

#### Common Questions

*What specific fermented foods should I eat?*

Any that require refrigeration and are low in sugar, and have no added sugars are good choices. Sauerkraut and kimchi are both excellent choices. However, take note that any sauerkraut, pickles, and such that are stable on the shelf have not been fermented and are not recommended. Kombucha is also great, though it contains small amounts of alcohol and is often high in sugar, and should therefore be consumed in moderation. Natto and miso, made from fermented soybeans, are also good choices and are widely available.

Many fermented foods can be expensive. Yogurt and apple cider vinegar are lower-cost items and easy to find in your grocery store. Kefir is a yogurt drink that is less common but carried by many markets, and also less expensive than some other fermented products.

It is possible to make fermented foods at home, but the process needs careful attention to avoid contamination with harmful bacteria or anything else that can cause a foodborne illness. Tim Ferriss offered a great protocol for homemade sauerkraut in his book *The 4-Hour Chef*, and that can also be found online. Pickling vegetables in miso is a relatively easy way to make fermented food at home. If you decide to make your own fermented foods, be sure to follow the recipe exactly, including all advised precautions.

*I get an unpleasant histamine response from fermented foods—itchy eyes, tingling in my hands, and brain fog. What should I do?*

This is not uncommon. I’ve had this experience too from eating broccoli and onions, and I never knew why. When I hosted Sean Mackey, MD, PhD, and chief of the division of Stanford Pain Medicine, on the *Huberman Lab* podcast, he told me about his experience with gut pain, one that defied all approaches… until someone suggested he cut out histamine-containing foods like onions.[^c4-169] I can live without onions, but love low-sugar fermented foods and the benefits mentioned above are motivation for me to eat them daily. But they can cause a histamine response. So I have taken the histamine enzyme diamine oxidase (DAO) before these meals. It’s inexpensive and it solved the issue for me.

### Nutrition Protocol 7: Consume Fatty Ocean Fish and/or Consider Omega-3 Supplements

#### What to Do

- **Make a point to consume some fatty, cold water fish once or twice a week.** Consider including salmon with the skin, sardines, mackerel, or herring as part of your weekly diet.
- **Take supplements of fish oil or krill oil, or, if you’re vegan, algae oil.** Aim to consume 1,000 milligrams of eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA) per day. Some people will benefit from consuming as much as 2 to 3 grams of EPA per day, although for most people getting that 1 gram of EPA per day will suffice. Some may even wish to ask their doctor to prescribe generic or name brand Lovaza, which is high in omega-3 fatty acids (at 465 mg per capsule), and is purified of all metals and other toxins. It is now rather inexpensive to obtain given it is available in generic form. I take it daily.

#### How It Works

Nutrition Protocol 5 included the somewhat bold suggestion that we build a healthier relationship with fat. The omega-3 fatty acids are among the best forms of fat. These compounds form polyunsaturated fats, which are found in some fish, some leafy greens, beans, many plant-based oils and some other foods.[^c4-170]

As discussed earlier, fatty acids, the building blocks of fat, help with metabolism, how our bodies respond to hormones, physical performance, and more.[^c4-171] The body can turn calories into stored fat. But we can’t make omega-3 fatty acids. We have to get them through our diet.

And we should make sure to do that because the evidence that omega-3 fatty acids are good for us—our brains, in particular—is persuasive. Research has found positive ties between omega-3s and memory, cognition,[^c4-172] the maintenance of mental health and heart health,[^c4-173] improved outcomes after heart disease treatment,[^c4-174] and relief from depression.[^c4-175]

Let’s get specific. Modern interest in omega-3 fatty acids can be traced largely to two Danish researchers who became curious about the diet followed by the Greenland Inuit.[^c4-176] The low incidence of heart disease and diabetes led the researchers to wonder whether something in their diet, which contained large amounts of seal and whale fat, was staving off these illnesses. Their 1971 paper comparing plasma lipid and lipoprotein levels, which are associated with coronary artery disease, among a population of Greenland Inuit and a population of Danish citizens (including a small group of Inuit living in Denmark) led the researchers to speculate about a connection between the high content of unsaturated fat in the Inuit diet and low incidence of coronary artery disease as well as diabetes. The publication launched decades of research about the value of omega-3 fatty acids.

Omega-3 fatty acids have been studied in numerous disease settings, with varying results. Among the more striking findings, aside from the clearly beneficial role in reducing the risk of heart disease, is a link to the reduction of depressive symptoms. In one study, researchers randomized sixty people diagnosed with major depressive disorder to treatment with 1,000 milligrams EPA daily, 20 milligrams of the prescription drug fluoxetine (more commonly known as Prozac), or both for eight weeks.[^c4-177] Among the forty-eight patients who completed at least four weeks of study treatment, EPA and fluoxetine were equally effective at treating depression, and the combination yielded better outcomes than either one alone.

I mentioned a few of these foods in Nutrition Protocol 5, but it bears repeating here for the particular benefits of omega-3 fatty acids they contain.

#### Common Questions

*Fish oil supplements can be expensive. Are they necessary? Which ones are the best?*

Indeed they can be expensive and concerns about them turning rancid are real. To get 1 gram or more of EPA per day, make sure the source is fresh and from a reputable, third-party tested supplement company. The liquid fish oil (usually cod, mackerel, anchovies, or some combination) sold in dark bottles to protect from light is most cost-effective. Just be sure to keep the bottle refrigerated after opening or it can go rancid. As I mentioned earlier, these days I take Lovaza, which is a prescription high-dose omega-3 capsule that has been purified of metals and other contaminants. It’s available in generic form now so it is inexpensive, but you do need a doctor to prescribe it.

*I don’t like fish oil or fish. Can algae or krill do the job for omega-3s?*

All these are decent sources of omega-3 fatty acids. For those who are allergic to fish oil or don’t want to take it for ethical reasons, algae oil supplements are vegan and rich with omega-3.

One warning: I know a fair number of people who tolerate fish oil well but for whom krill-based omega-3 gives them a rash that itches. I am one such person. So proceed with caution.

*What about just eating a lot of fish instead of taking supplements?*

Again, it is hard to consume enough fish. High-quality fish can be expensive. We also have to be careful about avoiding mercury, which now exists in many species at levels that are too high for frequent human consumption. King mackerel, swordfish, and bigeye tuna are among the fish with the highest mercury levels. Cold-water fish with the lowest mercury levels and that are excellent sources of omega-3s include inexpensive options, like sardines and herring. These and supplementation are going to be the easiest and most cost-efficient approaches to follow. And maybe some sustainably sourced cod, tilapia, or salmon with the skin on one to two times a week, if you like the taste.

## Chapter 5: Protocols for Light

![Chapter emblem](images/chapter-emblem.jpeg)

Of all the science I’ve studied over the years—as a research neuroscientist, in my role hosting many of the world’s most qualified doctors and scientists on my podcast, and in my own real-world experience—light, and the incredible influence it has on every aspect of our health, is the subject that has thrilled and surprised me the most.

As a master’s student I worked on the visual pathways that control circadian rhythms, and in graduate school and during my postdoc fellowship, and in my own lab, I researched visual circuits that convert light energy—photons, that is—into conscious visual perception, or what is commonly referred to as eyesight. My lab also spent a few years exploring the connections between our eyes and the cerebellum. Turns out, our eyes and our cerebellum—or “mini brain”—are in an ongoing dialogue that helps us orient in space. We will get back to the cerebellum later when we discuss learning in chapter 6.

But as my lab explored the visual system, papers kept coming out showing how light either supports or damages the health of our cells. In some cases these findings were about how light affects the skin. In other cases, it was about how light impacts our health via our eyes in ways that are separate from eyesight. Given that so much of my training centered around our visual system, that research intrigued me. Not just because it was in my wheelhouse but also because of how actionable it was. It could be applied easily to daily life, and impact health in potent ways. So I voraciously read every one of those studies. I also knew one of the pioneers in this field. Glen Jeffery, PhD, at the University College London, a former colleague of mine from the field of visual system development, began to study how particular types and sources of light either help or hurt human physiology. His lab also studied how light affected longevity.[^c5-1] I connected with him periodically to get a sense of what was on the horizon. While his is not the only lab working on the relationship between light and health, Glen is a leader in the formal study of this topic. We have him to thank for taking what were largely anecdotal observations put forth by niche online communities and testing them in controlled studies including clinical trials.

Over those years, I was also spending more and more time indoors, under LED lights—both during the day and at night. Such is life in a lab. My colleagues all did the same. So did my friends in medicine, tech, design, and, once smartphones hit the world full force in 2010, pretty much everyone else. I, and some of my more health-conscious colleagues, started to wonder if all that time indoors under the LED lights was part of the reason a lot of us were feeling so lousy.

Now we know that it almost certainly was. The lack of full-spectrum sunlight, and the use of LED light was no doubt directly damaging our bodies, inside and out, by impairing cellular health. Now of course, I can’t be sure it was *all* due to indoor lighting, but at one point my hair started falling out, I was always tired in the afternoon, and my joints ached. And I was exercising and eating well at the time, and my life was no more stressful than it is now.

Eventually I decided to use light as a tool, not just to get my sleep right but to improve other aspects of my health. I was amazed by what happened. My hair grew back—like crazy, in fact. I got far fewer colds and other respiratory infections. My mood even lifted. Mind you, I was in my forties then, and I’m in my fifties now, and still with the addition of a few simple protocols, my general health improved markedly. There are different levers of health but based on the data from Glen’s lab and others, I treat my relationship to sunlight and indoor lighting as key levers for health.

My experience is anecdotal, but we now have evidence to support why and precisely how the use of light can improve cellular, organ, and body-wide health. It is an area of health just as crucial as sleep, exercise, or nutrition. Moreover, we now know the best ways to capture the benefits of different types of light. Which is why it deserves its own chapter here.

While light as a tool for health is not discussed as often as it should be, it is not new, and its origins are definitely not fringe; we’ve long known that there was a connection between sunlight and well-being. And in many regions of the world, hospitals still take patients outside for the age-old practice of sunlight exposure to promote recovery from certain ailments.[^c5-2] And photobiomodulation has been studied and used by serious scientists and physicians since the early 1900s.[^c5-3] The Danish physician Niels Finsen was actually awarded the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1903 for his discovery that light can be used to treat various diseases including tuberculosis of the skin, or lupus.

Nowadays, photobiomodulation has been shown to be effective for treating acne,[^c5-4] accelerating wound healing,[^c5-5] and promoting hair growth,[^c5-6] as well as reducing pain[^c5-7] and even improving blood sugar regulation.[^c5-8] Studies have also demonstrated the efficacy of photobiomodulation for offsetting age-related vision loss[^c5-9] and for improving hormone health.[^c5-10] That’s not all; light has also been shown to improve heart[^c5-11] and GI tract health[^c5-12] and to help combat various autoimmune conditions.[^c5-13]

And of course, there are countless positive effects of viewing sunlight on your circadian rhythm. As you recall from chapter 1, viewing low solar angle sunlight in the morning and again in the afternoon sets your sleep-wake cycle correctly, increases your daytime mood, alertness and focus, and immune system function, and promotes better sleep at night. It is not exaggerating to say that light is medicine, especially sunlight.

And like any medicine, the effects of light depend on the type, intensity, duration, and timing of its delivery. For example, whereas sunlight in the morning and daytime is beneficial, viewing bright lights (especially from LED sources) too close to your bedtime spikes your cortisol levels, quashes your melatonin, and disrupts your blood sugar regulation (as discussed in Sleep Protocol 3). That affects your sleep that night and your energy the next morning. And certain wavelengths of light—in particular those emitted by most LED sources—may also accelerate cellular aging and promote disease progression by damaging cells in the retina, cornea, and brain, according to studies in animal models.[^c5-14]

While all these effects of light might sound tricky to navigate, it’s actually quite simple. You just need to know which types of light are beneficial to view, which are detrimental, and how and when to maximize one and minimize the other. In this chapter, I’ll teach you.

### What Is Light?

First we need to discuss what light is, exactly.

Obviously, light makes things visible. Any light source, be it the sun, a lamp, a candle flame, or the glow from a phone screen makes things visible because it emits energy. Light sources vary by type and amount of energy; that’s what makes them different from one another.

Recall from chapter 1 that light is comprised of a broad range of wavelengths, from very short wavelengths to very long ones. Some of these wavelengths are visible to humans—they make up what we call the visible spectrum of red, green, blue, and so on. Other wavelengths of light, such as ultraviolet and infrared, are invisible to us.

Short wavelengths of light are, as their name suggests, waves of energy where the peaks and the troughs of the wave are very close together. Long wavelengths of light are the opposite; the peaks and troughs of long wavelength light are relatively far apart.

The sun emits an extremely broad range of short, medium, and long wavelengths. The entire visible spectrum is held inside sunlight. That’s why sunlight through a prism comes through as a rainbow on the other side. The prism slows down and bends the light, and each wavelength exits at a different angle, spreading the light into the full visible spectrum of red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, and violet.

Green, blue, and purple light are shorter in wavelength compared to yellow, orange, and red light, which are longer. Sunlight (in the absence of a prism) appears white or pale yellow. The sky turns colorful at dawn and dusk because, as you may recall from chapter 1, when the sun is low in the sky, components of the atmosphere reduce the amount of shorter wavelengths reaching our eyes—a process called Rayleigh scattering—leaving us primarily seeing the longer wavelengths of red, orange, and yellow. The sun of course always emits the same wavelengths of energy regardless of where it happens to be in the sky. Which visible wavelengths arrive at our eyes is what determines how the sun appears to us, and the effect it will have on us.

Then there are the invisible wavelengths. Sunlight includes wavelengths shorter than blue or violet that are (unimaginatively) called ultraviolet (UV) light. We can’t perceive UV light but it’s there, radiating down on us all day. (Though interesting to note that bees can see UV, and squirrels can see it too, possibly to help them detect predators at night. Some species of flying squirrels actually have UV fluorescence that causes their bellies to glow a bubblegum pink.)[^c5-15] The sun also emits wavelengths longer than red light, appropriately called infrared (IR) light. We humans can’t see IR, but we can feel it as warmth. Though we have engineered technologies to see IR emissions—that’s what night vision goggles do.

The sun also emits small amounts of X-ray energy, which is made up of very short wavelength radiation, even shorter than UV. And, like with UV and IR, we can’t see X-rays, but they are there. X-rays pass through our skin but are absorbed by our bones, teeth, and other dense tissues. That’s how X-ray machines work: They are designed to send out concentrated X-rays so their patterns of absorption can be captured on film or by a digital sensor, allowing your doctor or dentist to see different structures inside your body that absorb those X-rays to varying degrees.

Whether visible or invisible, these wavelengths travel in a similar pattern—not as a line but, well, as a wave, moving up and down, up and down. Shorter wavelengths of light go through many more up-down-up-down cycles as they travel from one point to another; longer wavelengths go through fewer. Thus, we often refer to short wavelengths of light as high frequency light and long wavelengths of light as low frequency.

Mentions of UV light can trigger concerns, so let me address that now. Whether light exposure is harmful, beneficial, or benign depends on the type, intensity, duration, and timing. All light energy is radiation. Often when people hear the word *radiation* they think *radioactive*. The radiation from visible light is not harmful because it doesn’t have enough energy to perturb the atoms in our body. But here’s where type, duration, and the other factors matter. Some forms of non-ionizing light radiation can disrupt our cells if we are exposed to too much of it. For example, we need some UV light exposure each day. But excessive exposure can cause genetic mutations in our cells by causing the formation of abnormal bonds in our DNA.[^c5-16]

Wavelength and intensity of light are inversely related to one another. Put in practical terms, you can be exposed to a lot of long wavelength light, like red or IR light, without damaging your skin. It takes comparatively less exposure to short wavelength UV light to cause a sunburn. But that doesn’t mean short wavelength, high frequency light is inherently bad for us. Again, we come back to this core idea: Dosage matters. We all need some UV light from the sun to reach our skin, where it sets off a cascade of reactions that results in the production of vitamin D, which is critical for calcium absorption, bone health, immune health, and more.[^c5-17] But too much UV exposure can lead to a sunburn, as I mentioned above, and cause premature aging of your skin, as well as DNA mutations that lead to certain skin cancers.[^c5-18] And because long wavelength IR is so low energy (remember, wavelength and intensity are inversely related), we need relatively long sun exposure times to enjoy its benefits. The challenge is getting enough IR and NIR (infrared and near-infrared) light from the sun without also getting excessive UV exposure, but it can be done. There’s a protocol for it.

I’m aware that none of what I’ve shared with you thus far tells you exactly *how* light can change your cells. As wavelengths travel through space, in that up-and-down cycle, they hit various surfaces, big and small: a mountain range, a tree, this page, your hand. These surfaces absorb or reflect wavelengths. But sometimes they pass right through. Light can pass right through your body, for example, and as it does it can change the molecular properties of the cells it encounters and the components within them, such as in the example of excessive UV-altering DNA structure of, say, skin cells. Here are two more examples, this time with light playing positive roles in cellular function: Studies suggest that red, NIR, and IR light can enhance the functioning of your mitochondria, the energy producing organelles in your cells.[^c5-19] Data suggest that NIR and IR may also trigger the release of a gas called nitric oxide that acts on your vascular and lymphatic cells and causes them to dilate, allowing for more lymph fluid and blood to move through them.[^c5-20]

There are more examples in the protocols that follow. You’ll learn how to use light—in some cases sunlight, and in other cases artificial light of specific wavelengths—to improve your physical and mental health. Also here are recommendations for in-home lighting and light devices that emit or block specific wavelengths of light, which you can use to achieve specific benefits, such as increased morning and daytime energy levels, better glucose regulation, and even better eyesight. In chapter 1, we explored how light helps with sleep; now it’s time to see its immediate effects on other important aspects of our health.

As you read these protocols, remember this: While it might seem fantastical that light can do so many positive things for our brain and body, it actually makes perfect sense. Light is energy that the cells in our body can absorb and use. The very first law of thermodynamics is that energy can’t be destroyed or created de novo; it can only be converted from one form to another. So let’s discuss the ways you can convert light energy into cellular energy, which leads to improvements in physical energy, vision, skin, mood, and heart health… and more.

I hope this powerful lever will no longer be overlooked.

**Note:** *If you are reading this book from beginning to end, you’ll realize as you encounter Light Protocols 1, 2, and 3 that these are essentially the same as protocols covered in chapter 1 and chapter 3. You may be thinking, “Does he have a memory issue, or think I have one?” The answer is: no and no.*

*The practices I suggest in this chapter are indeed found in earlier ones. But, because many people may read this book out of order, I wanted to be sure that these crucial protocols would not be missed. Moreover, the information that follows is not a carbon copy of the protocols in chapter 1 or chapter 3. I include new information about the mechanisms behind the “critical window” in the first hour after you wake up, whereby your SCN can amplify your morning cortisol levels… if and only if you give it the right stimulus. I also cover new information about viewing light at specific times to adjust your cortisol rhythm, so you can avoid what is commonly referred to as “burnout,” but is often a mistiming in your daily cortisol peak. I also include more options for indoor lighting—some were mentioned only briefly in previous chapters; others are new. All that said, if you feel you are already versed enough in these first three protocols and most importantly, you are already doing them on a daily basis, feel free to skip to Light Protocol 4.*

### Light Protocol 1: View Bright Light in the First Hour After Waking to (Further) Increase Your Morning Cortisol Levels

#### What to Do

- **Get morning sunlight in your eyes as soon as possible after waking.** If the sun hasn’t risen yet, or is otherwise inaccessible, view a 10,000 lux artificial light. Either one will significantly elevate your post-waking morning cortisol levels, which is highly beneficial *if it occurs in the first hour of your day*.
- **The timing will vary based on when you wake up, and where you live.** Refer to the information below to figure out what’s best for you. Ten to thirty minutes is a good general rule, but even if you can only grab five, do it. Some is better than none.

#### How It Works

It is hard to overstate the positive impact of this protocol on your energy, mood, focus, stress levels, immune system, and, of course, sleep. If you’ve read chapter 1, you might be thinking: Does this protocol sound familiar? Yes, I’m recommending a similar behavioral tool here, but emphasizing different benefits. Stay with me.

I can hear all the questions running through your head, so for this protocol, let’s tackle these first.

You’re probably thinking, “Wait—I have to get up and watch the sunrise every day?” No. You don’t. If you wake up early enough, and the sky is clear, great! Do that. But most people can’t. And you don’t need to. The key thing here is to view bright light *in the first hour after waking*. This applies even if your normal wake-up time is noon.

“What if I wake up before the sun is out?” Another question I hear often. Again, not a problem. That is where a 10,000 lux artificial light can really help. It’s not a replacement for sunlight, but if you wake up before sunrise, I suggest getting one of these lights and looking at it for ten minutes or so upon waking. Then, if you can, get outside for some early natural light once the sun has risen. If you’re off to work at an office before sunrise, these lights are a game changer.

“I can’t see the sun where I live, so what should I do?” I have good news for you. You need to get sun*light* in your eyes, but you do not need to see the sun. Some days it’s clear, and other days it’s overcast. Sunlight still comes through on cloudy days. Maybe you’re thinking: “Not where I live!” Really? Consider how bright it is at 8:00 a.m. on a densely clouded winter day in Seattle, which is the northernmost major city in the contiguous US. Then consider what it’s like at midnight the night before. Unless you live at one of the earth’s poles in winter—which I’m guessing you don’t—there is always some sunlight during the daytime. So view it within an hour of waking. Let’s keep going with those common questions.

“Can I wear sunglasses?” It’s best to view morning sunlight without them. Wearing corrective lenses such as eyeglasses or contact lenses is fine, even if they include UV protection. Don’t wear a brimmed hat, however. The neurons in your eyes that you need to stimulate here respond to light coming from above and in front of your eyes, and a brimmed hat will block it.

“Can I blink?” Yes! Never force yourself to stare at sunlight, or any bright light for that matter. It can damage your eyes to do so. People vary in their sensitivity to light, so if this is hard for you, squint and look to the area adjacent to the sun as needed. This shouldn’t hurt.

“Can I get my morning sunlight through a window?” While better than nothing, the glass used for most windows filters out too much of the wavelengths of light you need. Thus, go outside. Bring your morning coffee, tea, or a glass of water. Bring your dog, kids, partner, or a friend along with you if you like. Yes, your dog will benefit too. After all, the same circuits and mechanisms that underlie this protocol are present in humans and dogs (and horses, goats, and squirrels, as I’ve mentioned, and all diurnal mammals). And of course you can walk, jog, skip rope, or do calisthenics as you view bright light too. If you take an hour walk, or schedule a run or a yoga session outside, even better, as sunlight and exercise can synergize to increase your early morning cortisol levels. Whatever you do, just don’t spend the whole time looking down at your phone. That will negate the effect you’re seeking.

“How long should I view morning sunlight to get the maximum effect?” As I mentioned, the answer depends on sunlight availability but a good general rule of thumb is this: On clear mornings shoot for a minimum of ten minutes, on partially cloudy days, get a minimum of twenty minutes, and on very overcast days, thirty minutes. If you view a 10,000 lux artificial light beforehand, for any of the reasons discussed already, you’ll need less time viewing sunlight—about half as much—to get the same effect.

It’s hard to be more specific than this because sunlight availability is shaped by the time of day, time of year, weather, and location.

And, once more: “What if I wake up before sunrise, then what?” This is by far the most common question I hear. Unless you have powers that I am not aware of, you will have to wait for the sun to come out to see sunlight. Get your in-the-first-hour-of-waking bright light by viewing a 10,000 lux artificial light. Ten thousand lux artificial light devices are not as good as sunlight, because they don’t contain the same array and balance of wavelengths present in sunlight as discussed in the introduction to this chapter. But they will elevate your morning cortisol levels, which is your goal in this protocol.[^c5-21] They cost about $100 to $150. Some are portable and suitable for travel. And, again, if you rely on a 10,000 lux light first thing in the morning, you’ll still want to get five to twenty minutes or so of natural sunlight exposure to your eyes once the sun comes out. Most people find that having a 10,000 lux light in their bathroom or kitchen works well for their morning routines.

If you do use a 10,000 lux light, you needn’t be obsessed with the viewing distance, nor do you have to worry about intermittently stepping or pivoting away from the light while preparing for your day. Just aim to be in front of it at a distance of about one to two feet for at least ten minutes total in the first hour after waking. More is fine, but again people vary in their sensitivity to light and some find that after ten minutes of 10,000 lux light they feel *too* awake! Other people can handle more exposure.

And if you have a question about my schedule: Because I typically wake up before the sun is out, I have a 10,000 lux light in my bathroom and my kitchen. I turn them on within a few minutes of waking and leave them on as I brush my teeth and prepare for my day. Once the sun is up, I go outside and view sunlight. That way, on days when I need to commute to work early or exercise before the sun is up, I know I have already spiked my morning cortisol. And when I travel, I bring a small portable 10,000 lux unit and use it in the same way. It’s a fantastic tool but it’s not a replacement for sunlight.

“Does viewing my computer screen or phone work to replace morning sunlight or 10,000 lux light?” Alas, no. Your phone screen is far too dim and far too narrow a spectrum to accomplish the effect here. Diabolically, however, your phone or computer screen is plenty bright enough to stimulate cortisol release if it’s viewed at night. And that is bad. And your phone or computer is plenty bright enough to suppress your melatonin levels. Also bad!

By now you may be asking (or shouting): “Wait, why in the world would I want to *increase* my cortisol levels? Isn’t cortisol a stress hormone? Isn’t that a bad thing?” Okay, maybe if you read this book in order, you already know the answer, but I’ll repeat it here: Most people think cortisol is a stress hormone to avoid, but you absolutely want to have high cortisol levels in the first hours of your day. The science shows us why.

##### The Natural Cortisol Cycle

Sleep Protocol 1 explains the science behind how viewing morning sunlight impacts your circadian rhythm. As a brief reminder: When you view sunlight, or a 10,000 lux light, it activates cells in your eyes that convert light into electrical signals. Those signals are relayed to the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN), your master circadian clock, located above the roof of your mouth in your hypothalamus. The SCN in turn releases chemical and electrical signals that coordinate the activities of the trillions of twenty-four-hour clocks found in every cell and organ of your body into a coherent set of rhythms. The physiological and psychological benefits that circadian coordination brings about are many.

But the SCN is not a one-trick pony. It serves another crucial role that is seldom discussed but, frankly, just as important. Your SCN can also stimulate a significant increase in your cortisol levels in the first sixty minutes after you wake up. It’s time restricted, meaning it can only occur in this short window. If you miss it, it’s gone—at least until the next day.

This is not a window you want to miss! Because whereas surges in cortisol are generally not advantageous if they occur in the afternoon, the evening, or at night, as I’ve mentioned, you actually want your cortisol levels to be very high in the first hours of your day.

Cortisol has gotten a bad rap. It’s been labeled the stress hormone and indeed, this hormone made in your adrenal glands is released during times of stress. But cortisol is also released when you wake up each morning. More accurately, you wake up each morning because cortisol is released. You read that right. Cortisol is the hormone that ensures you have the energy to get out of bed and lean into your daily activities. That is because cortisol’s fundamental role is to cause the release of stored fuels in your liver and muscles, which shifts the state of your brain and body from sleep to one of physical and mental readiness. The technical term for this process, which you might remember from chapter 3, is called the cortisol awakening response (CAR). Cortisol is not just a stress hormone. It’s an energy-releasing hormone. (See Stress Control Protocol 5 if you’d like a reminder.)

When we view cortisol in this way, we start to understand that it’s not something to be avoided at all. Rather, it is something to harness and use to our advantage. Our body has designated pathways and mechanisms to do just that. It allows for what’s called the healthy twenty-four-hour cortisol curve, which follows the pattern below:

1. Very low in the 1 to 2 hours prior to bedtime
2. At its absolute lowest in the first half of your night’s sleep
3. Rising slowly in the second half of your night’s sleep
4. Rising sharply in the 30 minutes prior to your desired wake-up time
5. Rising sharply even more in the first 1 to 2 hours after you wake up
6. Peaking about 30 minutes to 3 hours after waking
7. Gradually decreasing across the early and late afternoon
8. Repeat…

   Countless studies now show that allowing this natural cycle to operate without disruption helps optimize our sleep, cognition, and energy levels as well as mood and immune system function.[^c5-22] By contrast, altering this cycle such that evening or nighttime cortisol levels are too high (or morning cortisol levels are too low) can lead to problems in all these areas. Studies of night shift workers have been crucial in uncovering these connections.[^c5-23] A chronic disruption to the ideal cycle is referred to as a flattening of the cortisol curve. This flattening causes anxiety, sleep disturbances, low daytime energy, and mood disruptions as well as impaired immune resistance to viral, bacterial, and other infections.[^c5-24]

##### Cortisol and Stress

Keep in mind that just because we are framing cortisol as not purely a stress hormone does not mean it is not related to stress. It is. Stress triggers the release of cortisol.[^c5-25] If you experience stress at any point during the day or night, you can and should expect a spike in your cortisol to occur. That’s perfectly normal, healthy, and adaptive—because that spike will provide you with the immediate physical and mental energy you need to deal with whatever stressor you might face.[^c5-26] Stress-triggered cortisol levels typically return to baseline within about one hour or so. In fact, you can experience a lot of cortisol spikes above baseline per day (or night) before it ever becomes problematic for your health. I’m not suggesting you seek out stress, but as we discussed in chapter 3, humans evolved to deal with it in a variety of forms. Raising kids, traffic, difficult people, the pressures of work, school, or athletics, the state of the world… many of these are indeed stressful at times, and cortisol makes sure you have the fuel to deal with each one.

Cortisol spikes that occur shortly before sleep are where problems begin. That increase is often what prevents people from falling asleep, and what causes the classic stress-induced sleep disturbance of waking up at 3:00 a.m. and not falling back asleep. One night of that happening, no biggie. Two nights in a row? Hard, but manageable. However, three or more nights of stress-induced sleep disturbances really start to take a toll on your mental and physical health.

##### Cortisol and Light

And now we get back to the protocol suggested here. I discussed how to deal with both acute and chronic stress in chapter 3. What we didn’t discuss is that when you get your twenty-four-hour cortisol curve correct, it makes both kinds of stress much easier to deal with. And to get your twenty-four-hour cortisol curve correct we need to… view morning sunlight (or 10,000 lux light) in the first hour after waking. It not only boosts your morning cortisol levels, but also helps ensure your nighttime cortisol is kept low.
