This has immediate benefits you can feel within minutes and that last all day, among them improved mood, focus, and energy. Think of it as the optimal start signal for your day. Because from the perspective of your brain and body, that’s exactly what it is.

Here are the basics of how it works, plus some additional information pertinent to the twenty-four-hour cortisol cycle. Your cortisol level at any one moment, and your overall twenty-four-hour cortisol cycle, are controlled via the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis, which we discussed in chapter 3. Neurons in an area of your hypothalamus called the PVN (paraventricular nucleus) extend wirelike projections into your pituitary, a gland that resembles two small marbles in a sock hanging out the base of your brain.[^c5-27] One of those marbles sits in front of the other, and this is called the anterior pituitary. Your PVN neurons release corticotropin-releasing hormone (CRH) to cause your anterior pituitary cells to release adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) into your bloodstream. Next, the ACTH travels to your adrenal glands and stimulates the release of cortisol into your bloodstream. Voila! Cortisol then causes energy to be released from various organs and cells in your body. Cortisol does many other things, but one more that’s relevant here: Unlike adrenaline, which is also released from your adrenal glands and increases your energy level, cortisol can cross the blood-brain barrier. That means it has action on the body, such as mobilizing glucose for fuel, but also can increase the excitability of the neurons in your brain involved in alertness, focus, memory formation, and even motivation.

The PVN also detects when cortisol levels in your blood get high. It then *reduces* its release of CRH, which in turn reduces ACTH release, which results in less cortisol release. This is called a negative feedback loop; when the level of cortisol reaching the brain is very high, less cortisol is triggered to be released. In that way, it is like how many home thermostats work. For example, if the temperature in a room becomes too high from the level you’ve set, the thermostat shuts the heat off.

This self-regulation process takes a bit of time to take effect, which is why a short-term spike in cortisol is no big deal. An hour or so afterward, you’re back to your baseline level, appropriate for that time of day. But with frequent spikes, you start to alter your normal twenty-four-hour cortisol cycle. Cortisol surges at 9:00 p.m. for a few nights in a row and the next thing you know, your next-morning levels are lower than they should be *and* your PVN is then primed to release *more* cortisol later that night.

There is a name for this domino effect. It’s called chronic-stress-induced burnout. Alas, for many, this is the norm, especially now that a good number of people lie in bed looking at their phone in the first and last hour of each day, which, for reasons you’ll soon understand, sets them up for lower-than-needed cortisol levels in the morning and greater-than-desired cortisol levels at night.

So in a way, a better name for chronic-stress-induced burnout would be “wrongly-timed-cortisol-induced-burnout,” because, again, you want your morning cortisol high. I already listed some of the immediate benefits of stimulating cortisol in the hour after waking, but perhaps by now you can also identify another: If you do, you not only get enormous benefits in energy, focus, and mood right away, you also kickstart that crucial negative feedback loop that ensures that your levels of cortisol will be dropping as you head into the afternoon and evening. Your cortisol levels will be very low as you progress into sleep.

That’s how all the pieces come together: In that special window in the first hour after you wake up, when your SCN can also stimulate a significant increase in your cortisol levels, you can bypass the negative feedback loop and stimulate the release of more cortisol even though its levels are already high. In fact, your SCN does so both through the HPA pathway and via a separate, parallel pathway involving direct activation of your sympathetic nervous system.[^c5-28] We can refer to that second pathway as the MLIC pathway (for morning-light-induced-cortisol pathway). And, as the name indicates, the way to activate the MLIC pathway is by viewing bright light.

As a final note, researchers have studied the use of bright artificial light in the first hour of the day not just for this, but as a therapeutic intervention for seasonal affective disorder (SAD), a diagnosable mood disorder characterized by depression that fluctuates with the seasons, worsening in the colder, darker months.[^c5-29] Rates of this condition are particularly high among people who have major depression or bipolar disorder. In one study, people diagnosed with seasonal affective disorder were treated with twenty, forty, or sixty minutes of 10,000 lux light in the morning.[^c5-30] Even the shortest exposure was sufficient to relieve depression among the participants, according to a self-reported questionnaire. Other studies have shown similar results.[^c5-31] Newer studies have shown that reducing the amount of bright light reaching your eyes in the final one to two hours of your day leads to improvements in mood and sleep, and to various mental and physical performance benefits as well.[^c5-32]

In the last ten years, it’s become clear that far more people are suffering from SAD or SAD-like symptoms due to device usage in the early and late hours of the day. In chapter 1, we discussed the severe negative effects of shift work on long-term health, and the fact that nowadays most adults and kids—most (!)—qualify as shift workers due to this kind of device usage. How can that be? Well, remember—even the brightest device screens are too dim to trigger meaningful cortisol increases in the first hour of your day, and even the dimmest screens are more than bright enough to trigger cortisol increases at night. That is, unless you filter out the short wavelengths reaching your eyes—which we talk about in the next protocol.

#### Common Questions

*Does it matter if this light hits my skin or are the eyes all that count here?*

This protocol is concerned with viewing light only. Later protocols in this chapter will address the need for sunlight on skin and how to balance that exposure with cautions about sun damage.

### Light Protocol 2: View Sunlight in the Late Afternoon and/or Early Evening to Help Buffer You Against Negative Effects of Artificial Light at Night

#### What to Do

- **View sunlight in the afternoon and early evening, for five to thirty minutes.** Follow the same general guidelines as for Light Protocol 1. Simply go outside, take off your sunglasses (eyeglasses and contacts are fine), and face in the direction of the setting sun. Don’t wear a brimmed hat. And again, don’t stare at the sun; blink as needed.
- **Do not replace late afternoon/evening sunlight viewing with a 10,000 lux artificial light.** It’s too bright, and the wavelengths these devices emit can mess up your sleep-wake cycle.

#### How It Works

As discussed in Sleep Protocol 2, melatonin, which facilitates falling and staying asleep, begins to increase in the late afternoon and early evening and sharply rises in the hour before your natural bedtime (which, by the way, tends to arrive about fifteen to sixteen hours after your morning sunlight viewing). It continues to rise into the night, before gradually decreasing as morning approaches. Melatonin levels are lowest in the morning and highest at night. In other words, when cortisol is high, melatonin is low, and when cortisol is low, melatonin is high.[^c5-33]

Bright light robustly suppresses melatonin, and it causes the release of cortisol as explained in chapter 3.[^c5-34] Blue lights, screen lights, and LEDs, all of which emit lots of short wavelengths, are especially potent at suppressing melatonin. Bright LEDs, commonly used in bathrooms, bedrooms, and hallways, are short-wavelength enriched. It takes less than thirty seconds of bright LED exposure to the eyes to significantly reduce your melatonin levels. So if you pick up your phone at night, or flip on the lights… you’re exposing yourself to the kind of light that will suppress melatonin. Late afternoon and early evening sunlight viewing helps mitigate these negative effects.

Why do I suggest you not use a 10,000 lux artificial light as a replacement for evening sunlight, when I already suggested it as a replacement for morning sunlight in the previous protocol? The reason has to do with wavelengths, discussed earlier in this chapter. Low solar angle sunlight is lower in UV and the short visible wavelengths, which is why sunrises and sunsets often appear orange, pink, or even deep red. Those longer wavelengths help inform your brain that night is coming, and it should prepare for sleep. Too much short wavelength light—especially if it’s bright, and 10,000 lux is bright—will alter your sleep-wake cycle.

You’ll notice, just as in the previous protocol, that I’m not suggesting specific times to view late afternoon or early evening sunlight. Again, that is because schedules vary from person to person, and the time of day when the sun sets varies according to your location and the time of year. Luckily, you can get the desired effect without being overly precise about the timing. Just aim to view sunlight at some point after the sun is directly overhead and before it sets.

This doesn’t mean that you should avoid sunlight or artificial light during other parts of the day. Researchers from Rush University ran a small study where, for one week, people experienced bright light exposure for up to five hours by combining outdoor exposure to sunlight and indoor exposure to 10,000 lux light during the day.[^c5-35] They called it “the bright week.” The following week, the light exposure was dimmer; people spent two and a half hours outdoors at most, and wore light-obscuring goggles when they did. That was “the dim week.” The researchers found that light-induced melatonin suppression at night was greater during the dim week than during the bright week (though some participants showed greater differences than others). Bright light exposure during the day partially prevented light-induced melatonin suppression at night.

Seems paradoxical, given that light suppresses melatonin, right? Yes, until we look at another mechanism at work here. Another small study from the Netherlands measured melatonin levels, body temperature, and skin blood flow (all markers of circadian rhythmicity) of twelve women and noted how sleepy they reported feeling, according to when they viewed light in the evening and at night.[^c5-36] They divided subjects into three groups. One group viewed dim light at night. Another group also viewed dim light at night but also viewed bright lights beforehand, late in the evening. The third group viewed bright light in the early evening, and then dim lights at night. All three groups saw some reduction in melatonin, which is not surprising given that light viewing suppresses melatonin production any time of day or night. But the third group—the group that saw early evening bright light *plus* late-night dim light—had a less dramatic melatonin drop. This again supports the idea that early evening light exposure can partially inoculate us against the negative effects of bright light at night.

These studies may be small, but they point to the importance of viewing sunlight in the late afternoon and early evening, and avoiding bright light exposure at night. It’s worth noting that it may be especially important for adolescents to avoid bright light at night, as one study showed that early evening sunlight exposure did not protect them against the melatonin-reducing effects of bright light as it did for adults.[^c5-37] This may also mean that adolescents are particularly sensitive to the negative effects of bright artificial lights and screens at night.

The reasons to try to offset the negative effects of bright light at night are not just related to sleep. Animal studies have shown that bright light exposure to the eyes late at night activates pro-depression circuitries.[^c5-38] And as we’ve already covered, human studies have shown strong links between nighttime bright light exposure, cortisol increases, melatonin suppression, and mood disturbances. If you or your child happens to view bright light in the hours before sleep now and again, perhaps from a movie or a night out, that’s no cause for concern. If you make a habit of keeping bright artificial lights on late at night, however, and you notice your moods are shifting for the worse, that could be why.

As you’re probably realizing, modern life—with all its lighting options and screens everywhere—is not oriented around daylight fluctuations in the way it once was. Humans used to wake up and go to sleep with the sun. We had no choice but to be attuned to the solar cycle. The advent of artificial lighting changed everything, and the shift from incandescent to lower cost LED lighting further exacerbated the issues. In fact, in the last ten years, the amount and type of artificial light exposure humans experience has changed so dramatically that we can honestly say that, as a species, our whole relationship to light has been altered. Yet our biology hasn’t changed one bit in thousands of years. Hence this chapter.

#### Common Questions

*How do I make this work if I’m stuck in the office all day?*

There is no need to be obsessive about this—it doesn’t have to interfere with your life. Still, by making some concerted effort toward viewing sunlight (or a 10,000 lux lamp) in the mornings, and sunlight in the late afternoons or early evenings, and avoiding bright light at night, you can dramatically improve your mood and energy levels, metabolism, and sleep—which of course bolsters all the rest. So try to get outdoors at these times if you can. Better yet, take a walk in the direction of the sun. Or even just make time to turn toward the sun and pause (and not look at your phone) for a few minutes in the parking lot before leaving work.

### Light Protocol 3: Avoid Viewing Bright Light One Hour Before Your Bedtime

#### What to Do

- **In the one hour before your bedtime, use only as much artificial light as necessary to safely carry out your nighttime activities.** That recommendation holds until you wake up the next morning to begin your day.
- **Be especially mindful to avoid viewing bright short wavelength light at this time.** Avoid not just lights that appear blue, but also bright “white” LED lights, fluorescent lights, and screens, because they emit a lot of short wavelengths that stimulate cortisol release and inhibit melatonin.
- **If you can’t avoid viewing bright short wavelength light, consider wearing short wavelength light blocking lenses.** Not simply “blue blockers,” but these specific lenses. For anyone seeking an easier transition into sleep and better overall sleep, these glasses can be helpful.

#### How It Works

In the first hour of your day, it takes a lot of bright light to stimulate cortisol release and activate the neural pathways in your brain and body that increase wakefulness. By comparison, in the final hour of your day, it takes very little bright light to wake you up. Moreover, melatonin, the hormone that promotes sleepiness, is potently inhibited by viewing bright light at any time of day or night. That’s why viewing bright light at night is a double whammy to your system: It makes you more alert and it makes you less sleepy by at least two different pathways.

The whole light-sensing and cortisol-releasing system is just not the same in the morning and at night.[^c5-39] If you have ever felt that you are a vastly different person in the morning and at night, indeed you are. The key to using light as a tool to enhance your health is to understand this dynamic.

It all boils down to knowing when you woke up that morning and how many hours it has been since. Here’s a reference you can follow:

- **A Day in the Light**
- **Phase 1:** 0–1 hour after waking: You need to see a lot of bright light (Light Protocol 1).
- **Phase 2:** 6–10 hours after waking: Get some late afternoon or early evening sunlight in your eyes (Light Protocol 2).
- **Phase 3:** 10–14 hours after waking: Start dimming the lights, avoid bright light exposure to your eyes (this protocol).
- **Phase 4:** And finally, sleep…

  Though by now you may be asking (or shouting), “What is all this ‘0–1 hour after waking, 6–10 hours after waking, and 1–2 hours before sleep’ stuff? No one lives this way! Why can’t you just give me a clock time?”

I’ve said this before, and I’ll say it again here: People follow different sleep-wake schedules, with some sleeping from 8:00 p.m. to 4:00 a.m. and others sleeping from 11:00 p.m. to 7:00 a.m. Still others work the night shift. Variation in people’s schedules makes it impossible for me to say, “Dim the lights and avoid viewing LED screens between 10:00 p.m. and 5:00 a.m.” or even “View bright light within an hour of sunrise.”

Also, the length of days varies according to location and time of year, and things like daylight further complicate matters. So I suggest you frame your sleep-wake schedule according to four phases. Once you try this approach to your days, and use light (or avoid it) accordingly, I’m certain it will improve your health and well-being.

It’s worth noting again that the clock times corresponding to the four phases will change if you were to, say, sleep in an extra hour or two, or wake up an hour earlier than is typical, or go to sleep an hour earlier or later. Not a problem! When it comes to the effects of light on cortisol and melatonin, we care about your biology, not an alarm. Start phase 1, for example, when you get up to begin your day. The light prescription for each phase does not change. This ought to bring a sense of control over your time—after all, no one wants to have to take care of their health strictly by the clock. Work, school, and other commitments have us doing that already.

In case any of this is confusing, here is how I use this system to structure my days (and nights).

##### My Phase 1 (as of writing):

I woke up at 7:00 a.m. I usually wake up at 5:45 or 6:00, but I was a bit more tired than usual from a long week of work and travel and I forgot to set my alarm. My sleep tracker told me that I fell asleep last night at about 10:15 p.m. At 7:00 a.m., I went for a walk outside for about twenty minutes, without a hat or sunglasses, and walked east in the direction of the sun. It was light out but overcast, with no hint even of the sun’s outline in the sky. But because it was fairly bright, I knew I was getting a decent amount of sunlight in my eyes, and therefore stimulating cortisol release. I was not at all concerned that I had somehow missed the window to use sunlight to boost my cortisol because my usual wake-up time is about 5:45. I know it’s about getting light in my eyes in the first hour after waking, not at a specific clock time, that matters.

I returned from my walk and, just to be sure that I spiked my morning cortisol sufficiently, I flipped on a 10,000 lux artificial light that I keep in my kitchen and kept it on while I went about my morning activities. Today was my day off from exercise (yesterday was leg day and generally the day after leg day is a day off from exercise for me; see Exercise Protocol 2).

From 8:00 a.m. until 11:00 a.m., I worked (podcast preparation, emails, and calls) at my desk with the overhead indoor lights on their brightest setting, and I sat near a window. I managed to get a few minutes outside during one of my work calls, and I paced while on the call, which allowed me to get a few extra steps in and a bit more sunlight. Around 11:00 a.m., I paused work to eat lunch, and then went back to work at my desk until about 2:00 p.m. On a less busy day, I might have taken my lunch outside.

##### My Phase 2:

Given that I woke up at 7:00 a.m., this phase began six hours later at 1:00 p.m., and sure enough I started to feel a little sleepy around that time. I almost always experience a dip in energy about six hours after I wake up, even after a great night’s sleep. Some people don’t, but I do. I know it correlates, among other things, to the decline in cortisol that is normal, healthy, and expected at this time.

I know better than to push through this dip. I could take a prescription stimulant or slam an energy drink or two at that time, but why? I know there are other tools that won’t mess with my sleep. So from 2:00 to 2:30 I did a non-sleep deep rest (NSDR) session, which I described in chapters 1 and 3, and I emerged from it feeling refreshed. I drank some water and had a half cup of strong coffee and then dove back into work until about 5:00 p.m. (I can drink caffeine up until about 2:00 to 2:30 p.m. with no negative effect on my sleep, but for those more caffeine sensitive, take care.)

##### My Phase 3:

Phase 3 is from ten hours until about fourteen hours after waking, so for today, that meant from 5:00 to 9:00 p.m. I used this time for more work. I also took a brief twenty-minute walk outside, then prepared and ate dinner. Then I started to wind down for the night. I dim the lights in my home to less than full blast starting in phase 3, and I recently started using the medium and long wavelength only setting in the evenings on lights that switch from full spectrum to medium and long wavelength emitting only. (See Sleep Protocol 3 for more on these bulbs.) They appear yellowish-orange rather than white. Several companies such as Bon Charge and Ra Optics now make LED bulbs that switch from full spectrum to medium and long wavelength emitting only (without having to program them for a specific time). You just flick the standard wall-mounted light switch. I love this simple technology because it’s so aligned with what our system needs, and it’s easy to use with no Wi-Fi or an app. And because they are LEDs, they last a very long time and are cost-efficient.

##### My Phase 4:

This phase spans from the period starting fourteen hours after waking until the next morning when the new day starts. Today for me that meant from 9:00 p.m. on. For some time now, I have made it a practice to dim the lights in the final hours before I go to sleep. As I mentioned earlier in this chapter, people vary in their visual sensitivity to light. I am one of those who can be in front of a screen right up until I fall asleep. I have no trouble falling asleep, but it tends to make me wake up three to four hours later. When I started dimming the lights before bedtime, those mid-sleep awakenings all but stopped. I also switched to using long-wavelength-only light bulbs (red light) in the one to two hours before my bedtime. I still might wake up once in the middle of the night to use the bathroom but I have no trouble falling back asleep, and both my device-measured sleep scores and my subjective experience is that I am sleeping much better. If I’m out late or otherwise can’t use my typical indoor lighting in the hours before sleep—such as when I stay in a hotel—I wear ROKA Wind Down glasses that filter out short wavelength light. Often I wear them at home too, as I find they simplify this process.

Take note that phase 4 is where most people make seemingly small mistakes that cost them dearly in terms of health and well-being. There are two main reasons. With the advent of smartphones, and an endless stream of news, content, and the many other hooks that technology offers, it’s very easy to turn to a device. It’s also because most homes and hotels use LED lights nowadays, which emit short wavelengths that disrupt sleep. A bit later in the chapter, I’ll explain how to help with this. In the meantime, here are some ways to make phase 4 much easier and more effective:

- **Keep it low and keep it dim.** I suggest that any lighting you use in the final hours before you go to sleep come from desk lamps or floor lamps, that is, low light sources, and that, if possible, you avoid using overhead lights. The neurons in your eyes that signal to your brain that it is daytime are arranged across your neural retina (the light sensing tissue in the back of your eye) and they view the upper visual field, meaning the sky when you are outside and the ceiling when you are indoors.[^c5-40] Many people find that using low, dim light sources in the one to two hours before bed makes it much easier to fall and stay asleep.[^c5-41] This is pretty easy to do, and can make a big difference.

  You can go further still and use bulbs without short wavelengths, which thus appear yellow-orange, or even go with bulbs that emit purely long wavelengths, and thus appear red. Keep in mind this is not red light therapy. Red light therapy (explained later in this chapter) can be very beneficial for certain aspects of health but is altogether different from what we are discussing here. Medium-wavelength-only bulbs are relatively inexpensive and provide a nice yellow-amber glow. Admittedly, using long-wavelength-only bulbs will make your home look a little space age, but they are a great tool to help you sleep better. Either way, using dim, non-overhead lights without short wavelengths in the last one to two hours before bedtime reduces the activation of the retinal neurons that signal your brain to suppress melatonin and boost cortisol.[^c5-42]

  As mentioned above, several companies have conveniently engineered bulbs that are full-spectrum-emitting (white) for the daytime, and with a simple flick of the light switch, become medium and long wavelength only emitting (yellow-amber or red). Incandescent versions of these exist too and are best, but they use more energy than LEDs, don’t last nearly as long, and are more costly. They are also a bit hard to find.

- **Wear eyeglasses that filter out all short wavelength light.** This approach is very convenient if you don’t want to change the lights in your home, or if you don’t have control over the lighting conditions in a certain environment, such as on planes, in hotels or airports, out with friends, et cetera. I designed the ROKA Wind Down glasses for use during the final hours before sleep, and I use them at home and when I travel. They differ from traditional blue blockers because they prevent all short wavelength light, not just blue light, from reaching your eyes. (Don’t wear them while driving because they make anything that is blue or green much harder to see or even invisible, and that could cause an accident.)
- **Don’t worry about moonlight.** You may be wondering if bright moonlight or even a roaring fire will stimulate the wakefulness pathways in your brain. The answer is, perhaps surprisingly, no. Although these are concentrated light sources, a bright full moon is less than 1 lux and while candles, fireplaces, and bonfires mostly emit medium and short wavelength light, it doesn’t radiate very far. If you have ever been camping and turned around from a roaring campfire, you’ve noticed that as soon as you are just a few paces away from it, you need a flashlight in order to see. We discussed the physics of this in chapter 1. So while fire and candles are great nighttime light sources from a cortisol-limiting and melatonin-preserving perspective, they are not very practical. Of course, if you’d like to read by candlelight or gather around a fire with friends, great. Just make sure the flames are extinguished when you’re finished. Be careful not to start a fire.

  You may be wondering if all this attention to avoiding bright light in the hours before sleep is silly, neurotic biohacking. After all, you can find studies showing that blocking blue light improves people’s sleep to varying degrees,[^c5-43] and you may be one of those people who can pass out with the TV or computer still at full brightness right in front of you. Indeed, there is considerable variation in the degree to which short wavelength light exposure alters people’s sleep.[^c5-44] That said, having even just a dim 100 lux overhead light on while you sleep can alter the next-morning glucose levels.[^c5-45] And that’s while sleeping, with eyes closed. The point is, altered sleep is not the only reason to avoid bright light in phase 4. Nighttime bright light exposure increases blood pressure[^c5-46] and heart rate, and has been linked to weight gain and even a risk of obesity.[^c5-47] Studies have found nighttime bright light to negatively impact next-day cognitive function[^c5-48] and mood[^c5-49] independent of bright light’s negative effects on sleep.

None of this is surprising to biologists who have studied the so-called non-image-forming visual system or the many opsins other than melanopsin that are present in our skin and other tissues for the last three decades.[^c5-50] Myself included. We know, for instance, that the retinal neurons that respond to bright short wavelength light connect not only to your SCN but also to areas of your hypothalamus, such as the supraoptic nucleus, that are directly involved in sleep regulation. (I know, supraoptic sounds like suprachiasmatic but please don’t blame me, I didn’t name either one.) Your eyes also connect to your thalamus’s perihabenular nucleus, which has been nicknamed the anti-reward or disappointment center,[^c5-51] given it actively inhibits dopamine release and is thought to increase feelings of depression when activated at night by, you guessed it, bright light.

The broader field of medicine is starting to incorporate these discoveries. Disrupting the light-dark cycle can affect lifespan. An international team of researchers conducted an enormous study in which 88,905 people enrolled in the UK Biobank, a database for collecting long-term health information, were given wearable light sensors for one week.[^c5-52] The participants wore these wrist sensors for seven days, during which they went about their normal routine. The sensors recorded light exposure around the clock. At the end of the week, the researchers had data on 13 million hours of light exposure.

They grouped all the data according to daytime and night, categorizing participants according to light exposure during the day (between the hours of 7:30 a.m. and 8:30 p.m.) and light exposure during the night (between the hours of 12:30 a.m. and 6:00 a.m.). They then collected health data over a follow-up period of about eight years. For the 3,750 participants who died during the follow-up period, the researchers categorized mortality data according to cause of death.

They found that the brighter the night and the darker the day, the higher the risk of death; the link was dose dependent! The risk of death by any cause was up to 34 percent higher among those who got the most light exposure at night, compared to those with the least light exposure at night. The reverse was also true. The risk of death (by any cause) was up to 34 percent lower among the participants with the most light exposure during the day compared to those with the least. This connection held despite any other traits including age, sex, physical activity, smoking, drinking, and cardiovascular health.

There’s more. The analysis zoomed in on nighttime light exposure, grouping it into half hour increments and matching those increments with mortality data. The brightest lighting between 1:00 a.m. and 6:00 a.m. carried a risk of death by any cause that was 11 to 39 percent higher compared to the darkest lighting during this stretch of time. The risk of death due to cardiometabolic issues (heart attack, stroke, diabetes, nonalcoholic fatty liver disease) was 20 to 67 percent higher for the brightest lighting compared to the darkest lighting during this stretch of the night. The time frame here differs slightly from the one described in this protocol, but the exact times aren’t the point; the point is that viewing bright light at night is disruptive to your immediate and long-term health.

It’s true that this was a relatively brief study, using just a week’s worth of light exposure data. However, about three thousand participants repeated the study up to four times and the light exposure patterns were the same. Several other studies have found similar links.[^c5-53] And the sheer volume of light exposure data in this one makes a persuasive case. As the researchers wrote in the 2024 publication of their study in the *Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences*, “Across the general population, avoiding night light and seeking daylight may lead to reduction in disease burden, especially cardiometabolic diseases, and may increase longevity.”

In another large study, published in *Nature Mental Health* in 2023, researchers at the University of Manchester cross-referenced data on mental health with data on light, sleep, and physical activity from 86,722 individuals.[^c5-54] Their analysis revealed a link between greater nighttime light exposure and higher risk for several mental health issues, including major depressive disorder, anxiety, post-traumatic stress disorder, and self-harm behavior. Greater daytime light exposure correlated with a reduced risk of these issues. They also found that people who experienced darker nights had fewer mental health symptoms, an effect that occurred independent of daytime light exposure. That is, bright-light-filled mornings and days and dark nights independently and additively promoted better mental health.

These large datasets deliver a clear and important message, one that typically goes unmentioned: Keeping the lights off during the late hours of your night is not just about getting great sleep; it is fundamentally important for your health and well-being.

### Light Protocol 4: Expose Your Upper and Lower Body Skin to Sunlight During the Day

#### What to Do

- **Get twenty to thirty minutes of outdoor sunlight exposure to your skin at least three times per week, and ideally every day.** Wear the minimum amount of clothing that allows you to be comfortable and that is appropriate for your environment, without covering your entire body (for example, shirtless with shorts, or shorts and a tank top, or a swimsuit. In some cases, jeans and a short-sleeved T-shirt may be what’s called for). It is best that you do not wear a hat during this time. I discuss cold weather options below.

#### How It Works

There is no substitute for sunlight. You could turn on every light in your home in the morning and daytime, make sure they are full-spectrum incandescent bulbs or wavelength-balanced full spectrum LEDs, view a 10,000 lux artificial light within an hour of waking up, and it still would not replace sunlight.

Each of those technologies can serve as a health-promoting supplement on days when you can’t get enough sunlight, and they can help boost the effects of sunlight, but they should not be used as an everyday replacement for sunlight. Think of them the same way you would supplements relative to nutritious food; they can help bridge deficiencies, and in some cases they can afford you a real mental or physical performance advantage. Yet no rational person would ever replace all their food with supplements on a consistent basis. Alas, because most people don’t understand how powerful light is as a tool for health, and that sunlight is a uniquely beneficial form of it, they engage with light in a way that is analogous to trying to live solely on supplements.

Actually, in many cases it’s even worse than that. People are spending the first hours of their day in sunless, dark, or dim indoor environments, viewing screens, and then continuing their days under artificial lights that seem bright but that are actually dim compared to sunlight. After sundown, they stay under those same lights, which are now far too bright for what is needed at night, and many view mostly short wavelength emitting screens. This is, in no uncertain terms, as bad as living on highly processed junk food. And it’s making a lot of people sick, mentally and physically.

Getting sunlight on our skin is as much a cornerstone of health as sleep, exercise, or nutrition. It’s hard for most people to fully grasp this, especially given that we all have heard how damaging UV light is for our skin. Yet, we need to embrace what is special and beneficial about sunlight and incorporate it into our daily lives. And no, you do not have to live in California, or run around shirtless or in a bathing suit outside. You simply need to know how the energy present in sunlight impacts *every* cell in your body: your brain, hair, skin, liver, heart, your hormones, neurotransmitters, immune system, and on and on.

And so, on to the science.

Sunlight is the absolute best source of long wavelength light, from the red end of the visible spectrum into non-visible near-infrared and IR wavelengths. It is difficult to overstate how important these longer wavelengths are for our health, in particular for our mitochondria, the energy producing organelles within our cells. (I’ll cover the uses of LWL devices that purely emit red, NIR, and IR light in the next protocol.)

Sunlight contains short wavelength UV light, which as we discussed earlier in this chapter, triggers the production of vitamin D in the skin. Although this vitamin (which also acts as a hormone) is available in some foods, supplements can replace sunlight as a stimulus for vitamin D,[^c5-55] yet our bodies evolved to use sun-induced vitamin D in multiple ways that supplements may not mimic.

For example, vitamin D is important for hormone health and the reproductive system. A multi-institution study on mice and humans looked at the effects specifically of UVB (the ultraviolet wavelength that penetrates the skin) on reproductive-related hormones and behavior.[^c5-56] They found that mice exposed to UVB light for one hour per day showed enhanced mating behavior and physiology—greater attraction for one another, larger ovaries, and more testosterone—in both the male and female mice. Moreover, male mice showed a greater attraction to UVB-treated female mice, likely due to how elevated testosterone and estrogen levels in females impacted their appearance and scent, making them more attractive. More interestingly, the researchers saw similar patterns in people. According to their findings, published in *Cell Reports* in 2021, participants reported increased romantic interest in others following time in the sun. The data also showed heightened testosterone levels linked to this exposure in both men and women. Testosterone and estrogen levels—both of which impact romantic desire and feelings of well-being in men and women—were highest in the longer days of spring and summer relative to shorter winter and fall days.

This effect appears to relate to a molecule called p53 expressed in a type of skin cell called keratinocytes. Mice in which p53 had been removed did not exhibit the same changes following UVB exposure. This detail emphasizes the importance of having sunlight reach not only our eyes, but also our skin.

Here’s another: UV light from sunlight also reduces physical pain. In 2017, a group of researchers reported a study in which they exposed mice to UVB (midrange ultraviolet light, abundant in sunlight) radiation and then tested various parameters relating to the HPA axis.[^c5-57] This brain pathway is the core mechanism behind our stress response (as discussed in chapters 1 and 3).[^c5-58] They found a link between UVB radiation and the stimulation of corticotropin-releasing hormone, which helps us cope with social stress,[^c5-59] and endogenous beta endorphins, a type of opioid our body naturally produces in response to psychological distress.[^c5-60] Although this work focused on mice, the results point toward a potentially crucial and unappreciated role for sunlight, in particular UV light—which most people generally think of as the aspect of sunlight to be avoided.

Excessive UV light exposure will cause sunburn and increase your risk for certain forms of skin cancer. So, while UV light from the sun has many benefits, it is still important to avoid too much exposure and sunburn.

##### A Word About Sunscreen

Of course, no one wants a sunburn. One’s risk of sunburn and skin cancer varies depending on factors such as skin tone and inherited susceptibility to skin cancer. All dermatologists agree that any amount of sunburn is bad for us, so bear that in mind. And all agree that excessive exposure to sunlight leads to more rapid aging of the skin too. Excessive skin exposure to UV light, in particular, mutates our skin cell DNA and destroys keratinocytes, which give skin its suppleness. So the takeaway message is to avoid sunburn at all costs.

I don’t burn easily but if I am going to be outside at a time of day when the UV index is high, I either rely on a physical barrier—hat and long sleeves—or I apply a mineral-based sunscreen that uses zinc oxide (not nano zinc) as the only active ingredient. People debate whether chemical-based sunscreens are bad for hormone health and my read of the literature is yes, they can be; but that debate aside, no one argues whether physical barriers or mineral-based-only sunscreen are useful and safe. It’s therefore an obvious choice in my opinion, especially since purely mineral-based sunscreens now come in forms that don’t leave a white paste on your skin, are reef- and ocean life–safe, and aren’t too expensive. I use Le Rub, which is an all-day mineral-based sunscreen that comes in a metal tube. Why is that relevant? Well, I am among a growing number of people who don’t want more microplastics in my body if I can help it. After hosting Shanna Swan, PhD, professor of environmental medicine and public health at Mount Sinai School of Medicine, on my podcast, I did an audit of easy-to-eliminate endocrine disruptors, and I decided to find a non-plastic container, non-endocrine-disrupting sunscreen. Le Rub meets those criteria, smells great, and applies clear, unlike many zinc oxide sunscreens that remain as a white paste on the skin. I liked it so much that I became a partial owner of the company—so I am now very biased, but for the very reason that it’s the only sunscreen I’ll use.

Definitely check the UV index before spending a lot of time in the sun. A simple web search of “What is the UV index at different times today in \[enter city and country\]?” will yield you a result in less than ten seconds. It will tell you when to be careful about excess UV exposure.

But don’t avoid the sun entirely! Getting sun exposure on your skin not only supports various hormone production pathways as described here, it may also help you live longer. A Swedish study looking at mortality rates among 29,518 women found that greater sun exposure correlated with lower all-cause risk of death.[^c5-61] In fact, people who spent the least amount of time in the sun had nearly double the mortality risk during the twenty years of the study compared to those who spent the most time in the sun. Obviously, there are likely to be many factors at play here: More time outside usually means more fresh air, movement, social interaction, et cetera, not just sunlight. Yet the data correlating different amounts of sunlight exposure to health and longevity all seem to point in the same direction: Getting sunlight on your skin is beneficial. Interestingly, that work followed an earlier study of nearly forty thousand women that found a reduction in mortality linked to exposure to ultraviolet light coming directly from the sun, and yet an increase in mortality linked to ultraviolet light from artificial sources.[^c5-62]

Why would UV light from sunlight help and yet the (seemingly) same UV light from artificial sources harm us? One idea is that because sunlight has a balance of short, medium, and long wavelengths—each at particular energies and with their own unique health-promoting effects—they synergize. UV without adequate longer wavelengths—such as what comes from most LEDs—is thought to be detrimental to our cells.[^c5-63]

I’ll dive more into the ways that different wavelengths of light impact our cells in the next protocol, but for now here are some crucial things to know: No single wavelength of light is “bad” or “good.” Longer wavelengths of light are absorbed by the water in our mitochondria and help “charge” the mitochondria like batteries, making them more efficient at producing ATP[^c5-64] and possibly even helping cells to make more mitochondria. Longer wavelength light also helps offset the negative effects of reactive oxygen species (ROS)—a normal by-product of cellular function that, if in excess, damages our cells.[^c5-65] ROS are thought to be a major factor in the reduced energy levels and organ dysfunction we experience with aging.[^c5-66] Long wavelength light can pass through our skin, eyelids, our ribs, and even our skull to reach our brain and other internal organs, and so helps to promote their health, largely by improving mitochondrial function as described above.[^c5-67] How wild is that?! Sunlight also contains abundant amounts of medium wavelength light—yellows and oranges, or in technical terms about 500 to 620 nanometer light, which has been shown to reduce headache pain, stimulate blood flow, and reduce inflammation.[^c5-68]

Artificial lights of course contain some of these wavelengths but not in the same balance as is present in sunlight. Incandescent bulbs are better than LEDs in this respect, but nowadays LEDs and fluorescent lights are almost exclusively used for indoor lighting because they cost less, use less energy, and last longer. Most LEDs are enriched with short wavelengths which, unless balanced out by long wavelength light, have been shown to increase ROS and damage mitochondria.[^c5-69] Some LEDs and fluorescent lights even emit small amounts of UV.[^c5-70] This all becomes a problem for cellular health when we are under these lights all day and not getting the protective effects of long wavelength light or enough sunlight. It’s rather incredible that while so many people are afraid of UV from sunlight, they may be unaware how the many hours of daily (and nightly) exposure to short wavelength light can damage our health. The remedy: balanced wavelength exposure from sunlight, done safely of course. The protocols in this chapter represent the key times and ways to do just that. The other remedy: incandescent rather than LED indoor lighting, and limiting your short wavelength light exposure after nightfall.

Still not convinced that light is medicine? I mentioned above how researchers found that UV light from sunlight reduces physical pain, and there are studies of humans experiencing similar effects. In a study of eighty-nine patients who’d undergone spinal surgery, those who stayed on the bright side of the hospital, and were therefore exposed to 46 percent more intense sunlight than those staying on the dim side of the hospital, reported less pain-related stress and a bit less pain, and required 22 percent less pain medication.[^c5-71] Similar results have been reported in the relief of fibromyalgia among women[^c5-72] and in a small study of US military veterans, chronic lower back pain.[^c5-73] Preliminary research indicates that the underlying mechanism here brings us back to the intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cells, which don’t just connect to the SCN but also communicate light information (through a relay station) to the periaqueductal gray area, a region that is crucial to pain modulation.[^c5-74]

And, as discussed in other protocols in this chapter, regular, consistent light exposure also enhances mood.[^c5-75] Data suggest that individuals exposed to moderate amounts of UVB—which is abundant in sunlight—may have a lower risk for depression.[^c5-76] A review of seven different studies evaluating the link between ultraviolet radiation and mood concluded that the evidence supports this beneficial connection.[^c5-77]

The simple takeaway here is this: Get some sunlight on your skin for at least thirty minutes per day, as many days per week as possible. How much skin you can directly expose will of course vary by weather, location, and circumstances, but do it. Check the UV index and learn what you need without getting a sunburn. Don’t get a sunburn. And while sunlight through a window is not the same as going outside, if you can make your indoor environment brighter from sunlight, do it. Otherwise, think seriously about how much conventional LED light exposure you’re getting and, if it’s a lot, consider switching to full spectrum LED lights. And given the direct and protective benefits of long wavelength light, consider the next protocol.

#### Common Questions

*What if I live in a dark, gloomy place or it’s a dark, gloomy time of year, as it is in much of the UK, Scandinavia, or the Pacific Northwest, especially during the winter?* I’ve mentioned this elsewhere in this chapter, but time outside is still essential. Even on a cold, cloud-covered day, you’ll get more light exposure outside than from an indoor artificial light source. Cold days make people less inclined to be outside in shorts and short sleeves, and that is okay—but avoid the brimmed hat then so you can get more sun on your face and in your eyes. And if you can’t get outside into direct sun, do what you can. Sometimes you can only get time out on a covered balcony. Every little bit counts. It’s like getting your daily steps in. You need your daily light exposure too.

As a final note on this: If you live in a region where you just can’t get much sunlight exposure to your skin for many days of the year, you would be very wise to get a 10,000 lux artificial light (any brand will do), and a red and IR incandescent light. You might also use bulbs in your lighting fixtures that switch from bright, balanced full spectrum to medium and long wavelengths only simply by using the light switch.

### Light Protocol 5: Expose Your Skin and Eyes to Long Wavelength Light (Red, Near-IR, and Infrared)

#### What to Do

- **Use a long-wavelength-light-emitting (LWL) device for ten to thirty minutes, three to seven days per week.** For general health effects (energy, skin appearance, exercise recovery, etc.), the goal is to illuminate the largest area of your skin, face, and head that you can. This will obviously depend on what LWL device you have access to and the amount of time you can devote to this.

#### How It Works

Red light therapy has become a popular health trend. Red light saunas, red light panels, red light beds, masks, even red-light helmets to promote hair growth… the list goes on. Despite their space age look, this is a trend with genuine scientific support behind it. Several leading dermatology journals including *JAMA Dermatology* have published in-depth reviews on the use of red light to treat different skin conditions,[^c5-78] and other fields of medicine including ophthalmology are following suit by exploring how red light can be used to offset, or even reverse, age-related decline in organ function. Most of these devices also emit near-infrared (NIR) and/or infrared (IR) light as well. For simplicity and accuracy, I will refer to all such devices collectively as LWL devices. Of course, the exact wavelengths and intensities of light that different LWL devices emit vary. Some also emit short wavelength light. I’ll touch on some of the different features to look for when considering use of different photobiomodulation devices at the end of this protocol.

First, let’s discuss what photobiomodulation is really about. In the context of light, photobiomodulation involves exposing a portion (or all) of your skin to a specific range of wavelengths, typically long wavelength light, for ten, twenty, or thirty minutes, three to seven days per week. As I mentioned above, for general health effects the goal is to illuminate the largest area of your skin, face, and head that you can. Smaller handheld LWL devices that illuminate a limited area can be helpful for pain reduction and to promote wound healing in specific areas,[^c5-79] but the most impressive effects of long wavelength light photobiomodulation are generally achieved with whole-body long-wavelength light exposure using a large LWL panel, or a red light bed or LWL blanket, and by illuminating both sides of your body, either simultaneously or sequentially.

Long wavelength light can penetrate the skin’s surface and once inside your body, it can scatter up to 8 centimeters.[^c5-80] Longer wavelengths in the infrared range have been shown to even pass through thin clothing such as T-shirts and through your torso.[^c5-81] That might sound scary but remember that long wavelength light is low energy non-ionizing radiation, so it is safe, and all evidence points to long wavelength light having a protective and a health-promoting effect on your cells. Put simply, exposing your skin to long wavelength light in this way is a good thing. The main reason? It promotes mitochondrial health.

*Mitochondrial health* is a term used often these days, so before going any further, let’s further define what this means. As discussed several times already in this book, cellular energy is generated in the form of a chemical called adenosine triphosphate, or ATP. Mitochondria are crucial for ATP production, as well as for making our hormones and neurotransmitters. Mitochondria contain an enzyme called cytochrome c oxidase, and it can absorb light.[^c5-82] In that way, cytochrome c oxidase is similar to the photopigments in your eye that absorb specific wavelengths of light, and that kick off the cascade of events in your eyes and brain that lead to sight. The difference is that cytochrome c oxidase is inside the cells of your body and brain, and its job is to support the formation of ATP for your cells to use. The way it does that is by moving electrons from one protein to the next inside the mitochondria. (Briefly: Like any compound, proteins are made of molecules; molecules are made of atoms bonded together; atoms are made of subatomic particles including protons, which are positively charged, electrons, which are negatively charged, and neutrons, which carry no charge.) That process releases energy that moves protons, also in the mitochondria, and because protons carry an electrical charge, it sort of works like a battery.

The business of moving protons in mitochondria isn’t just about making energy; it takes energy too. The first law of thermodynamics is that energy can’t be created or destroyed, it can only be transformed. Long wavelength light energy from the sun that is absorbed by cytochrome c oxidase is transformed by your mitochondria to help create ATP. So, in a loose sense, we are solar powered.

The absorption of long wavelength light by cytochrome c oxidase also causes nitric oxide—a chemical that can impair mitochondrial function—to dislodge from the organelle, which then allows cytochrome c oxidase to use oxygen more efficiently. That enhances something called mitochondrial respiration, a process critical for converting nutrients in our blood into ATP.[^c5-83] Bam! Long wavelength light can enhance cellular ATP production through at least two proposed mechanisms.

Long wavelength light also may support mitochondrial energy production through a third mechanism involving the increased action of intracellular melatonin, which can help prevent oxidative damage.[^c5-84] Until now we have discussed melatonin only as a hormone produced by the pineal gland that promotes sleepiness. However, many cells throughout our body produce melatonin. Long wavelength light may allow intracellular melatonin to act more effectively as an antioxidant, helping to repair some of the oxidative damage that is a normal consequence of cellular metabolism. One potential benefit of this pathway is that it may reduce some of the harm caused by excessive UV light exposure.[^c5-85] As we discuss next, the implications of that are, literally, visible.

##### How It Affects Your Skin

Long wavelength light can promote the youthful look of skin, reduce acne, and accelerate wound healing.[^c5-86] Studies have also investigated long wavelength light as a tool to treat wrinkles, scars, burns, and other causes of discoloration of the skin.

In one study of ninety-three patients, administration of rapid pulses of 590- nanometer light was linked to reduced signs of aging.[^c5-87] In another study by the same research group, ninety patients were given pulses of 590-nanometer light in eight treatments over four weeks.[^c5-88] The investigators took digital images of the patients at the start of the study and over the following twelve months and found reduced signs of aging in the vast majority of participants. They also evaluated tissue samples from ten of the patients and found increased collagen, a protein that provides structure and elasticity to skin, in all the subjects who received this therapy. The wavelength measuring 590 nanometers is in the orange-red range of the visible spectrum and, as noted above, longer wavelengths (600–850 nm) can pass even deeper into the skin layers. Indeed, investigations found even more impressive reductions in wrinkles following treatment with 633-nanometer (red) light combined with 830-nanometer light, which falls in the near-infrared range.[^c5-89]

There also are benefits to combining long wavelength light with short wavelength light, at least for improving skin. Dermatologists at Mount Sinai Medical Center, in New York, treated twenty-two people with mild to moderate acne with eight sessions of light therapy that used alternating exposure to blue (short wavelength) and red (long wavelength) light, for twenty minutes per exposure.[^c5-90] Four weeks after the treatment ended, participants showed a 46 percent reduction in acne lesions. At eight weeks post-treatment, the reduction had reached 81 percent. A study from Imperial College of Science, Technology, and Medicine, in London, with 107 patients, reported similar outcomes.[^c5-91] That is pretty remarkable if you ask me.

##### How It Affects Your Metabolism

There’s another impressive effect of long wavelength light therapy. Exposing your skin to long wavelength light can reduce your glucose levels, and increase your metabolism. It seems unlikely, but it turns out to be true. All we have to do is look at the data. In a recent study, researchers shined a 670-nanometer light on subjects’ backs for fifteen minutes and measured their glucose levels in response to ingestion of a sugary drink—a classic research method to measure blood sugar regulation.[^c5-92] They observed a 27.7 percent reduction in glucose in comparison to control subjects that did not receive the light exposure. Measurements of oxygen uptake confirmed that their metabolism had risen significantly, which makes sense given that long wavelength light exposure can increase ATP production by as much as 100 to 200 percent.

I heard some people interpreting this study as meaning that eating under short-wavelength-only light sources like conventional LED lights lowers your metabolism, even going so far as to argue that obesity is on the rise because of short wavelength light overuse. While that *might* be the case, that is not what this study shows. It is reasonable, however, to conclude on the basis of this study that eating outside in the sunlight or even in the shade on a sunny day where long wavelength light is abundant, or eating near a LWL device, may be beneficial for those seeking to improve their blood sugar regulation. Getting exercise and proper nutrition per the recommendations in chapters 2 and 4 are the major factors for healthy blood sugar regulation. Nevertheless, long wavelength light can certainly be used to augment proper exercise and nutrition, and it may be a particularly useful tool for regulating blood sugar and metabolism when exercise is restricted due to injury, weather, travel, and the like.

##### How It Affects Your Eyesight

The effects go on. Long wavelength light has been helpful in preserving eye health too. First, a little bit about your eyes: The photoreceptor cells in your eyes consume more energy than any other cell in your brain or body.[^c5-93] Think about that for a second: more than any other cell, meaning more than all the rest of your brain cells, your liver, even your muscle cells… and that is true even if you were to run a marathon and use those muscle cells, every single day! Your photoreceptors are almost always active, even in the dark. The point is your photoreceptors produce and use a ton of energy around the clock. The energy they draw on comes in the form of ATP, and ATP production, as you now know, depends on mitochondria. Not surprisingly, your photoreceptors are packed with mitochondria[^c5-94] and they produce a ton of ATP, but with all that ATP production comes a high amount of free radicals, and as I mentioned earlier in this protocol, those impose stress on the cells, which over time damages the mitochondria. Exposure of the eyes to long wavelength light—the red, near-infrared, and infrared end of the spectrum—both reduces the presence of free radicals[^c5-95] and helps stimulate the production of ATP by the mechanisms discussed above. So it makes sense that long wavelength light therapy might have a role in preserving or improving our photoreceptors… and therefore, our vision.

And indeed, that’s what the data show. Work by neuroscientist Glen Jeffery (mentioned at the start of this chapter) investigated whether direct viewing of long wavelength light could improve people’s vision. In one study, he and his team enrolled twenty-four people between the ages of twenty-eight and seventy-two to look at a 670-nanometer beam (red light) from a flashlight for three minutes per day for two weeks.[^c5-96] Participants under the age of forty showed no change in vision. But those around forty years and older showed a greater ability to discern colors at the end of the experiment. In a second study, the investigators used the same intervention but at a less intense level, meaning the light was not as close to the participants’ eyes (though it was still 670 nanometers, or red light) and found that to be sufficient to boost vision for one week, again among those about forty years old and over.[^c5-97] The improvement in vision in these studies reached 20 percent among some participants, which is a significant and compelling result. The researchers also observed a reduction in drusen, which are fat deposits that accumulate in the eyes as we age[^c5-98] and that are connected to age-related macular degeneration.

Importantly, the second study by Jeffery and colleagues found that the timing of the long wavelength light therapy mattered. The benefit to vision occurred only if the red light was seen in the morning, likely because mitochondrial function changes across the twenty-four-hour cycle, with a particular sensitivity to light then. It is worth noting that the range of benefit was wide; some individuals experienced a greater boost than others. The underlying reasons of who benefits and who doesn’t are not yet clear. Studies ongoing in Glen Jeffery’s lab are now focused on the use of long wavelength light therapy for advanced macular degeneration, retinitis pigmentosa, and glaucoma.

To be clear: The most common causes of vision loss—cataracts, glaucoma, macular degeneration, and diabetes[^c5-99]—are unlikely to be caused by lack of long wavelength light exposure, although that possibility hasn’t been ruled out either. All these forms of vision loss are typically associated with aging, and some forms have a clear genetic contribution as well. Everyone should get an annual eye exam and get their eye pressures checked for glaucoma once a year. Do not rely on this protocol as the only way to treat or prevent these conditions. That said, the ability for long wavelength light to slow, halt, or reverse vision loss is gaining more and more support.

Along those lines, you might be wondering how exactly to adopt this protocol. Turns out it’s very easy: Expose your face to long wavelength light from a concentrated red light source (not laser!) for five to ten minutes once or twice per week, and do it within three hours of waking. You don’t need to put the light source terribly close to your eyes either; it’s best you do it at a distance that is comfortable and doesn’t force you to close your eyes. However, in this and other long wavelength light protocols, you are welcome to close your eyes. It won’t hinder the effect unless you wear dark occluding glasses—the ones that make it look like you’re going into a tanning bed (which is UV by the way; I do not recommend those for reasons that ought to be obvious by now). Long wavelength light easily passes through your eyelids to reach your photoreceptors. You can get enough retinal long wavelength light exposure as a consequence of whole body long wavelength light illumination too. There is no evidence that more frequent or longer exposures than five to ten minutes once or twice per week are needed for the visual system benefits, but also no evidence that more would be harmful. Remember, the effects were only observed in people forty and older and only if it was done within one to three hours of waking.

##### Sources to Consider

You have a lot of options when it comes to long wavelength light sources for photobiomodulation—for this use, and others. I will discuss these in order from the least to the most costly.

##### Option 1: The sun.

The sun is rich with long wavelength light and it’s zero cost, but you get less long wavelength light exposure on overcast days and for most, it’s not practical to expose your whole body to it for ten to thirty minutes, three to seven days per week. And while UV light is less of an issue when the sun is low in the sky around sunrise and sunset, for people who miss those windows of opportunity, you will need to take measures to avoid getting excessive UV exposure. As mentioned above, check the UV index for your location. Of course, never, ever, force yourself to stare at the sun. Blink as needed to protect your eyes. The reflex to do so is the guide to follow. Or close your eyes; remember, long wavelength light radiation will reach your eyes just fine through your eyelids as long as you’re not wearing sunglasses. It’s fine to wear corrective lens eyeglasses or contacts for the reasons discussed in chapter 1.

##### Option 2: A LWL device.

There are tons of options out there on the market now, and they vary a lot by cost. It’s a bit overwhelming. You’ll often see claims from companies that their LWL device is best because it has “more power” than others on the market, but that’s a bit misleading. Differences in the intensity of devices are negligible when you consider that just getting closer to a device and/or extending the duration that you use it can compensate for most differences in intensity. Which you decide to use will likely be dictated by your budget and access. Small handheld units the size of a sandwich can cost $500, some full body panels $10,000 to $12,000, and the LWL “red light beds” and capsules can cost from $25,000 to more than $100,000. (Sunshine when the UV is low may be sounding pretty good right now.)

Some people like LWL face masks or helmets for skin or hair, respectively. A review of the research on a phototherapy mask, published in the *Journal of Clinical and Aesthetic Dermatology* in 2018, concluded that this light therapy device was effective for treating acne and psoriasis, healing wounds, and reducing actinic keratosis, rough and scaly skin that can result from years of sun exposure.[^c5-100] This study was not funded by the device manufacturer, but it was authored by the head of a private dermatology research institute rather than an academic laboratory research group. That said, there is no reason to think the results with a mask would be any different from the results with a light panel, except that the light is hitting a smaller area of skin. I think the panels are the most versatile as you can expose whatever body areas you want but obviously cost compare and decide for yourself.

After deciding what is affordable for you, the most important factor in selecting a LWL device is that it exclusively emits long wavelength light of about 600 nm or longer. (We don’t see infrared light, which is why these are often called red light devices.) Generally speaking, the broader the range of long wavelengths that a device emits, the better the results. In other words, the most effective devices emit red, near-IR, and IR (600–850+ nm) light. The Jeffery lab studies used red light at wavelengths of about 600 to 670 nanometers to produce the visual system benefits, while light at wavelengths of 850 nanometers and above penetrated into and through the body—which again, is a good thing. As another rule, LWL devices that feel warm to the skin at the distance you use them are going to be more effective, because that encourages more blood flow and lymphatic flow, and in doing so helps improve the anti-inflammation effects of long wavelength light. Some LWL devices also include non-UV short wavelength light, which can be helpful for pain relief.

Most LWL devices use LEDs, but a few use incandescent bulbs. Lasers, which deliver a focused ray of light, tend to be higher in intensity—and they are brighter. I don’t recommend these for home use. Low-level laser therapy (LLLT) is a medical intervention and anyone using it to address aging or skin issues that are often treated with topical creams or other prescription interventions, such as wounds, acne, or other chronic skin conditions, should consult with a physician to ensure this approach is safe for you.

As mentioned above, I strive to take brief walks outside throughout the day just before or after meals, and pace outside when on work calls, if I can. Obviously I wear clothing during these times, but even with most skin covered, I’m sure to get some long wavelength light exposure, especially on clear days. I also use a JOOVV LWL panel for ten to thirty minutes once a day, generally three to five days per week. The JOOVV panels are medical grade and emit red and IR light; note they are a *Huberman Lab* podcast sponsor. I also really like the LWL incandescent bulbs from SaunaSpace as they generate heat, and emit 600 to 1,000 nanometer light. They make actual red light saunas too using those same bulbs; they look like a small canvas tent with a large-bulb long wavelength light–incandescent panel inside, and they are terrific because they too generate a lot of heat—which is what you want for a sauna session—and have all the features of long wavelength light photobiomodulation.

I confess I am not a fan of most other long wavelength light, or red light, saunas that use LEDs because they generally don’t get hot enough to trigger the benefits of dry or wet traditional saunas.[^c5-101] Dry heat saunas can have great benefits for cardiovascular health, for growth hormone production, and for enhancing red blood cell production leading to endurance performance enhancement, but those effects are generally seen using temperatures ranging from roughly 180 to 210 degrees Fahrenheit. Most red light saunas just don’t get hot enough to create those benefits. Rather than view any one LWL device as “the best,” consider what you are able to access and afford, and use that. And remember the best and least expensive long wavelength light emitting source: good ol’ sunlight.

## Chapter 6: Protocols for Focus, Motivation, and Learning

![Chapter emblem](images/chapter-emblem.jpeg)

Our ability to get and stay motivated, to focus, and to learn new things is at the heart of what it is to be successful in life. Not just in school and work, but in creative endeavors and athletics. Consider the effort it takes to study for a big test or remember the material needed for a big presentation, or even stick with a new approach to a painting or new musical instrument practice, or try to respond to a social situation in a new way.

The question then becomes, “How?” How can we get motivated when our energy or natural impulses pull us toward apathy, overthinking, or procrastination? How can we tap into heightened focus, on demand? How can we learn faster and more effectively?

It turns out these are states of mind and body that we can learn to deliberately access.

My second year of college is when I first started to discover this. I learned that motivation can happen automatically as the consequence of, say, being excited or intrigued by something but it can also be deliberately fostered.

As I mentioned a bit in the introduction, I went from being a good student in my early life to falling behind my peers in high school. I touched on why that happened, but I make no excuses. Those were ultimately my own choices and actions. And those challenges both in and out of school, and watching my peers face those challenges too—seeing some soar and thrive while others struggled—would all become a blessing in many ways. It forced me to realize that no one was coming to save me and that I had to change things on my own. That realization scared me, but it’s what motivated me to turn my life around. I never quite had the exact words for what went through my head at that moment until recently, when a very wise friend and mentor said something and I thought, “THAT! That’s what I was hearing in my head! THAT!”

I can’t say I came up with it, but it’s something that I have heard in my head in fragments, over and over since I was nineteen. I still remind myself of it every day:

*Losers take the negative things that happen to them and the feelings that come from things that suck… and they wallow and they use it for self- or outward destruction.*

*Winners however take whatever they feel—even if it sucks—and they transmute those feelings into actions that are good for themselves and for the world.*

I chose to do something. And through that choice, I learned that while motivation can result in action, it’s possible for action to result in motivation too.

As a sophomore in college, I decided to study as if my life depended on it. I didn’t care if I liked the subject. I decided it made no difference, that eventually I would find the right path if I kept moving forward but I was going to move forward no matter what. Sure enough, my motivation to learn grew more and more, and morphed into a desire to get a PhD in a topic I fell in love with, to run a lab, to teach, and to build a career in science. Somewhere early along the way that fear I described dissipated. My love of certain topics and lab skills grew, but it often came *after* I had forced myself to learn them. Sure, sometimes it was there prior—I’ve always had a love for biology for example—but often it was only after I immersed myself in a subject that I truly fell in love with it. The hardest courses I took in college turned out to be the ones I loved the most, and years later those subjects would be among the major focuses of my lab. The most useful thing I learned back then was that I realized that I could access the state of urgency that we call motivation whether I loved something or not. Reason and persistence, not excitement, anchored my effort.

And the act of being able to access a state of motivation gave me confidence to tackle what I wanted to go after or what was placed in front of me. I wasn’t a grade-chasing automaton; I had a sense of agency over my life and that kept me going.

Just as my motivation grew, so too did my ability to focus and learn. At first, I had to take drastic measures to force myself to do both. While studying biology in university, I would set a timer for several hours and force myself to study without breaks until the timer went off. Having been so checked out in high school, I had a lot of catching up to do. This was extremely difficult at first. Long bouts of studying required a level of focus I did not have back then. But over time, my ability to focus got better—and kept getting better.

I later came to discover that the early stages of focus and learning are supposed to include agitation. That feeling comes from the shift in your brain and body’s neurochemical milieu that sets the stage for learning to take place. You are asking your brain to change, and your brain doesn’t want to change. Changing is very energetically demanding for brains. This uncomfortable feeling is something I often refer to as “limbic friction.” It’s not an official scientific term, but it refers to a state of elevated autonomic arousal where you’re funneling into focus, and it takes constant or near-constant effort to get there and stay there. It’s a mental edge of sorts. Once I understood that this limbic friction was not only normal, but essential, focus and learning became easier. I started seeking it out. And it felt good. I share this backstory simply to help illustrate that motivation, focus, and learning are states of mind and body. They have neural and hormonal underpinnings, much in the same way that REM sleep has its neural and hormonal underpinnings, as does stress, and so on. And that’s good news, because it makes what might otherwise be nebulous, clear. We know what to aim for.

This is a physiology-first approach to focus, motivation, and learning. It’s rooted in how we work, which is why the approach works.

In this chapter you’ll learn how to enhance your ability to focus by leveraging that. You’ll also learn a powerful tool for “getting motivated” that is unlike all others you’ve likely seen before. And you’ll finally get the truth about neuroplasticity—the rewiring of neural circuits that underlies all forms of learning (and forgetting), and that is often referred to simply as *plasticity*. Most everyone has heard of plasticity but honestly, most of the ways I’ve seen it discussed publicly are flat-out wrong.

Perhaps you’ve heard that “Every experience you have changes your brain.” That is not true. Or “It takes twenty-one days to form a new habit.” Wrong again. It can take a few days or a year, based on your level of motivation. Perhaps you’ve heard that “Your brain makes new neurons for your entire life.” (The official term for that is neurogenesis.) Alas, barely any new neurons are added to the brain after puberty except for in your olfactory system, which allows you to smell, and those are mostly to replace neurons you’ve lost. Starting to get depressed? Well don’t, because despite these myths, we all possess a tremendous ability to rewire our brains and to learn at any age.

The key is to understand the *type* of plasticity you’re after. What we’re talking about here—the rewiring of our brains that occurs as part of learning at any age—is a process that involves *a specific set of steps that must be completed in a specific sequence for learning to occur*.

I call these steps self-directed adaptive plasticity (SDAP). Mastering these steps opens the doors to learning pretty much anything you set your mind to. And that’s what this chapter is about.

> **The Steps and Sequence of SDAP**
>
> Let’s start with an overview of how SDAP occurs:
>
> - **Get alert.**
>
>   SDAP requires you to focus on the material at hand. Alertness sets the stage for focus; it’s a precursor. I’ll explain all this in the pages ahead.
>
>   So get alert and…
>
> - **Get and stay focused.**
>
>   Focused on what? On implementing a specific strategy during your learning bout.
>
>   As you go…
>
> - **Maintain a state of urgency.**
>
