>   Your internal state really matters as you learn. You can’t be too relaxed, but you can’t be stressed either. I define a state of urgency as simply a state of persistent motivation. It’s the state to aim for because it has you stay alert but not too alert and…
>
> - **Embrace errors.**
>
>   Errors that arise from genuine attempts to do something are key signals for triggering plasticity. Your nervous system is stimulated to rewire largely based on what you fail to do, not what you do correctly.
>
> - **Rest.**
>
>   Sleep is when neural rewiring actually occurs, especially during REM sleep the first night after a learning bout. There are other ways you can incorporate rest—like non-sleep deep rest (NSDR) and short breaks—to improve performance.
>
> - **Repeat.**
>
>   Consolidate newly learned material or skills through repeat performance, either through physical repetition or taking yourself through the material or skill using your imagination (seriously). Mental self-testing is especially effective for reinforcing newly formed brain connections.
>
>   Each of these six steps is valuable in its own right, and can be applied to various areas of life. Thus, although this chapter is framed in the context of plasticity, each of the protocols has other important applications too. I’ll explain more as we go.

### Types of Neuroplasticity

Before we explore each step of SDAP, let’s get clear on what we’re talking about when we talk about plasticity.

All sustained behavioral and cognitive change is the result of plasticity. These changes come in two broad types: adaptive and maladaptive. Adaptive changes are desirable—this is the plasticity that accompanies learning a new language or a new artistic or athletic skill. Maladaptive changes are the ones that make life harder. Consider when a brain injury renders someone unable to produce coherent speech, or a traumatic event leaves someone stricken with PTSD. That’s still plasticity but obviously not the sort you want.

These two types of plasticity happen in different ways. Maladaptive plasticity, as in the brain injury I described above, tends to occur fast and is hard to undo. Adaptive plasticity, like learning that new language, takes more effort, and reverts somewhat easily, at least at first. I realize that’s not convenient but the sooner we accept that reality, the further along we can all be in our efforts to learn new things.

Understanding why and how maladaptive brain changes occur will help illustrate how to get the adaptive brain changes that you want, and make them happen more quickly. Psychologically traumatic events trigger astonishingly fast and stable changes to nervous system wiring.[^c6-1] This rewiring happens not just in the brain but in the patterns of brain-to-body and body-to-brain connections, and hormone-control pathways.[^c6-2] The duration of a traumatic event can be very brief—no more than a few seconds—yet bring about persistent or recurring anxiety, sleep disturbances, and physical challenges, like chronic pain,[^c6-3] rashes,[^c6-4] gut issues,[^c6-5] and more, that last for years.

This is essentially *one trial learning*. Something happens and we are (seemingly) forever changed. The evolutionary logic is straightforward: One trial learning from traumatic events helps ensure we avoid similar circumstances in the future. It keeps us safe.

How one trial learning happens brings us back to an analogy discussed in chapter 3. Remember the autonomic seesaw? A stress-inducing event or thought causes your autonomic nervous system to increase your sympathetic tone, which makes you alert. That sharpens your focus. If sympathetic tone is too high, however, it feels like anxiety or panic.

When we experience a traumatic event, our brains quickly trigger the release of a lot of adrenaline into our bodies and a lot of norepinephrine in our brains.[^c6-6] Together, these two neuromodulators create all the necessary conditions for plasticity to occur. We’re not talking about a bit of normal life stress. We’re talking about something you perceive as really scary that causes a large and rapid shift in the neurochemical milieu of the body and brain. This shift during a traumatic event may sound like a good thing, because it helps you move away from the person or thing stressing you out, but in the long run many times it’s not. If the stress response is too big, it triggers the rapid modification of multiple brain circuitries all at once and can result in an unhealthily low stress threshold going forward.[^c6-7] In some cases, one’s stress threshold becomes set so low that anxiety and panic arise from innocuous events of everyday life. Undoing the kind of rewiring that results from traumatic events takes dedicated effort. Fortunately, it is possible. I discuss one way to do that in the next chapter.

The conditions experienced during this kind of one-trial learning are also at play in SDAP. “Uh-oh,” you may be thinking, “is he going to suggest that I get stressed out to learn?” No. In fact, if you’re too stressed, and your sympathetic tone is too elevated, you won’t be able to focus, and you absolutely need to focus in order to learn. But you do need to be alert. My point here is that a shift in neurochemical milieu is crucial to achieving that state—alert but calm. Not stressed.

### Conditions for Neuroplasticity

SDAP is all about desired forms of learning: a new musical instrument, a new language, a new physical skill, a new healthy habit, et cetera. For SDAP to occur, you must focus intensely on what you are trying to learn. To focus intensely on what you are trying to learn, you have to be alert. And to be alert, your autonomic nervous system has to be in a somewhat sympathetic-dominant state.

That seesaw shift in the nervous system signals to the relevant circuits in your brain and body that what is happening is unique and important, and that they need to change to become better equipped for similar circumstances in the future. Another useful way to think about it is that your brain must get the message that there is a gap between its current configuration and the demands you’re facing—a deficit of sorts that it needs to overcome. The deficit is resolved by making new brain connections.

Now of course your neurons don’t talk to each other in words. They don’t say, “This is important, and we have a deficit between where we’re at and where we need to be, so we need to change.” Neurons communicate in the language of chemicals and electricity. So this message is communicated electrochemically, as a shift in your brain and body’s neurochemical milieu that in turn alters the amount of firing in the brain circuits that need to change for the desired learning to occur. And when it comes to shifting neurochemical milieus—that is largely the job of neuromodulators.

The neuromodulators dopamine, serotonin, adrenaline, norepinephrine, and acetylcholine each serve different purposes, depending on where they are released in your brain or body.[^c6-8] It’s incorrect to say that dopamine alone drives motivation, for instance, or that serotonin controls mood. It’s far more varied and nuanced than that. In terms of plasticity, all these neuromodulators can alter the level of electrochemical activity in the circuits I just described. In other words, these neuromodulators can change the amount and the volume that neurons “talk” to each other.

In fact, in the context of plasticity, you can think of a neuromodulator as a microphone lowered over a specific conversation in a crowded stadium. Like a stadium on game day, brains are noisy. They are busy carrying out all kinds of everyday electrochemical duties. The “microphone” makes a conversation louder against the background noise. This is one common way plasticity occurs. The faster and greater the shift in the activity of a given circuit relative to its previous levels, and relative to the background (more electrochemically active), the more likely that circuit will alter its structure and connections—in other words, the more likely plasticity of the circuit will occur. It’s also true that if neural circuits are quieter (less electrochemically active) against the chatter of usual background brain activity, they can weaken.

Different contexts spike the release of different neuromodulators alone or in combination, which amplifies the conversation of the neural circuits active in that context. For example, dopamine is a major neuromodulator released in response to novelty and surprise, which facilitates plasticity for learning and memory.[^c6-9] And acetylcholine is released at high levels under conditions of heightened focus, but not all over the brain; rather, it’s released specifically at the sites in neural circuits that are active.[^c6-10]

Regardless of which neuromodulator or combination of neuromodulators is released, what happens next is largely the same. Since the brain is homeostatic—that is, it seeks balance—rather than maintain high levels of activity, the neurons that are part of a given conversation modify themselves so they become more easily active should that context occur again. They may add more receptors to render themselves capable of capturing more neurotransmitters or they may sprout a tiny neurite, an axonal (output) or dendritic (input) branch that becomes part of a new set of synaptic connections with other nearby neurons.[^c6-11] All this changes the threshold for activation of that circuit going forward, and on and on.[^c6-12] Voila! That is learning-driven plasticity. Other forms of plasticity involve similar cellular and molecular changes but the conditions that create them are different.

SDAP is about creating this situation of specific neural circuits rewiring in specific ways on purpose. The steps involved in this process are designed to help you do just that.

### Where to Begin

Above, I noted that the first step of SDAP is getting alert and the second is getting focused. These two work together in a positive feedback loop.

The cool thing is even the mere act of trying to focus shifts us into a slightly more elevated sympathetic tone, which causes our levels of alertness to increase, which then causes activity in the circuits for focusing to increase, which further causes levels of alertness to, you guessed it, increase. For those who struggle with focus, take solace in the fact that the circuits involved with focus are amenable to plasticity too. As you move through the SDAP process described in this chapter, and practice the various protocols here, you’ll learn new things, but you’ll also get better at focusing, which will help you to learn more new things, and so on.

There are multiple ways to create the increase in alertness and focus needed for SDAP. I’ll cover all your options—behavioral, supplement based, pharmacologic—below.

But remember this: Alertness and focus are necessary but not sufficient for plasticity and learning. To trigger learning, you’re also going to have to make errors from genuine attempts, what I refer to as repetitions, or reps. Not deliberate errors, and not half-baked efforts, but rather, errors that emerge from truly exerting yourself to learn new information, new movements, even new modes of thinking. Consider this: If your nervous system can already generate the activity patterns that enable you to do a certain task—perform a dance step, for example, or order coffee in a foreign language—why would it change? It doesn’t need to! You’re already equipped with the neural circuits to accomplish that task. You need to try, and fail, and try again. This is tough to accept, especially for perfectionists, but all who embrace it thrive. Especially those who come to recognize limbic friction, the slight agitation that accompanies effective learning, as a state to seek, not shy away from.

The importance of making mistakes and trying again doesn’t mean you have to toil endlessly. SDAP can be enjoyable. You’ll likely experience some limbic friction but guess what? Once you learn to expect it, and you realize that it helps not hinders your ability to learn, you too will be seeking it out.

You may be wondering “Why all these conditions for plasticity? Isn’t there a plasticity pill?” No. As I mentioned earlier in this introduction, plasticity is energetically expensive. Strengthening and reshaping neural circuits requires a lot of ATP, the energy our cells need to function.

And this process applies to everyone. It’s true that when it comes to neuroplasticity, children have it easier than adults. Their brains are more malleable because almost every experience is novel to them. In fact, many aspects of developmental plasticity emerge with no effort or need to deliberately focus at all. Good examples include the way that a baby’s visual and auditory systems are shaped by their early visual and sound experiences. Those things just happen. The automaticity of plasticity in our youth isn’t always a blessing however. If a child has a temporary eye injury or if a child’s eyes are misaligned due to an imbalance in the muscles that help move the eyes, it can cause longstanding maladaptive changes in brain wiring.

Yet even at an early age, many forms of plasticity still require focus. Cognitive skills like language and motor skills like walking or eating with utensils all take deliberate focus to learn. In that sense, the process for motor and cognitive skill learning is inherently the same for all ages. Your states of mind and body, alongside the agitation you experience from errors while making genuine attempts to learn, are what ensure that your brain gets the message: This thing happening right now is unique and important; we’re going to have to rewire.

### As You Proceed

An important point for anyone wishing to establish new brain patterns is that following each step of the SDAP process in its proper sequence is more important than any one tool listed here. This will be an important reframing for a lot of people.

I mentioned that there wasn’t a pill for plasticity, but people love to think about what they can take to increase neuromodulator levels to heighten focus. Adderall, energy drinks, nicotine, modafinil, microdoses of psilocybin, et cetera, are used by many people working in business, tech, sports performance, finance circles, and beyond to try to focus and learn better. The use of such stimulants is widespread on college campuses and among high school students in the US,[^c6-13] and millions of adults use them daily too.

Their widespread use merely speaks to how hard most people find it to focus intensely enough and push through limbic friction. I’m not judging anyone. For example, I, like most adults in the US,[^c6-14] use caffeine daily to increase focus. I occasionally rely on other pharmacologic tools for focus too. In this chapter, I’ll cover the popular as well as the rarely discussed ones.

That all being said, the main focus here is behavioral tools. They may not seem as sexy, but many rival the pharmacologic tools.

It truly doesn’t matter what you use to get alert and focused, as long as it’s safe. If you opt to use nicotine or modafinil or meditation or good ol’ sleep and hydration, those obviously have different safety profiles. You can use white noise or various sound tones.[^c6-15] These all have data to support them in the context of focus and learning. You can cycle different tools in and out, by the day or by the month. The point is: You have choices. Think of them as tools in your SDAP arsenal.

### Stick with It

We know a lot more about plasticity now than we did twenty-five or even just five years ago. Prior to the 2000s the widely held belief—even among neuroscience researchers—was that the opportunity for adaptive plasticity mostly closes after age twenty-five.[^c6-16]

That idea is now dead. We know people can rewire their brains and learn throughout their lifespans.[^c6-17] Also mostly dead is the idea that learning-associated plasticity involves the addition of new neurons. Plasticity in humans is almost exclusively the consequence of changes to existing neural circuits, not adding new neurons to those circuits.[^c6-18] And yet, the results you can achieve when you incorporate the best of what we know about SDAP can be extraordinary.

Here is an overview of SDAP, once more:

- Get alert.
- Get and stay focused.
- Maintain a state of urgency.
- Embrace errors that arise from genuine attempts.
- Rest.
- Repeat your performance.

I’ve listed these again because the steps and the sequence are non-negotiable. Not because I say so, but because that’s how our neuroplasticity works. There are things you can do to accelerate the process: all the tools I mentioned above (and more), along with micro-pauses, post-learning-bout NSDR, adjusted sleep protocols, and hypnosis. I cover all these in the pages that follow.

I began this chapter with this basic process because it can be applied to learning anything.

Similar to exercise, SDAP is not easy. But with time, each step becomes familiar. If you think of SDAP this way—as a process that consistently leads to a desired end—it can become a pleasure.

### Learning Protocol 1: Shift into a State of Alertness and Focus

#### What to Do

- **Getting alert and focused is the first step in SDAP.** You have to be in a state of elevated autonomic (sympathetic) arousal, but not stressed.
- **Use tools to help you achieve this state.** Such tools are many and varied, and fall into three general categories:
  - **Foundational**
  - **Behavioral**
  - **Pharmacological**
- **Put your phone away.** You may think you have an issue with getting focused, but it’s likely that you are distracted by something in your surroundings—the smartphone being the major culprit. Studies show that even just having your phone in the same room in a bag behind or under your chair reduces your ability to focus on cognitive tasks and/or increases the energy that it takes.[^c6-19]

#### How It Works

You might be thinking “Why would anyone need a protocol for focus?”

Fair question. Most people can easily get (and stay) focused on texting, scrolling social media, playing a video game, or watching their favorite sports team or TV show for an hour or more, with no protocol required.

But when it comes to SDAP—pushing your brain to understand or do that which it currently cannot understand or do—focusing is hard for most people, young or old.[^c6-20] One recent, albeit small, study of fifteen people engaged in a work-related task found that their focus wavered every 3.5 minutes, on average.[^c6-21] The latest data say that most people switch tasks every couple of minutes, or even less.[^c6-22] And that number drops further when people are trying to focus on challenging material. That is why I refer to a dedicated session of trying to learn something as a learning bout. It is a fight—with the material you’re trying to learn, and with yourself as you try to stave off frustration and resist the temptation to quit.

Yet it’s in that state of mild agitation that plasticity is sparked. But only if we focus intensely on what it is we are trying to learn.

We can all take solace in the fact that getting and staying focused has always been hard. History shows that we humans have long sought tools to make it easier. In the early 1900s an inventor by the name of Hugo Gernsback designed the Isolator—a metal helmet that covered the entire head and face, with eyeholes and a breathing tube cut into the front.[^c6-23] It resembled the helmet of an old-school scuba diving suit. The rationale was simple: Block peripheral vision and outside noise to help people focus. The Isolator did not become popular, but 117 years later it inspired the Helmfon, an oversized motorcycle helmet designed to be worn while seated at a desk, created by industrial design company Hochu rayu.[^c6-24] The rationale was the same, all that time later: Block out peripheral vision and outside noise to help people focus. The Helmfon, as you might imagine, also did not gain traction. Even if it had, the advent of social media and other online activities essentially moved the outside noise of the entire world directly into one’s central field of view. So much for helmets.

Other long-used tools include non-amphetamine stimulants such as caffeine, which blocks adenosine receptors in the brain that would otherwise trigger sleepiness, and nicotine, which triggers the release of several neuromodulators discussed in the introduction to this chapter. The use of caffeine in the form of tea or coffee dates back more than two thousand years. But coffee and tea didn’t become popular in Europe until the seventeenth century, the result of invasions and trade.[^c6-25] Today, approximately 90 percent of the world’s adults—that’s estimated as more than five billion people (!)—drink caffeine every single day. Later I’ll explain how to use caffeine specifically to enhance focus, but meanwhile those stats reveal that caffeine is the most popular drug on the planet by a huge margin. (If you’re wondering, alcohol and nicotine are in a distant second and third place, respectively.)

Nicotine, mostly in oral forms like pouches, gum, and mints, has made a big comeback as a focus aid in recent years. I recently gave a talk to several thousand undergraduate men and women at an East Coast university and asked the auditorium for a show of hands of “who in here takes nicotine daily?” About 30 percent of them raised their hands. (In a more private setting—a smaller group of about fifty male students—about two-thirds said they use nicotine two or more times per day every day.) This is obviously not a controlled study, nor did I count each hand, but even if these are artificially high estimates, it’s still pretty shocking. Or is it? Nicotine is an unusual stimulant because it makes people alert but calm—a highly desirable state for learning. Unless smoked, vaped, dipped, or snuffed, nicotine does not cause cancer, but it is highly addictive and it raises blood pressure.[^c6-26] Later, I’ll explain how, assuming you’re okay with the risks, nicotine can be used to enhance focus. There are a few safer alternatives, some of which work through the same mechanisms.

And there are the amphetamines. First synthesized in Romania in the late 1880s, amphetamines are compounds that increase levels of some of the key neuromodulators discussed in the introduction to this chapter, like norepinephrine and dopamine.[^c6-27] These stimulants were initially marketed in the 1930s as a treatment for narcolepsy, but soon hit the college scene when research showed a link with increased scores on intelligence tests.[^c6-28] They were also investigated for the treatment of attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and as appetite suppressants starting even back then.[^c6-29] A decade later, both German and Allied forces used amphetamines during World War II to stay awake and alert.[^c6-30] Recreational use of amphetamines exploded in general popularity starting in the 1950s, partly due to a surplus from World War II. By the 1960s, there was an epidemic of amphetamine dependency and abuse in the United States.[^c6-31] They were made illegal for non-prescription use in the early 1970s, classified in the same way as cocaine and morphine, and their use dropped. That is, until the FDA approved amphetamines for the treatment of ADHD in 1996.[^c6-32] Drugs marketed for ADHD like Adderall, Vyvanse, et cetera, are amphetamines, and they work quite well to increase alertness and focus. Current exact rates are hard to come by, but it seems that up to 35 percent of college students use stimulants at some point during their undergraduate years.[^c6-33] For people without a genuine clinical need for amphetamines, their use can be problematic. They are effective for helping people complete work that relies on skills they already have, but far less effective for learning new skills. They are lousy for contemplative thinking, too, and creative endeavors. And they are very habit forming, and in many cases addictive.

That’s the history. And while getting and staying focused has always been hard, it seems it’s now harder than ever.

The good news is that accessing a state of focus necessary for SDAP is possible for anyone. It starts with understanding the states of mind and body you’re after. You’ll recall that negative experiences automatically set off the learning process. No coffee, no tutor, no motivational video or mantra required. The fast, massive increase in sympathetic tone caused by adrenaline and norepinephrine ramps up activity in relevant brain circuits. It’s proof that if the right electrochemical systems get triggered, we all have the capacity to focus. Again, I’m not saying seek out stressful situations. But this points to adrenaline and norepinephrine as potent pro-focus and pro-plasticity molecules. That is knowledge we can use.

Work in the 1990s from neuroscientists James McGaugh and Larry Cahill at UC Irvine showed that if adrenaline and norepinephrine are elevated using drugs, exposure to cold water, or emotionally activating visual images, the resulting increase in sympathetic tone opens the door for the learning process.[^c6-34] Interestingly, the beta-blocker propranolol, which prevents an increase in sympathetic tone, impairs learning and memory of emotional events.[^c6-35] Conversely, if sympathetic tone is artificially increased before, during, or even immediately after a learning bout, memory is enhanced.[^c6-36] And not just for emotional events or information.[^c6-37]

Importantly, the relationship between autonomic arousal and learning follows an inverted U-shape curve, a finding first documented in 1908 and reconfirmed since.[^c6-38] If autonomic arousal is too low, learning doesn’t occur. If autonomic arousal is too high, learning also doesn’t occur. Only if autonomic arousal is somewhere on the top of the inverted U-shape curve does learning occur.

Keep this in mind anytime you begin SDAP. The key is to enter a learning bout alert but calm, then to move through it in such a way that your level of autonomic arousal continues to increase—but never to the point where you start to feel overly stressed.

The best way I can describe that level of autonomic arousal is if I ask you to imagine the kids’ game sometimes called “hot hands.” It’s where one person places their hands out, palms up, and you put your hands on theirs, palms down. The person with palms up flips their hands over to try and tap the top of your hands before you can pull away. You don’t know when they will make their move. You’re alert and focused, anticipating something will happen. Learn to recognize that state. That’s the ideal level of autonomic arousal for a learning bout. With a bit of practice you’ll be able to sense when your autonomic arousal is climbing too high or dropping too low, and keep yourself in that ideal state. In other words, you learn to get better at entering the learning process.

##### Is Being Focused the Same as Being in a Flow State?

No. Don’t confuse this state with a flow state. In flow states we forget the rest of the world (and even ourselves), and we do things as if on autopilot.[^c6-39] Flow states are ideal for task performance—executing cognitive and motor skills we have already mastered. We don’t learn in flow states, we implement what we already learned.

The person who first described flow states—the Hungarian psychologist Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi—accurately described this feeling as when the challenge of a task is matched with your existing skill level, not too easy, nor too hard… just challenging enough to engage you and “an absolute sense of control.”[^c6-40] That last part—“an absolute sense of control”—means your brain already has the neural circuits in place that it needs to execute the task. And as we discussed above, that means no rewiring… no plasticity is triggered, and no learning occurs.

To trigger plasticity and start learning, you must push past your current abilities. You have to get stumped, miss the mark, and most importantly, you have to feel the agitation of making errors. Recognize that as limbic friction, and seek it out.

Ask any elite performer how they got so good at their craft and they will tell you, “Practice, lots of practice.” But there are two kinds of practice. There are the hours upon hours spent drilling what we already know how to do and there is the practice of pushing ourselves to learn new skills. The latter is accomplished by making errors through genuine attempts. As the great Twyla Tharp, world-renowned choreographer and dancer, put it, “The more you fail in private, the less you will fail in public.”[^c6-41] Twyla understands that elite performance requires genuine attempts—failing and failing again (and again), until the gap between one’s goal and actual performance is reduced to zero.

##### The Learning State

The experiments that perhaps best illustrate the vital role of focused attention in learning come from the work of neuroscientist Mike Merzenich, PhD, and his lab at University of California, San Francisco.[^c6-42] The studies were done in the 1990s using monkeys and later adapted to studies in humans. The monkeys were trained to place their fingers on a rotating cylinder that had both coarse and fine bumps laid out in rows across its surface.[^c6-43]

The monkeys quickly learned that if they detected a difference between the coarse bumps and the fine bumps, they earned a reward. To signal when they noticed that difference, they used their other hand to move a joystick. Over time, the researchers made the task harder by making the difference in the bumps progressively smaller, which required more focus from the monkeys. Not only did the monkeys learn to perform the harder task, but the researchers observed significant changes in the brain areas representing sensations in the fingers that were touching the cylinder. In other words, they observed plasticity associated with that learning. These were adult monkeys, too, showing that plasticity was not just confined to developmental critical periods as had long been believed.

That was interesting but it was just the beginning of the story. In other studies from Merzenich, monkeys had to learn to discriminate between different sound tones. In that case the regions of the brain responsible for hearing changed. Perhaps not surprising, except that the monkeys were experiencing bumps on their fingers at the same time they heard the tones. So why did only the auditory areas of the brain change? Because the monkeys received rewards only for learning sound tones, so that’s what they focused on. Together, these two sets of experiments showed that mere experience doesn’t cause neuroplasticity. Learning-associated brain plasticity only occurs in the circuits associated with where our attention is placed.

Since those landmark studies, there have been thousands of experiments exploring the conditions required for learning and plasticity. Consider the often-cited studies from neuroscientist Eleanor Maguire, PhD, and colleagues of London taxi drivers, who must learn to navigate the complex streets of their city by memory (this was prior to the advent of GPS and Google Maps, mind you).[^c6-44] They found that, compared to bus drivers, taxi drivers had larger hippocampi, a key brain area for encoding new memories. Then there is the study showing more concentrated patterns of brain activation among professional violinists for finger movements compared to amateurs.[^c6-45] And there are studies showing significant brain circuit changes as people learn to juggle,[^c6-46] as well as reversion of those newly formed circuits if people don’t practice in the first weeks afterward.[^c6-47]

All these studies—the taxi drivers, the violinists, the jugglers—suggest that intense focus is a foundational need in order for SDAP to occur. But suggestions aren’t proof. There is, however, one study that really hammers home the relationship between focus and plasticity in humans. In 1993, two researchers from Hebrew University in Israel asked people to practice detecting a slight shift in the angle of a line relative to the angles of a bunch of surrounding lines. The people got better at that task.[^c6-48] Not surprising. Also not surprising was that when participants were asked to detect a slight shift in the angles of *all* the lines, they got better at that task too. What is surprising is that performance on one task did not improve performance on the other task, despite the fact that what they saw in both tasks was exactly the same. The only difference between the two conditions was what the participants were instructed to pay attention to. The finding leads to a profound insight: that the plasticity they experienced was tied to the act of *looking* for something and not solely to the success of *finding* that something. As the authors concluded, “Learning will occur only in those neurons that are activated by the stimulus and that are at the same time relevant for the task. Which neurons are relevant \[for neuroplasticity\] is dictated by the mechanism or strategy used for task performance (and not merely a stimulus-response correlation).”

These results, along with the earlier studies mentioned here, point to the crucial role of focus in plasticity and learning.

Which brings us to the common saying “fire together, wire together.”[^c6-49] People often use this phrase to capture the idea that habits form from neurons being activated at nearly the exact same time. The thinking goes that neurons firing simultaneously or one after the other causes them to become wired together, which will lead them to readily fire together in the future. But the term “fire together, wire together” is actually unrelated to the kind of learning we are talking about in this chapter—achieving new skills, developing new behavioral patterns, et cetera. This is not a trivial point. This phrase is often attached to the false notion that people can learn when in passive or semi-engaged states. It implies that we can simply expose kids to music to enrich their brain. Not so. It also implies that simply reading or doing something repeatedly is enough to create new brain patterns. Alas, not so. Oh and the “fire together, wire together” phrase is constantly misattributed to psychologist Donald Hebb when in fact it was Carla Shatz, the developmental neurobiologist, who said it first—in the context of developmental brain wiring, not learning.[^c6-50] The point is this: Whether young or old, if we want to learn, we need to focus intensely on new information, or in the case of cognitive or motor skills, on our attempt to perform them. The good news is that with the right tools and a little practice, anyone can access focus… and learn.

##### Tools for Focus

As I mentioned in the introduction to this protocol, we humans have long sought tools to make this endeavor easier. Here’s where science puts us today.

There are three categories of tools to get alert and focused.

1. Foundational
2. Behavioral
3. Pharmacological

   The tools offered here can be used for learning bouts, as described above, or even for what I call work sessions—time when you’re not necessarily tackling new information or skills, but grappling with some work or physical challenge that simply requires intense focus.

###### Foundational Tools for Focus

These tools are the bedrock upon which all the other suggestions in this protocol depend. Without them, the rest of the tools in this protocol will be far less effective. Get the foundational tools right, and you’ll greatly amplify the potency of all others you opt to use.

###### Foundational Tool 1: Sleep

In chapter 1 when I said that sleep is the foundation of mental health, physical health, and performance, that included learning of all kinds. When we do not get enough quality sleep, or if our sleep timing is altered by more than an hour or two from our normal schedule, our levels of alertness get harder to regulate and so focusing becomes an even bigger challenge. Thus, aim to get adequate sleep using the protocols in chapter 1. (See Sleep Protocols 1–6 for a reminder on the basics.)

###### Foundational Tool 2: NSDR

If you’ve had less than adequate sleep and you’re trying to lock in on a learning bout, consider doing ten, twenty, or, if possible, thirty minutes of non-sleep deep rest (NSDR) at some point prior to starting that learning bout. NSDR, while not a replacement for sleep, is your best bet to restore mental and physical vigor if you didn’t get enough sleep. As mentioned in Sleep Protocol 8, NSDR is preferable to naps, because it doesn’t create sleep inertia so you won’t finish a session feeling groggy, nor does it disrupt your normal sleep schedule. A short nap of thirty minutes or less can also restore mental and physical vigor, but midday napping for more than thirty minutes can really mess up your nighttime sleep. Refer to Sleep Protocol 7 for best practices.

###### Foundational Tool 3: Stress Control

The other key to an effective learning bout is to make sure you don’t show up in a state of excessively high sympathetic tone, or what we commonly call stress. Stressing about something other than what you’re trying to learn steals your focus. If you’re worrying about your to-do list, it’s hard to focus on learning a new song on the guitar. And stressing about what you’re trying to learn prevents you from staying in the alert but calm state you’re after. Chapter 3 provides tools you can use “offline”—meaning when you aren’t actively engaged in a learning bout—as well as tools you can use during a learning bout, such as the physiological sigh. Both types of tools are effective to help maintain your level of arousal near the peak of the inverted U-shape curve that is ideal for learning.

###### Foundational Tool 4: Nutrition

If you’re even mildly dehydrated, your focus won’t be at its best.[^c6-51] Drink water and, if you need to, add some electrolytes, which aids the rehydration process. The same goes for your blood sugar levels—make sure yours are relatively stable by not reaching for sugary foods when you know you want to be focused.

Chapter 4 described how to eat to fuel your body for all types of activity, and that includes learning bouts and work sessions. Those protocols offered guidelines, but there are options for how you adapt them for your schedule when it comes to learning. For example, in the first two to three hours of my day, I focus best if I’m fasted. I make sure I’m hydrated, and that I’m caffeinated, too, but unless I wake up especially hungry (a rarity for me), I don’t eat yet. If I already exercised that morning, however, I eat, and then I start work.

You don’t want to be distracted by hunger or thirst during a learning bout, nor do you want to be lethargic from an overly large or starch-and-fat-laden meal. Figure out what is best for you. And don’t burn valuable mental energy trying to get conditions perfect. That effort can easily use up the self-control available to us, which tends to be finite. If we’re mentally exhausted from trying to be perfect, we’ll have nothing left for the actual task, a state that psychologists sometimes refer to as ego depletion.[^c6-52] Studies show that if people do a lot of decision-making prior to a mental task, they perform less well on the task compared to those who don’t.[^c6-53] That means no obsessing over your pre-learning nutrition. You’ll short-circuit your ability to learn. (See chapter 4 to make sure you’re hydrating and eating right.)

###### Behavioral Tools for Focus

The ability to deliberately set and maintain focus is a superpower. It is a skill that carries over to all sorts of professional, educational, physical health, and relational activities, not just to plasticity and learning. That said, one of the best ways to get better at focusing is to engage in learning bouts.

The act of continually adjusting your state of autonomic arousal so it’s not too high and not too low, while engaging with new information or new skills is work. It involves a lot of top-down control as neuroscientists say, which as discussed in chapter 3, is a loose reference to how your prefrontal cortex repeatedly directs and redirects your mental attention. And while no magic pill or ninja move will instantly give you that superpower, there are behavioral tools that can significantly improve your ability to focus. Some assist the transition into a state of focus, and others help you stay there.

###### Behavioral Tool 1: Meditation

Meditation can take many forms. One shown to improve focus is as follows: Set aside about ten to twenty minutes, sit or lie down, close your eyes, and direct your mental attention to the location between your eyes, or concentrate on your breathing, or both. As you strive to maintain those points of focus, thoughts, sensations, and outside noises inevitably distract you. Keep redirecting your attention back to the location between your eyes and/or breathing, over and over again, as many times as needed until the allotted time elapses.

From novice to expert, no one is expected to maintain perfect focus for the whole session. It’s the redirecting of your attention that is the key component. It’s analogous to the final few repetitions of a weight lifting set. It’s what drives the nervous system changes that make it easier to focus the next time you meditate, or in any other activity. It’s training; it’s what is meant by the phrase “meditation is a practice.”

A study by researchers at New York University found that meditating in this way for just thirteen minutes per day improved participants’ ability to deliberately focus and to regulate their emotions, two strong indications that this behavioral tool can enhance and speed up learning that requires concentration.[^c6-54] Shorter meditations of five minutes per day have also been shown to help.[^c6-55] You may be thinking this seems like the micro meditation described in Stress Control Protocol 4, or any other meditation… and you would be right. All meditation is perceptual exercise where you intentionally limit what you pay attention to. Remember the Isolator? That was a perceptual filter designed to restrict your visual field—that is, intentionally limit what you pay attention to. Knowing that, it should make sense that what you elect to focus on during a meditation is less important than the act of directing, and redirecting, your attention back to the same place. You can close your eyes and focus on the top of your head, your feet, your lower belly, and your breathing, or you can open your eyes and focus on a point on a wall in front of you (allow yourself to blink as needed, of course).

Studies show improvements in focus stem from all such meditations, because meditation is a perceptual exercise for improving focus.[^c6-56] It just so happens that it also helps reduce stress,[^c6-57] boost mood,[^c6-58] and improve sleep.[^c6-59] A recent study even showed that meditation can induce a similar glymphatic washout process—that is, the removal of metabolic waste from the brain—as observed during sleep—albeit to a lesser degree.[^c6-60] With a year or more of experience, meditation can allow for profound insights into how our thoughts arise (and pass) and for some people it can be transformative for understanding consciousness, but those are not the immediate benefits. Nor should anyone wanting to improve focus shy away from meditation thinking they have to experience those sorts of major insights for it to “work.” Meditation done simply as a perceptual exercise is powerful. And the effects show up fast: less procrastination, less impulsivity, and better learning.

If you are very limited on time, here’s a simple ten-breath meditation to try immediately upon waking, while still lying in bed: Keep your eyes closed and focus on your breathing for ten slow breaths. If your mind wanders before you reach ten, restart at one, and do that as many times as needed until you reach ten focused breaths. Then get up.

After a few days, you’ll notice improvement. Of course, five minutes, as described in Stress Control Protocol 4, and eventually ten, fifteen, or twenty minutes of meditation would be even more beneficial. I’ve heard from many people who do this regularly—meaning three to seven times per week—that they can focus better, and redirect their focus if it wanders. You’ll experience the other positive effects of meditation explained above, such as stress reduction and improved sleep too. My lab found that just five minutes a day of meditation provided these benefits.[^c6-61]

What time of day or night you meditate is far less important than if you do it regularly. In fact, there is no bad time to meditate as long as you’re in a safe location. If your back or knees ache from sitting cross-legged on the floor, remember that you don’t have to do that. Make yourself comfortable. Sit in a chair or lie down in bed.

In my experience, it is the rare person who adheres to a daily meditation practice consistently over many years. Most become the “I used to meditate every day, I need to get back to it” people, not unlike the “I used to work out every day, I need to get back to it” people. I believe that happens because we shoot for ten to twenty minutes of meditation every day right out the gate. We make progress but then stop when life gets too busy, and the benefits of meditation disappear slowly so we don’t notice until the habit is broken that we are struggling to focus.

That is why I suggest you set a *very* low bar, just ten breaths. Do that every morning for two weeks, then shift to doing five minutes of meditation as described in Stress Control Protocol 4. Do that three to seven days per week for a month, then increase the duration to ten minutes, still aiming for three to seven days per week for the next month. Then increase it to fifteen minutes three to seven days per week for the following month, then twenty minutes three to seven days per week… indefinitely. Mark the days you do it on your calendar to keep track of your progress.

Or just stick with five minutes if that feels right. Be the person who sticks to things rather than the person talking about all the healthy stuff they used to do.

For the time investment needed, what meditation provides in terms of ability to focus, along with stress reduction, better mood, and improved sleep is extraordinary.

###### Behavioral Tool 2: Hypnosis

Hypnosis. I know the word alone might cause some readers to hesitate before continuing. But keep reading. Maybe the word hypnosis makes you picture people squawking like a chicken, unaware their friends are laughing until they emerge from a trance. But that is stage hypnosis. Clinical hypnosis is completely different. I wish it was called *directed neuroplasticity* instead of hypnosis.

Clinical hypnosis is supported by solid research as a tool to treat chronic pain, and to help with smoking cessation, sleep challenges, anxiety, even gut health issues.[^c6-62] Through decades of research, including brain imaging and randomized controlled trials, Stanford University psychiatrist David Spiegel and his lab discovered that clinical hypnosis stimulates specific types of plasticity that allow for better autonomic self-regulation.[^c6-63] For example, hypnosis appears to reduce activity in the part of the brain called the dorsal anterior cingulate cortex, indicating diminished self-monitoring. An accompanying increase in connection between the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex and the insula indicates that the brain is doing a better job of regulating the body. These and other findings point to a state in which people are simultaneously less self-conscious and yet better at self-regulating.

Hypnosis won’t allow you to immediately speak a new language or perform the perfect golf swing, but it is very effective for teaching people how to access otherwise inaccessible brain and bodily states, such that they can more easily re-access those states once hypnosis is over. For example, someone with an intense fear of public speaking can experience being alert but calm while onstage in front of a big audience. With just a few sessions and the occasional brush-up session, people can get very good at this kind of autonomic self-regulation. Hypnosis, in other words, is about learning how to set your state of mind.

If you have trouble with focus, or any of the other issues mentioned above, you may consider hiring a licensed clinical hypnotist to work with in person or online. Alternatively, some years back, Dr. Spiegel developed an app called Reveri that provides this tool to all (I’m an advisor for Reveri). It has you listen to a brief recorded hypnosis script (in Dr. Spiegel’s voice) on your phone, a few times per week. Reveri has hypnosis scripts for improving focus, and also for improving sleep, reducing chronic pain, and much more. Each takes about eight minutes to complete. If you try Reveri, remember this: It’s not magic. It’s also not mind control and it’s most definitely not stage hypnosis. It is a tool for teaching your brain how to access different states, including focus.

###### Behavioral Tool 3: 40 Hertz Binaural Beats, 20 Hertz Oscillatory Induction, and White, Brown, and Pink Noise

The use of sound as a tool for focus is all about entrainment, or the matching of our internal rhythms to an external sensory event—in these cases, the frequency of sound waves. You may remember the term entrainment from chapter 1 and chapter 5. There, I talked about entraining your circadian rhythm to light, for example, by viewing bright light in the first hour after waking up. There are also ways to entrain to events in the outside world. For example, when you exercise at roughly the same time of day, you experience an increase in catecholamines and certain hormones at that time. Then after about three days or so, you automatically start to feel an increase in energy just prior to when you usually exercise. Entrainment works based on your nervous system’s expectation of certain things happening.

Sound waves can entrain our brain, too, and they do so very quickly. When we hear certain frequencies or rhythms, our brain starts to entrain to the predictable features in the sound by our neurons firing in regular fashion. Scientists have figured out how to leverage that and have created specific sound patterns that increase brain activity in areas that underlie focused states.

One example is binaural beats. Two distinct frequencies of sounds are played in each ear. When that happens, a cluster of neurons in your brainstem called the medial superior olivary nucleus performs a subtraction of the two frequencies. So if a 400 hertz (Hz) sound arrives at one ear and 440 Hz at the other ear, it leads you to perceive a 40 Hz beat. That sound frequency, in particular, has been shown to improve levels of focus, and even certain forms of memory.[^c6-64] The precise mechanisms for this are still being parsed but there is evidence that 40 Hz sound can do this in part by causing release of acetylcholine from the medial superior olivary nucleus and the release of dopamine in the striatum, a brain area involved in movement and motivated attention.[^c6-65]

Some evidence even shows that 40 Hz sounds can trigger the brain circuits involved in focus and memory to enter what are called gamma oscillation states, a pattern of neural activity that is favorable for learning.[^c6-66] (Interestingly, there is parallel evidence that activating these circuits using clinical devices may also help offset some of the early symptoms of age-related cognitive decline in Alzheimer’s disease.[^c6-67])

Not everyone appears to benefit from this tool however. It seems if people already have elevated levels of these neuromodulators prior to the sound exposure, the benefits of binaural beats are less apparent or even absent.[^c6-68] Alas, without doing an fMRI and blood draws, there is no way to know your baseline dopamine and acetylcholine levels. Considering 40 Hz binaural beats are safe and cost nothing (there are dozens of free apps, videos, and audio recordings of these on Apple music, Spotify, and YouTube), why not try them and see? You have nothing to lose and perhaps something significant to gain in your efforts to focus better.

Here’s how: Try listening to 40 Hz binaural beats for five minutes prior to a learning bout or work session. Once you determine if that works for you, try listening to the beats continuously throughout. (Of course, if you are trying to learn something that requires you to listen to instructions, you’ll only be able to use the 40 Hz tones prior to the learning bout.) Also, note that it’s recommended you use headphones for binaural beats as it’s the best way to entrain your olivary nucleus and other brain circuits to 40 Hz gamma frequencies.[^c6-69]

There are exciting new data suggesting that sounds of about 12 to 20 Hz—which cause the brain to entrain to beta, not gamma, waves—may also improve concentration and reduce mental fatigue.[^c6-70] Music with 20 Hz as the dominant frequency may be especially effective here.

I personally have tried 40 Hz binaural beats, using one of the many free binaural beat apps out there (I like BrainWave). I’ve also used white and pink noise, both of which have been shown to improve focus, albeit in a small number of studies.[^c6-71] I’ve heard anecdotal evidence that brown noise can also be helpful. (In case you’re wondering, white noise is noise with all sound frequencies present at equal energy, pink noise sounds less “hissy” than white noise, and brown noise is lower pitched than either white or pink noise.) Brown and pink noise work a bit to increase my focus but I was not terribly impressed by the magnitude of the effect. I have also tried Brain.fm and, for me, it works well (I have no affiliation with Brain.fm, I just like their product). I listen to it while reading, and during learning bouts and even writing sessions lasting anywhere from one to three hours. (I do take a break every fifty to ninety minutes, and avoid looking at my phone in those breaks… more on phone use to come.)

###### Behavioral Tool 4: Music

The data on listening to music to enhance focus is very clear: Silence is best. (That is unless the music is 12–20 Hz binaural beats, per the above.)

If you like to listen to music when reading or learning, music with no lyrics is better.[^c6-72] All that said, some people like to work in cafés, in airports, or in busy offices. The backdrop of auditory noise helps them focus. I suspect there is a lot of individual variation when it comes to this. You’ll have to experiment and see what works for you, and when.

As I write this I am in a completely silent room and it’s early evening—the only audible noise is the air conditioner and the keys of my computer, but this morning I listened to Brain.fm for two full hours while I worked on an earlier part of this chapter. I felt extremely focused during both sessions, so go figure. Be a scientist of yourself, and customize your own protocols for focus. One thing is certain: Sound can be a powerful tool for entraining brain states required for learning.

A note before we continue: Throughout this chapter I’ve been highlighting the important role that adrenaline and norepinephrine play in focus, and the formation of memories and learning. Soon we will cover ways to boost these and some other closely related neuromodulators, like dopamine, using pharmacology. But first, there are established behavioral tools to significantly and safely increase adrenaline and norepinephrine without taking anything. These won’t surprise you because I covered them earlier, in different contexts.

###### Behavioral Tool 5: Physical Exercise

Physical exercise causes meaningful increases in adrenaline through now-*well*- understood neural circuits, stemming from your motor cortex in your brain all the way down to your adrenal glands near your lower back.[^c6-73] Any vigorous physical activity that involves the large musculature of your legs and core (abdominals, lower back, etc.), will trigger the release of adrenaline, in a manner that scales with the intensity of the activity. Think: compound lower body exercises like squats or deadlifts, running, martial arts, tennis, and on and on. Adrenaline does not cross the blood-brain barrier, but it binds to receptors on your vagus nerve—the two-way neural superhighway that bridges your body and brain.[^c6-74] That, in turn, stimulates the release of norepinephrine from your locus coeruleus (remember that, from chapter 1?) and other brain areas involved in generating a state of focus.[^c6-75] That’s one mechanism, but there are others at play, including increased blood flow and brain oxygenation, and lactate-induced elevations in brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) (which you’ll recall from chapter 2… see how all of this comes together?). The effects of all this on your focus and cognition are significant, and can last several hours afterward.

One of the best ways to use exercise as a tool for focus is brief high-intensity interval training (HIIT)—for example, after a five- to ten-minute warm-up, I like to do a thirty-second near-all-out sprint, followed by thirty seconds of rest, and again, for a total of eight sprint-rest cycles.

Other HIIT options work too. You can find dozens of ideas for these online with a simple web search. It’s crucial to warm up for a few minutes before the first round and important too that you select a form of exercise that you can perform without getting injured. I like to run outside on a track or use a stationary assault bike, but you may prefer to swim, use a rower, a stair climber, et cetera.

There are also studies showing improved focus and cognition after sustained twenty to forty-five minute cardio training sessions at lower intensity (60–75 percent of maximum heart rate), although the effects of this on focus appear more transient compared to more intense exercise.[^c6-76] That makes sense, given HIIT elevates adrenaline and norepinephrine more than lower intensity steady state cardio.[^c6-77]

Fewer studies have explored how focus might be increased after resistance training. But assuming the sessions are not overly long or intense, I would expect them to impart a similar focus-enhancing effect as cardio training sessions (see chapter 2 for more on the ideal duration and intensity for those sessions).

Experiment to find the form of exercise you like best to enhance focus. Make sure to time the duration and adjust the intensity of effort so it doesn’t exhaust you.

###### Behavioral Tool 6: Proper Breathing

Sleep apnea is a condition where people under-breathe during sleep. Nasal obstructions, excessive weight, and certain medications cause it. If you snore, there’s a good chance you have sleep apnea.

The result? Your brain is deprived of oxygen at night.

Sleep apnea is a dangerous condition, because the health impacts creep up over time—causing fatigue, cognitive impairments, heart issues, and more.[^c6-78] Some of these can be reversed with tools to correct breathing while you sleep, but long-lasting impairments can occur.

Why am I discussing sleep apnea in a protocol on focus? Because many people have daytime apnea that impairs their focus too.[^c6-79] Daytime apnea is when you hold your breath while working. Chronic mouth breathers experience the same. When your brain doesn’t get enough oxygen, you get tired and you can’t focus. To feel alert and focus intensely, you need to fix sleep and any daytime apnea.

Luckily, it’s easy to do. First, make sure you’re breathing through your nose anytime you don’t have to speak, eat, or exercise hard. Second, learn to breathe with your diaphragm, also known as *belly breathing*, in which your belly expands as you inhale. This approach increases the amount of oxygen in the blood and promotes a more relaxed state. You’ll be amazed what a difference that will make for your energy levels and focus.

Check right now. If you’re mouth breathing, switch to nasal breathing. Does your belly move out as you inhale and move in as you exhale through your nose? If so, great, you’re nasal diaphragmatic breathing. If you’re having trouble, imagine inhaling through your nose as if trying to direct the air backward—in other words, think about drawing the air “in and back” through your nose at an angle parallel to the roof of your mouth, as opposed to inhaling “up” your nostrils toward the top of your head. I know that sounds weird, but try it. You’ll notice that you immediately shift. And no, you don’t have to think about your breathing all day. After two to three breaths done consciously that way, it will carry on reflexively. Nasal diaphragmatic breathing in the daytime also helps you default to the right breathing pattern when you sleep, which can help offset sleep apnea, so it’s a twofer.

A few other issues with breathing to address here. If you have a badly deviated septum or challenged nasal breathing brought about by cartilage growth in your nasal passages, you need to fix that. The simplest way to open your nasal passages is to, again, practice nasal diaphragmatic breathing. Your sinuses are not fixed, but over time this effort will help open them up. Extreme cases of nasal passage collapse or other blockage may require surgery. People can often achieve some results from wearing a magnetic nose bridge for a few hours a day and/or at night. They gently pull your nasal passages open and lead to instant improvement in airway flow. Yes, they look silly. No, you don’t have to wear them in public. And it won’t make your nostrils or nose bigger. Intake Breathing makes a product that is easy to use. It certainly helped me breathe better at night and when I wore it for a few hours each day, the improvement in breathing, alertness, and focus was immediate, and significant. (Note: I have no affiliation with Intake Breathing.)

Keep in mind that it’s 100 percent normal to be able to breathe more easily through one nostril than the other at any one time, and which nostril switches every ninety minutes or so due to a neural circuit mechanism governed by your autonomic nervous system.[^c6-80] That’s right: The whole right versus left nostril breathing thing practitioners often talk about in yoga classes is supported by modern science, although the reasons for it remain unclear.

Nasal breathing has been shown to improve learning and memory. The reason is simple. It allows for better blood flow and oxygenation of the brain, and thus elevated activity of neural circuits involved in learning and memory.[^c6-81]

So find out if you snore. Again, it’s an indicator that you may have sleep apnea. There are lots of free apps that record you while you sleep and track your snoring patterns. If you snore, address it. Try different devices and exercises. You may need to get fitted with a CPAP machine. Talk to your doctor to explore your options. Eliminating sleep apnea is a big deal for your health, and it will powerfully impact your ability to feel alert and focused.

###### Behavioral Tool 7: Cyclic Hyperventilation

Cyclic hyperventilation might sound familiar, but there’s new context for this powerful tool.

It’s quite simple. You hyperventilate. Intentionally. Not a bunch of quick shallow breaths—that’s panting! Instead do ten to twenty cycles of a big deep inhale through your nose, using diaphragmatic breathing as described in the section above, and exhale, letting the air passively “fall out” from your mouth. You don’t have to heave into the inhale to get the effect you’re seeking. Work up to it gradually, and focus on long, diaphragmatic inhales through the nose. Increase the vigor after a few repetitions. After ten to twenty breaths this way, you will reliably feel much more alert.

As covered in chapter 3, you can spike your levels of adrenaline and norepinephrine and dopamine—the so-called catecholamines—and thereby increase your alertness and focus, by breathing in this specific way. It works by causing increased discard of carbon dioxide, which is called hypocapnia, and increased alkalinity of your blood pH, which is called alkalosis. That in turn triggers fast and significant increases in adrenaline and norepinephrine release in your body and brain.

If you think breathing to shift catecholamine levels is not very potent, think again. This tool works fast and extremely well to increase alertness, so you can focus on whatever task lies before you. It’s a causal relationship. In experiments where people hyperventilated through an air mask with artificially elevated CO[^c6-2], their epinephrine and norepinephrine levels did not increase, nor did they achieve alkalosis.[^c6-82] This tells us it’s not just the mechanics of deep breathing, it’s about increased discard of CO[^c6-2]. By the way, that is why people having a panic attack are told to breathe into a paper bag; it’s to encourage them to re-breathe the CO[^c6-2] they expelled, and bring their epinephrine and norepinephrine back to baseline.

When you do cyclic hyperventilation, you won’t have a panic attack as long as you pay attention to your autonomic state as you do. If you feel alert after ten breaths, stop. If not, do ten more breaths. If you want, complete twenty breaths, then take a long exhale and hold your breath for ten to sixty seconds until you feel the gasp reflex, and then start another round of cyclic hyperventilation. When you’re as alert as you want to be, resume normal nasal diaphragmatic breathing.

Sure, cyclic hyperventilation looks a little wacky but so what? It costs nothing, and it works. It may also have benefits for your immune system.[^c6-83] Just don’t ever do it in or near water, or while driving, because when your CO[^c6-2] is low, the impulse to breathe is delayed. People have drowned practicing this breathing pattern as a way to extend how long they can hold their breath underwater.

###### Behavioral Tool 8: Deliberate Cold Exposure

Deliberate cold exposure works very well to increase alertness and focus for hours afterward. That’s not surprising: As you now know, it can more than double or triple your circulating levels of epinephrine and norepinephrine and dopamine—our now-familiar friends, the catecholamines—and it does it within seconds. The data on deliberate cold exposure and learning and memory are mixed because most studies have explored if people can learn during deliberate cold exposure, while they are in the cold.[^c6-84] You can already guess what happens there: Deliberate cold exposure generally puts people at the far end of the inverted U-shape curve of autonomic arousal, where focusing ability sharply drops off. That is not the idea here.

This is: Try thirty seconds to three minutes of deliberate cold exposure, then shower and start your learning bout or work session. It’s about using deliberate cold exposure to create a long-lasting window of moderate catecholamine increase. Depending on the duration of the cold exposure, the increase in alertness and focus can last for many hours afterward.

The challenge is there is no one-size-fits-all protocol for this one because people’s cold tolerance varies.

My suggestion is that if you decide to use deliberate cold exposure as a tool to increase focus, select your method, then choose an uncomfortably cold (for you) but safe temperature. Refer to Stress Control Protocol 2 for more information. If you’re using a shower, get all the way under the water. If you’re submerging yourself in a plunge or pool, submerge your feet, legs, and torso completely, up to your neck. And yes, put your hands in the water, too, unless you need to grip the sides for safety. The water should be cold, but shouldn’t cause pain. Remember that the first ten to thirty seconds are going to feel like mild panic. Your breath will quicken, but then try long, slow, and controlled inhales and exhales. You can opt to distract yourself, or not. It makes no difference. Deliberate cold exposure bypasses most all attempts to reframe the experience as enjoyable. Pretty much the only thing that helps is to remember that it never feels good to be in the cold, but you’ll feel great when you get out.

When you do get out, towel off and take a warm or hot shower (or if you’re a real masochist, cold), get dressed, and go about your day. Again, to derive the focus-increasing benefits of deliberate cold exposure you don’t have to do it immediately before a learning bout or work session because the effects last hours. Enjoy! (Getting out of the cold, that is.)

###### Pharmacological Tools for Increasing Focus

“What can I take to focus?” is one of the most common questions I get. So here goes.

###### Pharmacological Tool 1: Caffeine

With 90 percent of the world’s adult population drinking caffeine every day, it’s hard to run a study on how caffeine affects alertness and focus… because most participants would be caffeine adapted, meaning they drink caffeine just to achieve normal, or what I call baseline, levels of alertness. This is an important concept to understand.

So many people rely on caffeine for basic alertness that pretty much any experiment comparing one group that takes caffeine to another that doesn’t ends up telling us more about the effects of caffeine withdrawal in the control group than anything else. Alas, most people just won’t quit caffeine for two to three weeks—which is the duration needed to get through the withdrawal—to participate in research. So we are left with very limited studies, all of which point to caffeine as a good way to enhance alertness, but not focus per se.

Let me explain. As we discussed in chapter 1, caffeine staves off fatigue by thwarting the action of adenosine, a molecule that builds up in our brain while we are awake and that causes us to feel sleepy as a result. If you drink caffeine regularly, you’re getting some modest focus-enhancing effects, as alertness is a prerequisite for focus.

Caffeine also increases adrenaline and norepinephrine in a dose-dependent manner.[^c6-85] A single cup of strong coffee—about 250 milligrams of caffeine—can increase circulating adrenaline by more than 200 percent over baseline levels, and norepinephrine 75 percent over baseline levels.[^c6-86] Ingesting caffeine daily also may increase the density of brain dopamine receptors, allowing the same amount of dopamine to impart a greater effect.[^c6-87] The largest alertness and focus-enhancing effects of caffeine are likely to be felt if you don’t regularly drink caffeine, or if you were to ingest more caffeine than is typical for you.

A note of caution: Remember the inverted U-shape curve that relates arousal and focus? If you are not a regular caffeine user and you suddenly consume 100 to 250 milligrams more caffeine than is typical for you, it will excessively elevate your sympathetic tone, and you may find it challenging to focus.

I drink caffeine every day, usually in the form of cold brewed or hot yerba maté. I have done that for more than three decades, and by now my caffeine tolerance is very high. Like most people, I swear that it helps me focus though it probably just does that by bringing my levels of alertness up to baseline. If I were to stop drinking caffeine, and push through the withdrawal, I could find my non-caffeinated baseline level of alertness… but I’m uninterested in doing that experiment. I love yerba maté and I love coffee. I sip caffeine from about an hour after I wake up until about 2:00 p.m. daily, and most days I do at least one, and often two or three, long learning bouts or work sessions in that time frame. You’ll need to experiment to see what is best for you. I know people who avoid caffeine entirely, those that only use it as a tool for alertness and focus, and I know many like me who use it every day. (Return to Sleep Protocol 11 for more about how caffeine affects your sleep as you experiment with this tool.)

###### Pharmacological Tool 2: Theanine

I suggest at some point you try taking 100 milligrams of theanine alongside your caffeine. The caffeine-theanine combination can heighten focus, even for those who consume caffeine regularly.[^c6-88] What’s more, the combination of theanine and caffeine has been shown to improve task-switching capacity and reduce susceptibility to distractions,[^c6-89] in part because it’s thought to increase alpha wave brain activity, which allows for selective attention.[^c6-90] It also increases levels of the inhibitory transmitter GABA, serotonin, and dopamine, which can help make the alert state created by caffeine feel a little more relaxed. For non-regular caffeine users, it reduces any jitteriness caffeine might cause, as it prevents some of caffeine’s vasoconstrictive and blood pressure elevating effects.[^c6-91] In fact, even though at doses of 100 to 400 milligrams (depending on someone’s body weight and tolerance) caffeine is considered safe for adults without anxiety, taking 100 to 200 milligrams theanine with it may further improve caffeine’s safety profile for non-regular and regular users alike.

Theanine may even allow you to get more of a focus-enhancing effect from less caffeine. In one study, people who ingested as little as 40 milligrams of caffeine combined with 100 milligrams theanine experienced improved focus.[^c6-92] Keep in mind that most commercially sold 12 ounce coffees deliver about 200 to 300 milligrams of caffeine depending on the roast, and 16 ounce coffees can contain as much as 400 to 500 milligrams.

Together, the caffeine-theanine combination tends to induce the “alert but calm” state of mind favorable for learning bouts. With its focus-enhancing effect, and various health benefits—such as reduced blood pressure and anxiety—I consider theanine a good tool for caffeine users, which means for nearly everyone.

###### Pharmacological Tool 2: Alpha-GPC

I consider alpha-GPC a valuable tool for increasing focus and energy levels, if it’s used correctly and very occasionally.

Even small increases in acetylcholine—a neuromodulator—can improve focus.[^c6-93] Alpha-GPC does that by increasing the amount of choline that reaches the brain, which in turn indirectly raises acetylcholine levels.[^c6-94] Research has found an enhancement of concentration and cognitive flexibility in subjects who take alpha-GPC about thirty minutes prior to a learning bout,[^c6-95] and at least one study showed modest improvement in cognition in people with dementia.[^c6-96] Other studies, however, show a minimal effect.[^c6-97] The variation in outcomes may reflect people’s baseline levels of acetylcholine before they take alpha-GPC, similar to what we discussed earlier with people’s baseline levels of dopamine before they listen to 40 Hz binaural beats. If a person’s natural levels of a given neuromodulator are already high, adding more may not help. If natural levels of acetylcholine are low to moderate, however, boosting it seems to have a positive effect.[^c6-98]

Alpha-GPC is often added to energy drinks, and most nootropic formulas (that is, substances marketed for improving cognition). If you’re looking to experiment with ways to increase focus for late afternoon or nighttime work or workouts, and you don’t want to disrupt your sleep, you can try 300 to 600 milligrams of alpha-GPC taken thirty minutes or so before you begin. Limit your intake to two to four times per week, because your system will quickly adjust to it.

If you take alpha-GPC, make sure to take 600 milligrams of garlic extract (in capsule form, to avoid the taste and smell of raw garlic) at some point in the same twenty-four hours, to help offset the increase in TMAO that alpha-GPC can cause.[^c6-99] TMAO is a metabolite formed by gut bacteria in response to high levels of choline and it can pose a cardiovascular risk if elevated too frequently. Garlic contains an antimicrobial chemical called allicin, which may help offset the buildup of TMAO, and garlic extract is very inexpensive.[^c6-100]

Some of you may be wondering if you can combine caffeine and alpha-GPC, or even combine caffeine, theanine, *and* alpha-GPC. Yes, that combination works very well to increase focus and energy levels… but it might be too stimulating for some people, raise blood pressure too high, and increase anxiety, too, so don’t go from none to all three. I can take 200 to 300 milligrams caffeine, 600 milligrams alpha-GPC, and 100 milligrams theanine together before a particularly demanding exercise session or learning bout. I probably take that combination once or twice a month. And I still practice the foundational tools described in this chapter: getting great sleep, practicing NSDR, exercising, et cetera. Stimulants and things that increase neuromodulators tend to work best on that solid foundation. I can’t emphasize that enough: Great sleep is still the most important tool for focus. Pharmacologic stimulants taken when you are very sleep-deprived sets you up for cardiac issues. Supplements should be used to augment a stable foundation. Not just for safety, but because that is how they work best.

###### Pharmacological Tool 3: L-tyrosine

This amino acid is used in the body to synthesize dopamine, as well as adrenaline, norepinephrine, and certain thyroid hormones.[^c6-101] It comes from foods we eat but, as a nonessential amino acid, our body can also make it from other compounds if needed. That said, consuming more L-tyrosine from foods or supplements leads to a net increase in catecholamine levels.

L-tyrosine is abundant in nuts and seeds, meats, and some cheeses. Parmesan Reggiano has so much tyrosine that you can often see the L-tyrosine crystals on the surface of the cheese block. Yes, it’s safe to eat those L-tyrosine crystals, and yes, that is one of the reasons some people like certain cheeses so much—the taste combined with the dopamine increase it causes is highly reinforcing.

L-tyrosine gets converted into L-dopa by the rate-limiting enzyme tyrosine hydroxylase, which means flooding your system with L-tyrosine is not sufficient to increase dopamine—the amount of tyrosine hydroxylase is the bottleneck on dopamine production.[^c6-102] Nonetheless, there is some evidence that supplementing with L-tyrosine can improve alertness, focus, and learning under certain conditions.[^c6-103] The problem is that most studies used ridiculously high dosages of L-tyrosine to observe these effects—as much as 8 grams or more delivered in capsule or pure powder form. I do not suggest taking that much all at once!

Anecdotally, many people find that supplementing L-tyrosine at doses of just 500 to 2,000 milligrams can help improve alertness and focus, but the published studies indicate L-tyrosine supplements really only help when people are stressed or fatigued.[^c6-104]

I have tried 500 to 1,000 milligrams L-tyrosine and I’ve tried *Mucuna pruriens*, an over-the-counter naturally occurring form of L-dopa. Both increased my alertness, focus, and energy levels for a few hours but, at least for me, they both led to a significant dip in energy afterward. Some people love L-tyrosine at 500 to 1,000 milligrams before work or exercise sessions, and swear by the focus-enhancing effects. That is why L-tyrosine is found in a lot of energy drinks and pre-workout formulas. I take it from time to time because it happens to be in one of the energy drinks I sometimes consume. So now to energy drinks.

###### Pharmacological Tool 4: Energy Drinks
