More than a third of the world’s adult population consumes at least one energy drink per month, and about 9 percent consumes them every day.[^c6-105] Studies of adolescents aged thirteen to nineteen have reported that a quarter of those who regularly consume energy drinks have at least one a day, and another quarter have at least two per day.[^c6-106] In 2024, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention noted that 30 to 50 percent of adolescents report some amount of energy drink consumption.[^c6-107] These rates are enormous.

To be clear, if you swallow a capsule of 300 to 600 milligrams of alpha-GPC, another capsule of 100 to 200 milligrams theanine, and down both with 100 to 300 milligrams of caffeine from coffee, tea, or diet soda, you’re basically making your own energy drink. But there is an important difference. Many commercially sold energy drinks contain anywhere from 200 to 400 milligrams caffeine, 400 to 900 milligrams alpha-GPC, and 100 to 200 milligrams theanine *per serving*, and contain one to two servings per can. Many also include L-tyrosine, and more are starting to include huperzine A, an alkaloid that blocks the enzyme that breaks down acetylcholine, leading to overall increases in acetylcholine levels in the brain.[^c6-108] Many energy drinks are also now starting to include racetams, a family of synthetic compounds that lead to increased activity of acetylcholine and other neuromodulators in the brain.[^c6-109] Now you know why energy drinks are so habit forming: They are carefully engineered neuromodulator-increasing cocktails that taste like candy. They can even cause withdrawal effects if you regularly drink one or more per day, and then try to suddenly stop.

I rarely drink commercially sold energy drinks, preferring instead to get my caffeine from yerba maté or black coffee, and sometimes also taking theanine and/or alpha-GPC in capsule form. If I do have an energy drink, it’s usually before a particularly hard workout, as opposed to a learning bout.

I suggest that kids under the age of eighteen avoid energy drinks or pre-workout formulas, which are similar. We have no idea how all that neuromodulator augmentation impacts brain wiring. I hear from people young and old saying they “can’t focus,” only to learn that they drink one to three energy drinks per day, or a 20 ounce coffee every morning. That’s likely 600 milligrams of caffeine just to feel baseline levels of alertness.

Homeostasis is a nonnegotiable rule of biology. If you want to boost focus and energy levels from caffeine or other substances, a daily high dose is not recommended. Put differently: Whatever stimulant you take every day will soon be needed to merely reach your baseline levels of alertness. Better in my opinion to use stimulants as an augmentation, not a requirement.

That said, I am not going to give up my daily caffeine. I enjoy the taste and the feeling far too much. I drink just enough of it to bring about a mild increase in my level of alertness. Coffee has also been shown to benefit longevity by a variety of mechanisms, and yerba maté and green tea both have additional health benefits from the antioxidants and polyphenols they contain.[^c6-110]

Most days I rely on the foundational tools described here: good sleep, nutrition, and hydration. I practice the brief daily meditation I described, and I add caffeine. These generate the alertness and focus I need for learning bouts, work, and exercise.

I include over-the-counter pharmacologic tools like alpha-GPC and theanine here because they *do work*, and I and many others have derived benefit from them. I also consider them a far safer and less expensive alternative to nicotine and prescription drugs for focus. Which brings me to nicotine.

###### Pharmacological Tool 5: Nicotine

Ah, nicotine. Humans love the effects of nicotine so much they keep coming up with new delivery methods and every time there is a health hazard associated with one way, they develop another.

This plant alkaloid has been used for centuries to increase focus. It was put into soldiers’ kits in the early 1900s because of its known stimulant and stress-reducing effects.[^c6-111] By the 1960s, more than half of adults in the United States and Europe smoked tobacco daily, with many starting upon waking and only stopping at bedtime.[^c6-112]

Nicotine, the primary psychoactive ingredient in tobacco, increases alertness and focus, and also heart rate and blood pressure,[^c6-113] but it has the unique property among stimulants of inducing relaxation.[^c6-114] It makes you feel “alert yet calm”—that state where the autonomic seesaw is tilted ever so slightly toward increased sympathetic tone. It’s the perfect state for focus. It also didn’t hurt tobacco sales that smoking alongside a stranger or asking for a light was an icebreaker, and that nicotine reduces appetite. Pair all that with advertising that romanticized the act of smoking, and the cost, foul odor, stained teeth, and stagnant breath that smoking causes all went largely overlooked.

Of course, until people finally realized that smoking, dipping, chewing, or snuffing tobacco is dangerous. It significantly increases cancer and stroke risk.[^c6-115] And yet, that went largely overlooked for a long time too. Public health announcements started to make these risks clear in the mid-1960s, but it was a rather slow and reluctant campaign until the 2000s, when the tobacco industry started to be heavily taxed and regulated.[^c6-116] By 2010, the tobacco industry—formerly one of the most powerful in the world—saw its sales plummet. I was born in 1975 and I can still remember people smoking in airports and on planes, and how every dining table had an ashtray on it. Even the squat racks in the first commercial gym I joined back in 1993 had ashtrays molded into them so you could set your cigarette down while you performed your set! How times have changed.

Or have they? From 2005 to 2015, as smoking was progressively banned from most every indoor and even some outdoor public spaces, the use of electronic cigarettes, aka vaping, exploded. Vaping is somewhat safer than smoking, but carries its own risks.[^c6-117] Nicotine itself doesn’t cause cancer, though the contaminants in vape solutions cause lung damage. Also, since nicotine is highly addictive, people struggle to quit vaping just as much as they struggle to quit cigarettes. Health warnings about vaping have curbed the market significantly in recent years, but because no other substance creates that alert-but-calm state like nicotine does, as they always have, people make sure to find a way to get their fix.

Which is why since 2020 the use of oral nicotine products like pouches, gums, and mints has exploded in popularity.[^c6-118] Notice the pattern? I get asked about oral nicotine almost daily. “Is it safe? Is it addictive? Is using four 6 milligram pouches worse than vaping?” Some people even use it when exercising; millions more use it to work. An increasing number of women and teens are using oral nicotine products now too.

So, here is what you need to know about oral nicotine: It absolutely works to sharply increase focus… if you take it occasionally. Meaning no more than two to three times a week, at a dose of 1 to 6 milligrams each time. If you take nicotine daily, you’ll soon need that same dose just to reach your former baseline levels of alertness, and without it you’ll be in a mild state of withdrawal. You’ll feel foggy and more tired than usual. And it is very habit forming. That is why so few people can limit their oral nicotine use to 3 to 6 milligrams once per day. I hear from countless people who started with that amount, loved the effect, then increased to 3 milligrams twice per day, and now use 4 to 6 milligrams or even 8 milligram pouches pretty much all day long.

There’s more to discuss as you consider this tool. Nicotine may also protect against Parkinson’s and Alzheimer’s. You read that right. Nicotine may prevent the neuronal degeneration underlying Parkinson’s and Alzheimer’s disease.[^c6-119] Clinical trials show, however, that once these diseases start, nicotine is unlikely to be of benefit.[^c6-120] Whether any neuroprotection that nicotine provides is great enough to offset the other health problems nicotine is known to cause is also still unclear. Remember, nicotine itself doesn’t cause cancer—it’s not mutagenic. But it may accelerate tumor progression.[^c6-121] It also raises blood pressure and causes vasoconstriction, which increases heart attack and stroke risk, and because of its vasoconstrictive effects, it has the potential to cause sexual side effects too, especially in men.[^c6-122] Experts on oral health are noticing that patients who use nicotine have more gum disease. Experts on skin health observe that it may cause premature aging of skin.[^c6-123] Both are likely as a result of its vasoconstriction effect (i.e., reduced blood flow to the gums and skin). That all makes sense, as reducing the blood supply means less oxygen and nutrients get delivered to an organ or tissue, and fewer waste products of cellular metabolism are removed from it.

Curious about the oral nicotine hype, I tried 4 milligrams nicotine gum and it worked to make me feel alert but calm. And it worked quickly, like flipping a switch. The next day, however, I felt a bit less mentally sharp. I also felt I needed to clear my throat a lot. I spoke to an MD friend who works on neural pathways for speech, and he told me that nicotine binds to both nicotinic and muscarinic acetylcholine receptors—the latter of which are abundant in the smooth muscles of the throat, larynx, and pharynx. He explained that after nicotine wears off, those muscles go into a slight spasm. Sure enough, taking 4 milligrams nicotine again fixed all that right away… until the next day. That experience was enough for me to end the experiment. Fortunately, the throat issue resolved after about three days.

I share this story because it made me understand the appeal—the focus-enhancing effect of nicotine is remarkable—and yet, people should know all the effects, which I’ll recap one more time here to underscore them. There’s addiction potential, increase in blood pressure and vasoconstriction, and of course how quickly the cravings begin and many of the positive effects evaporate. I have friends who are otherwise very health conscious, and they need nicotine to do any sort of focused work or exercise. It’s become part of the way they just get to baseline. Are they addicted? The classic definition of addiction is continued use despite harm to self or others. One way that I define addiction is something that causes a progressive narrowing of the things that bring you pleasure. According to both definitions, they are not addicted to nicotine (unless you consider the long-term health harms). But I do think they are dependent on it.

As with all things, my motto is this: Do what you want, but know what you’re doing. If you want to use nicotine, use the lowest possible dose that is effective for you. Stick to pouches, mints, or gums because the cancer risk appears to be lower than with cigarettes, but be aware that we do not yet have enough data to know this risk conclusively.[^c6-124] Limit your use to two to four times per week, and at most 6 milligrams per use (2–4 milligrams would be even better). That is, if you want the potent focus-enhancing effect of nicotine to last.

###### Pharmacological Tool 6: Prescription Drugs: Adderall, Ritalin, Modafinil and Armodafinil, Sunosi, Wellbutrin

These are the heavy guns for pharmacologically increasing alertness and focus. Collectively, these drugs are referred to as sympathomimetics: They increase levels of sympathetic tone by directly increasing levels of dopamine and norepinephrine in the brain, albeit each through different mechanisms.[^c6-125] Some block reuptake of dopamine and norepinephrine at synapses, leading to more availability of these two neuromodulators in the brain; others stimulate more release *and* block reuptake. Some also weakly increase other neuromodulators like serotonin. But they all potently increase alertness and focus.

I hesitated to include these drugs in this book, because they were developed to treat specific clinical conditions like ADHD (Adderall, Vyvanse, and Ritalin), or excessive daytime sleepiness (modafinil and Sunosi), or depression and smoking cessation (Wellbutrin), and they were not developed or marketed for merely increasing alertness and focus. The reality, however, is many millions of people get them prescribed or obtain them illicitly for that purpose. Knowing how they work and their margins of safety therefore feels warranted. Also, I hear often from parents wondering if they should medicate their child for ADHD. Or I hear from someone who thinks they themselves may have mild to severe ADHD, and they want to know what to do about it. They know I am not an MD, but they tell me it is hard to find a US doctor who doesn’t almost immediately default to prescribing these medications. They are confused and conflicted about what to do.

Here is what everyone should know: All prescription drugs for focus have side effects. These vary by drug, dosage, and by person in ways that can only be determined empirically, meaning by trial and error. Also—and this is very important—the dosage at which some of these drugs are effective is enormously variable. Adderall works to treat ADHD in some people at 5 milligrams, whereas others need 40 milligrams or even more.[^c6-126] It’s simply impossible to know how someone will respond, and it requires time to find the minimum effective dose. Of course, all the drugs in this section require a prescription to acquire legally. Illegal and questionably legal sources carry significant risk. Fentanyl—a deadly opioid—has frequently been found in counterfeit Adderall.[^c6-127]

The reason I call these “the heavy guns” is they work so well that people quickly become dependent on them, and some, such as the amphetamine-based stimulants like Adderall, carry abuse potential because they can create euphoria.[^c6-128] It’s also important to note, however, that failure to treat kids or adults who have ADHD puts them at a much higher risk for addiction than not, due to the impulsivity associated with ADHD.[^c6-129] That said, amphetamines may stunt growth,[^c6-130] cause sleep disturbances,[^c6-131] and even lead to psychosis if abused or taken by people with bipolar depression or a predisposition to psychosis.[^c6-132] And all these drugs are hard to quit.[^c6-133] When someone does try, they often suffer from excessive daytime sleepiness and mood and focus issues, aka withdrawal. It’s much worse than caffeine or nicotine withdrawal, which is why most people don’t quit—they use these drugs indefinitely. Thus, the decision to medicate a child or adult with Adderall or Vyvanse (both amphetamines) or Ritalin (a non-amphetamine stimulant) needs to be carefully considered.

There are also a lot of nondrug therapies for ADHD that can be effective and/or can help reduce dosage needs. They are the foundational and behavioral tools mentioned above. What about supplements? Can alpha-GPC replace a genuine need for Adderall to treat ADHD? Unlikely, but a lifestyle that follows the foundational behaviors described in the protocols here (sleep, hydration, nutrition that favors stable blood sugar levels and satiety, etc.) along with regular meditation or hypnosis for increased focus, and timed use of caffeine and theanine, may allow people to use a lower dose of a prescription drug for ADHD. There are also many cases where these lifestyle changes have allowed people with ADHD to stop taking their medications and still thrive, or thrive even more. It’s all highly individual.

That’s ADHD. What about the person who doesn’t have ADHD, but wants to use a prescription medication to induce states of intense focus one to three times per week? They may be doing everything else correctly, adhering to the foundational tools I’ve described in this chapter, but they want an “edge.” And what about the many millions of people who, due to smartphones, have what clinicians are now calling *mild ADHD*, which is not a diagnosis but a catch-all for no longer being able to focus? Should they take a sympathomimetic? We can no longer pretend that smartphone-induced mild ADHD doesn’t exist. My stance is that we should be aware of all the tools available for focus that are legal, and consider their relative potency and risks.

**RITALIN**

This non-amphetamine stimulant has largely fallen out of favor for the treatment of ADHD and for focus purposes because it’s short acting, and people prefer the stronger, longer lasting effects they get with Adderall and Vyvanse.[^c6-134] A recent brain imaging study found that methylphenidate—the active ingredient in Ritalin—did not actually increase activation of attentional networks in the brain.[^c6-135] It merely reduced the feeling of fatigue and the effects of sleep deprivation on attention. It also made boring work feel more tolerable, and even rewarding—thus allowing for more sustained effort at tasks. The study didn’t look at other stimulants, but this may be a general theme of the drugs covered in this section because few if any stimulants directly increase focus. Raising dopamine levels can reduce background “noise” in the brain, and therefore the tendency to get distracted, and raising norepinephrine increases alertness.[^c6-136] Together, that can make trivial things feel more engaging. It’s important to know that people with ADHD can focus quite well—they just have a much harder time focusing on things they don’t enjoy than do people without ADHD. Alas, much of life requires focusing on things we may prefer not doing. Apparently, stimulants like Ritalin trick the brain into ignoring our preferences.

**ADDERALL AND VYVANSE**

Make no mistake. These are amphetamines, aka speed, but they are not meth. There is a prescription drug for ADHD called Desoxyn, which is pharmaceutical grade methamphetamine, but it’s rarely prescribed due to the addiction and abuse potential.[^c6-137] (Only a few hundred prescriptions exist in the US currently.)

Adderall and Vyvanse are similar to each other but the former works faster, within minutes, and lasts four to six hours; whereas Vyvanse’s effects come on more slowly and last ten or more hours. An estimated 16.5 million people (adults and kids combined) take these amphetamines every day in the United States.[^c6-138] Some for ADHD, and some just to help with focus. They get them with valid prescriptions from board-certified MDs. If that is surprising, consider that despite being 5 percent of the world’s population, the US accounts for more than 80 percent of the prescribed Adderall and Vyvanse taken worldwide.[^c6-139] You can be sure that it is not all being prescribed for clinical levels of ADHD.

Here is my suggestion: If you are considering using these drugs for focus and don’t have diagnosed ADHD (and even if you do), first do an inventory of the foundational and behavioral tools for focus that are listed in this chapter. Are you getting enough sleep and exercise? Are you drinking enough water? Have you tried brief meditation or hypnosis for focus, and perhaps the caffeine, theanine, and/or alpha-GPC combination I described? If not, I suggest you do before resorting to use of prescription-level amphetamines. (Also, see the section “A Note on Phone Management” at the end of this protocol, as the phone is a severe impediment to focusing for many people.)

To be clear, I am not against prescription drugs per se, and if you do take one, don’t stop suddenly. Talk to your doctor. Many prescription drugs have their place in treatment, but unless there is a genuine clinical need, using stimulants as powerful as Adderall or Vyvanse on a regular basis will soon cause dependence, and other tools you try will pale in comparison.

**MODAFINIL AND ARMODAFINIL**

These drugs were designed to treat “excessive daytime sleepiness” caused by narcolepsy or sleep apnea or jet lag. Today, they are commonly prescribed to people simply wishing to improve their focus for work or school. They are not amphetamines, but they can similarly disrupt sleep and appetite, and they still pose some cardiac risk—a feature of all sympathomimetics because they elevate blood pressure and heart rate.[^c6-140] These drugs are interesting because while they raise alertness and focus, they also have the rare feature of also improving cognition, in particular executive functions that allow for orchestrated task switching and working memory—the ability to hold relevant information in mind for only as long as is necessary.[^c6-141] At the same time, they may impair creative divergent thinking.[^c6-142]

In speaking with psychiatrists who prescribe these drugs, I’ve learned that people’s sensitivity to modafinil and armodafinil varies tremendously. Some find 50 milligrams much too stimulating and their sleep is disrupted; others need 200 milligrams to achieve the benefits and sleep just fine. I have tried both armodafinil and modafinil and found they can erase my jet lag but they impair my recall memory. Armodafinil is essentially longer lasting modafinil, but even at the lowest dose of modafinil (I broke a 100 mg tablet in half), I struggled to fall asleep later that night. That said, I have a colleague who takes 100 to 200 milligrams of modafinil four to five times a week, which was prescribed to him for “mild ADHD,” and he has no issues sleeping afterward. These drugs used to be expensive—but the release of generic versions made it less than one dollar per 100 milligram pill. That, combined with their mild cognitive-enhancing effects, makes me think that modafinil and armodafinil use will increase in years to come.

**SUNOSI**

This is a relatively new drug that also acts to increase dopamine and norepinephrine in the brain.[^c6-143] It is FDA approved for offsetting excessive daytime sleepiness due to sleep apnea, and recently it performed well in clinical trials for ADHD,[^c6-144] making it likely to soon be approved for that purpose as well. I know people have already started using Sunosi by off-label legal prescription either daily for ADHD[^c6-145] or occasionally for enhancing focus. Sunosi is not an amphetamine, and thus has less abuse or addictive potential than the other compounds mentioned above. It does not cause euphoria, nor does it seem to cause withdrawal on days it is not taken. Provided the dosing is correct (typically 75–150 mg taken in the morning), it does not seem to disrupt sleep either. Interestingly, Sunosi is a much lower affinity dopamine and epinephrine reuptake inhibitor than Wellbutrin, Adderall, or modafinil and it may have some mild serotonin-increasing effects too. That might explain why people find it less stimulatory and anxiety promoting than other pro-alertness and focus drugs. As with all drugs that increase dopamine, people with conditions that cause mania or psychosis should be cautious about using Sunosi.

**WELLBUTRIN**

This dopamine and norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor is much more noradrenergic than dopaminergic as compared to the other compounds in this section.[^c6-146] This means it raises norepinephrine more than it raises dopamine. It was developed to help with smoking cessation, and to treat depression, while bypassing the sexual side effects caused by many SSRIs. Eventually it was adopted by the ADHD community—a mix of psychiatrists and online patient groups that found it useful for its off-label use to increase focus.[^c6-147] At higher dosages—200 milligrams or more—Wellbutrin increases risk of seizures in those who are seizure prone, and it carries the usual anxiety and cardiac health warnings of all sympathomimetics.[^c6-148] Because of its low dopamine-promoting activity, it has low abuse risk.

I know many people who take 100 to 150 milligrams of Wellbutrin daily—typically the sustained release versions—purely for its energy and focus increasing effects. I have taken 75 to 150 milligrams specifically for that purpose and it worked well, but I found that Wellbutrin impeded my memory, especially for names. I am not sure why or how, but it was a potent and reproducible effect for me. Fortunately, my memory reverted to normal as soon as the drug wore off. I mention this side effect knowing that everyone responds differently to compounds and simply to illustrate how individual the effects of sympathomimetics can be.

> **A Note on Phone Management**
>
> It’s clear we messed up. Smartphones are a great technology for many things: texting, apps, and more. And I do think social media can be used to inform, learn, and teach, and of course for entertainment and social connection (of sorts) too. With most powerful technologies, however, humans tend to go overboard before they course-correct. The time for that course correction is now.
>
> People can’t seem to set their phones down and even if they do, their phones still interfere with the ability to think. A study that looked at the effect of having your phone on your desk versus in a bag in the same room versus in an entirely separate room found that having your phone on your desk or even zipped up in a backpack reduces your working memory and fluid intelligence—the ability to figure things out on the fly—compared to when your phone is placed in a different room.[^c6-149] The authors of the study were able to disentangle focus—people’s ability to direct their attention to a task—from how much mental energy they could devote to what they were focusing on. They found that, even when people could focus on the task at hand, having their phone within physical reach reduced their cognitive ability. Apparently, even if we are not consciously thinking about our phone or seeing notifications, if it’s within our physical proximity our brain devotes mental energy to resist the temptation to pick it up. The takeaway thus is simple: To maximize focus, put your smartphone in an entirely different room from where you are.
>
> Another very useful tool is to restrict your social media apps to an old phone that has a completely different phone number. I did this, and now I purposefully limit my time with my “social media phone” to sixty minutes or less per day.
>
> If you do both those things and still find yourself continually looking at your phone, I suggest getting a timed lockbox that has a no-code-out option—meaning there is no way whatsoever to open the box until the timer has elapsed. I use a no-code-out lockbox for my phone, and find it helps for getting work done. I don’t have ADHD but I find that once the phone is truly inaccessible, my ability to focus is massively increased.
>
> The best analogy I can come up with for the smartphone as it relates to the topic is this: Just as sleep apnea or daytime apnea reduces the amount of oxygen reaching your brain, smartphones cause attentional and cognitive apnea. They lessen the amount of neural activity in our brain circuits for focus. To focus on a work session or a learning bout of any kind, get your phone far out of reach. Your mild-to-severe ADHD may be more phone-proximity-driven than you realize. Perhaps partially, perhaps entirely. There is only one way to find out!

### Learning Protocol 2: Use Mental Contrasting to Achieve a “State of Urgency” and Reach Your Goals

#### What to Do

- **Think of being in “a state of urgency,” rather than a state of motivation.** Urgency is an experience we are all familiar with. We tend to know what it feels like in our mind and body. Motivation can be vague and ephemeral.
- **The most reliable method to create this state is a psychological tool called mental contrasting.** It asks you to imagine your goals, and the obstacles to achieving them, in a structured way. Even if you’re already on your way toward your goals, this strategy can further assist you.

#### How It Works

“Motivation is everything.” We hear this all the time and know it’s true, yet people vary in their abilities to get and stay motivated. Especially to do things that require sustained focus and energy.

The tools I mentioned in the previous protocol were based on physiology as the primary lever. The idea is if we increase sympathetic tone and deploy catecholamines, we can create the neurochemical milieu required for plasticity. I made no mention of psychological tools.

Mental contrasting is a psychological tool, and a powerful one.

Imagine being able to instantly switch on a state of urgency whenever you want. Someday we’ll have that. I’m certain because my colleague at Stanford, neurologist Joe Parvizi, MD, PhD, conducted incredible experiments showing that if activity in a brain area called the anterior midcingulate cortex (aMCC) is increased, people feel an immediate surge in mental energy and readiness to lean into challenges.[^c6-150] Alas, currently the only way to instantly and selectively switch on your aMCC is to drill a hole in your skull, lower an electrode into this region, and pass an electrical current into it. It will be a while—probably five to seven years—before selective aMCC stimulation can be achieved noninvasively. In the meantime, if we want to activate a state of urgency we’re going to have to rely on something else. There is a pill to make you feel more alert and focused, but there is no pill that can make you feel motivated to do a specific task.

Fortunately, a solution does exist. It’s this psychological tool that can reliably shift your mindset, allowing you to become more mentally and physically able to exert effort. But first we should get clear on what a mindset is.

People use the word mindset all the time nowadays but in the context of motivation psychology, it has a very specific meaning and purpose. Alia Crum, a professor of psychology and researcher who directs her own lab at Stanford, explained it best: “A mindset is a setting for your brain.”[^c6-151] Meaning, a mindset is a psychological stance that makes certain thoughts and actions easier to access, and other thoughts and actions harder to access. Alia’s definition also speaks to the power of mindsets to simultaneously influence different aspects of your physiology—your brain directs many systems, including your nervous system, your hormones, even your immune system, in specific ways.[^c6-152] That, in turn, guides our behavior. When we switch to a mindset that embraces a challenge, it activates neural circuitries and chemical reactions that make us feel more capable of running that extra mile, putting in extra study hours, or going for one more hour of piano practice. Physiology is also a lever here, but a secondary one.

You may have heard the term “growth mindset,” coined by Stanford psychologist Carol Dweck. The term refers to the belief that ability is not fixed but rather can improve with effort.[^c6-153] With a growth mindset, a teenager who is failing calculus understands that studying hard will lead to better comprehension. That state unlocks the possibility for even more: You believe in the effort that learning requires, and take the action that it requires too. Upholding a growth mindset means you actively avoid identity-based and valuation labels of being good or bad at something. You aren’t “good” or “bad”; you simply haven’t put in the effort and taken the action yet. A growth mindset never says, “I’m not a math person”; it says, “I can get better at math if I work at it.” Experiments from Carol and others show that adopting a growth mindset can drive significant improvements in learning, especially when paired with a stress-can-enhance-performance mindset.[^c6-154] That last bit—that stress can help with growth—implies that challenge can improve your outcome, rather than limit you.

Maybe you are wondering: If stress is so great for learning, then why aren’t we all great learners? We all certainly feel stress. I think it’s because for most of us, the feeling we have when we fail at doing something difficult overrides the desire to keep striving. That is one reason I continually share ways for real-time autonomic self-regulation, like the physiological sigh described in chapter 3. These protocols are designed to lower stress not only to help people feel calm, but also to expand people’s sense of what’s possible to learn. If we have the tools to control stress, we can seek out more challenge.

No matter how well we control our stress, however, we are still left with the challenge of how to activate a growth mindset and stress-can-enhance-performance mindset. In other words: How do we actually get motivated? Should we use self-talk? Watch an inspirational clip on YouTube? Fantasize about achieving our goal? Scare ourselves with the fear of not achieving it? How many milligrams of fear should we take? Just kidding. Sort of.

The answer starts, I believe, with swapping the word *motivation* with *a state of urgency*. Here is why:

- A state of urgency is less prone to parsing than motivation, which immediately raises questions about context. Friedrich Nietzsche offered powerful wisdom when he wrote, “*Hat man sein warum? des Lebens, so verträgt man sich fast mit jedem wie?*”[^c6-155] Some readers may be more familiar with the English translation made famous by Austrian neurologist, psychiatrist, and Holocaust survivor Viktor Frankl: “He who has a why to live for can bear with almost any how.”[^c6-156]
- Sometimes the why is clear. But what about when it isn’t? What about the many aspects of learning and life that require persistent effort and for which the why, the deeper meaning and larger purpose, is unclear? Often the why only becomes clear during, or even after, the how. Maybe a person is forced to take a course they hate in order to get a degree. Once they complete the course, however, they may realize the new opportunities have been made accessible to them only because of the material they learned in the course; it wasn’t just a means to an end after all. A state of urgency doesn’t require you to have all the answers yet.
- A state of urgency stimulates catecholamine release, which further increases sympathetic tone, which therefore increases focus.[^c6-157] This helps dim distractions, both internal and external, which improves performance… and increases your state of urgency.[^c6-158] It’s a positive feedback loop.
- It’s obvious why a sense of urgency would help you maximize the number of repetitions that you can do in a given time frame. That’s huge because genuine attempts are the fundamental unit of all forms of learning.
- It’s specific enough that we know what to aim for, experientially, but broad in the sense that it applies to all activities and pursuits. Motivation drives you to try something, a state of urgency keeps you practicing.

So now the question is not, “How do we get motivated?” It’s “How do we create a state of urgency?”

The answer is mental contrasting, which is a tool based on the research of Gabriele Oettingen, PhD, a professor at New York University and the University of Hamburg.[^c6-159] The term is the result of her deep dive into understanding two psychological tools long thought to be helpful to this topic: positive thinking and visualization. The terms are likely familiar to you. Positive thinking refers to the practice of deliberately holding an optimistic view about an outcome as a way to help that hoped-for result come true. Visualization refers to the practice of imagining a desired future outcome, again as a way to help that result come true. Research had shown that a positive mindset can have beneficial effects on health and well-being.[^c6-160]

But as Oettingen and others have discovered, although positive thinking and visualization are great, they often undermine motivation just as easily as they can increase it. And get this: Too much positive thinking about goal outcomes undermines performance.[^c6-161] Apparently, visualization causes people’s brain reward mechanisms to get sufficiently activated, so they feel less energy to continue to strive for the goal.[^c6-162] And positive thinking provides a big but transient boost in motivation.

All that is consistent with what we know about dopamine in the context of goal seeking and rewards. As Anna Lembke, an expert on dopamine, put it, dopamine is about wanting, not about having.[^c6-163] That’s another downside of positive thinking: It activates the “want” circuitries but not the “have” ones. Anna further pointed out that the neural circuits underlying motivation evolved in times of scarcity, where effort almost always preceded reward—think hunting, gathering, seeking shelter, finding a mate, and so on. Because of the abundance of stimulation in modern life, which was designed to satisfy and even exploit our dopamine circuitry, most of us have recalibrated our motivation and reward circuits to expect more reward from less effort.[^c6-164] And while Anna’s work has mainly focused on addictive and compulsive behaviors, we’ve all seen this play out for goals too.[^c6-165] Too much reward prior to effort, or too much reward without effort, undermines future effort.

A friend of mine, an MD turned successful startup investor, warned me to be careful about telling too many people about a big goal. Most will respond, he explained, by saying “You would be great at that, go for it!” Unless you have a lot at stake, the reward of all that positive feedback can undermine your drive to actually pursue the goal. I asked him if he thought it would be better if we responded instead by saying, “Don’t try, you’ll never succeed!” “I don’t think that helps either,” he replied.

He was right. Oettingen found that if people focus too much on the challenge they’ll likely face, that too prevents them from pursuing goals, at least in the long run.

So much for just “Focus on the journey not the destination.”

We can thus all be grateful to Oettingen for carrying out experiments that tested various common motivational tools, alone and in combination. She also explored their efficacy for helping people achieve different types of goals: learning cognitive skills, learning physical skills, making better food choices, exercising more, and on and on.[^c6-166] She eventually discovered that it is the contrast between visualizing the goal and thinking about the obstacles to achieve it that creates a state of heightened physical and mental energy, and that state is what leads us to be more likely to start—and to persist.[^c6-167]

In other words, Oettingen figured out how people can activate a state of urgency. She calls the approach mental contrasting, and she calls the way to implement it WOOP, an acronym that stands for *Wish, Outcome, Obstacles, Plan*.[^c6-168] The four steps of WOOP can be done in your head, but it works best if you record your answers. Try writing them down, or hitting the record button on your phone. It works for both short- and long-term goals.

**WISH: Name the big, overall goal. What do you want to happen?**

- **For example:**
  - “I want to learn guitar well enough to play with a band live in front of a thousand people.”
  - “I want to get a PhD in neuroscience from a top program.”
  - “I want to learn to speak fluent German.”
  - “I want to paint well enough to make a living selling my art.”

It takes only a few seconds to complete the *W* step in WOOP. You don’t need to include a lot of detail, but some helps. For instance, “I want to be happy and successful” is too general. Instead of focusing on what you want to feel, name skills, credentials, and proficiencies that you’re hoping to achieve.

**OUTCOME: Here is where you think about what you want to feel from having**

**achieved the goal.**

- **For example:**
  - “I will experience the thrill of performing live with other great musicians and knowing that I’m giving people the live music experience I know and love so much too.”
  - “I will feel the freedom and excitement of being able to work for any number of different companies exploring for cures to neurodegenerative diseases.”
  - “I will enjoy going to Germany to visit my spouse’s family, be able to relate to them better, and maybe even work and start a life there someday. And I can help our kids become bilingual.”
  - “I will finally get to indulge my desire to be creative. And I can sleep in late and stay up late painting while listening to music, which is what I always wanted!”

You’ll notice this outcome step is aspirational—you’re encouraged to daydream about how you want to feel. I gave short examples here but feel free to expand on the many things you look forward to feeling. The reality check is next.

**OBSTACLES: Get clear on the obstacles you anticipate en route to your goal.**

Be hyperrealistic. Record the roadblocks you might face. Include how you might feel as you do. People’s temperaments vary, but you know yourself—so be honest about how you’ll react when things don’t go to plan.

- **For example:**
  - “I tend to be really tired from work at the end of the day. I’m going to feel frustrated when I am too tired to practice guitar or when traffic makes me late to guitar lessons.”
  - “I will miss the chance to attend weddings and go on fun vacations with my friends because I’ll be in the lab doing experiments or studying. I won’t have much money because PhD students don’t get paid much.” “It will be a long time before I am truly fluent in German because I learn really slowly. And writing in German is even more difficult than speaking it, so I will get discouraged a lot.”
  - “The art I make is not likely to appeal to a lot of people because I like melancholy themes and darker tones, and most people seem to buy art that is happy and playful.”

Again, feel free to expand as much as you want to for this step.

**PLAN: Come up with if-then statements to address the obstacles you anticipated.** These are *action* steps.

- **For example:**
  - “On days when I’m too tired to practice guitar after work, I will go to sleep early and get up thirty minutes earlier than usual the next day. That way I can get fifteen to twenty minutes of practice done in the morning. My mind is much sharper then anyway. Playing in the morning also makes me feel good for hours, so maybe work might not feel so exhausting. If I’m late to guitar practice because of traffic, then I will do my best to stay calm and practice in my head on the way there. I will add a few minutes of practice in my car after the lesson to really drill in what I learned.”
  - “When I can’t attend fun events because of time or money restrictions, I will remember that having a PhD in neuroscience puts me at a unique advantage for job choices and long-term financial security because there is so much still to discover about nervous system diseases… and we still don’t have cures to most all of them. Also, a lot of my friends who make more money than me now are bored with their jobs or have already maximized their earning potential. I will be able to consult and/or invest in biotech companies because I really understand where the field is and where it might grow. Also, I will remember that I love doing experiments.”
  - “If I feel frustrated at my slow progress learning German, I will remind myself that the frustration is a signal my brain is getting the message to change, and that a lot of learning happens in bursts; it’s rarely linear. I will ask my spouse (who is fluent) if we can do an only-in-German dinner once per week as a family, so I and the kids can practice. I will use AI to generate some free German language quizzes for me that I can listen to when I’m alone in the car.”
  - “I will remind myself that the best art has always come from people who really care about the work they are doing, and that I really feel and believe in the messages that motivate the art I create. I’ll set up a website and social media platform so I can connect with other artists with similar tastes, and learn from them about marketing my work.”

  You may have noticed what happened there. Mental contrasting quickly moves you from idealizing and making aspirational statements about goals and feelings to concrete action steps… and, more importantly, clarity about how you will deal with setbacks. It customizes the process of getting motivated. If you’re optimistic and unflappable and start new projects all the time or if you’re pessimistic and tend to talk yourself out of things or if it depends on the circumstances or the time of day or the goal, mental contrasting still works. It also serves as a strategy setting session. It’s not a pep talk. It’s a preparation exercise that has been proven to help people get started and persist in pursuit of their goals. It’s also zero cost, and takes around ten minutes at the outset. It’s a real gift to us all, and we have Oettingen, along with the students and postdocs that ran the experiments, to thank for it.

##### In My Experience

I used mental contrasting for a goal that I had been procrastinating on forever. I followed the WOOP process. I typed out the WOOP answers into a word processing document and hit Save. That took about ten minutes.

And it worked spectacularly well for me. It somehow cleared away the laziness and analysis paralysis and all the other stuff that had been holding me back, and I enjoyed two solid work sessions that very day, and then two months of steady effort toward the goal thereafter, even though I was in my busiest season of work and I had many other commitments.

When I started feeling a bit unmotivated again, I reread the document. I made some edits and additions based on new changes in life. That only took about five minutes. I now do mental contrasting for learning goals, for work goals, for fitness goals, and for personal goals too. I reread and update the WOOP documents whenever I am feeling a bit unmotivated. It’s become reflexive. I don’t share my WOOP answers with anyone, they are for me and for me only, but you can decide if you want to keep yours private or not.

##### The Mechanisms Behind Mental Contrasting

I was struck that mental contrasting seemed to increase my motivation across the board, not just for my specific goal. I procrastinate far less on everything now. I’m not aware of any data showing that doing mental contrasting rewires specific brain areas, but given what we know about the aMCC, I wonder if it might. Recall how Joe Parvizi conducted incredible experiments showing that if activity in the aMCC is increased, people feel an immediate surge in mental energy and readiness to lean into challenges. Especially since every instance of learning—whether that’s a new behavior or a new piece of information—is the consequence of plasticity and our aMCC is the brain structure most closely associated with tenacity.[^c6-169] It has been shown to increase in volume in successful dieters, people who push themselves to stick to a new exercise program, and other situations where thinking about and overcoming a challenge is called for. Parvizi discovered the role of the aMCC in 2013, and only recently has it been discussed in the larger field of neuroscience and media, so I doubt that Oettingen was aware of its potential role in WOOP. I look forward to a day soon when someone explores whether the aMCC is activated by going through the steps of the WOOP Protocol. In the meantime, I plan to keep using mental contrasting any time I need to generate a state of urgency for something, and I hope you’ll consider it too.

##### Why Some People Will Avoid Mental Contrasting

This may surprise the dreamers and go-getters, but a lot of people are afraid to strategize around—let alone think about—their big goals. Some of that is cultural[^c6-170] but in my observation a lot of people are afraid to change, even if they are unhappy with their current circumstances. It’s just not reflexive (and in many cases it feels aversive) for them to do so. Before you conclude that a resistance to change is just the way you’re wired, consider the experiment where people preferred to get strong electrical shocks they knew were coming at specific times… versus weaker electrical shocks that arrived without warning.[^c6-171] The same general conclusion comes from studies of pain. People like what’s predictable, even if it isn’t good. That defies logic until we remember that our nervous systems are prediction machines that seek to minimize energy expenditure.[^c6-172] So, while mental contrasting is merely a mental exploration of a goal, I anticipate some people will shy away from it… because change is hard. I hope you don’t and instead, go with the data. Put it to work for you. WOOP is a really cool tool to explore new things, and I’m grateful Gabriele Oettingen and colleagues came up with it. And learning to switch on a state of urgency to increase focus and achieve your goals and get things done in life is a valuable superpower, for SDAP and beyond.

### Learning Protocol 3: Embrace Errors to Improve Your Performance

#### What to Do

- **Embrace the fact that errors are an essential trigger for learning.** Errors that come from genuine attempts to learn something are the signal for plasticity to occur. This is true for all forms of skill development: cognitive, motor, musical, mathematical, et cetera, and why it’s an essential step in SDAP.
- **Strive to perform at a level of difficulty just slightly beyond your current ability.** Studies show that the right level is such that it produces an error rate of 15 to 30 percent. The 30 percent level tends to work best for learning motor skills, whereas 15 percent is the approximate level to shoot for with cognitive skills.
- **Don’t make errors deliberately.** That won’t have the same result. Work on pushing yourself past what you think you can do and using your mistakes as learning tools.

#### How It Works

If you can do something with proficiency, your nervous system won’t change. The gap between your current level of ability (even if it’s zero!) and the level you are striving for is what triggers learning and plasticity. No gap, no change.

Before I dive into this protocol, I need to make something clear. There are many forms of learning and plasticity that don’t require making errors. Just look at what happens with children. As every parent knows, a toddler learns that ice cream is delicious in a matter of seconds, and never forgets it. They also learn that tablets and phones can display cartoons after seeing them only once. No errors needed. (By contrast, learning to walk, to speak, or to eat with utensils are all examples of learning and plasticity that require errors to eventually master.) Traumatic events, at any age, are also examples of error-independent learning and plasticity. So is the learning that comes from experiencing a welcome surprise. Let’s say you drop by a friend’s party expecting to say hello and then go home early, but you end up meeting someone you really like there. You can be sure you will remember their name, their job, et cetera. Should a great long-term relationship emerge from it, you’ll no doubt maintain fond memories of the party, the friend who hosted it, and the events of the entire weekend when the party occurred.

You can thank dopamine for that. Dopamine helps us learn by linking our memories of prior actions, and the contexts in which they took place, with our sense of whether things went better or worse than we expected—a phenomenon known as *reward prediction error*.[^c6-173] It makes perfect sense why this evolved: to help us find and remember the paths we took to life-sustaining resources—food, water, shelter, potential mates, et cetera. Unwelcome surprises, even if they are not traumatic, shape our memories, help us learn, and guide our future actions too. Whereas positive events simultaneously increase dopamine and lower serotonin, negative events do the opposite. Say that instead of meeting a new friend at a party, you unexpectedly run into an old boss you hoped to never see again. That would shape your expectations and motivations around future gatherings at that house. It may even change your feelings about the friend—a phenomenon known to neuroscientists as *context-dependent plasticity*.[^c6-174]

##### Why We Need To Make Mistakes

You’ll notice that none of the examples of learning I just described require that we make errors. Stuff happened, for better or worse, and learning occurred. It speaks to the many types of plasticity.

SDAP is different. We *need* to make errors. With errors often comes some amount of agitation, of limbic friction, which by now you know is a good thing because it increases the release of catecholamines that facilitate focus and plasticity. But also, perhaps more importantly, mistakes provide the signal that sets the size and type of neural circuit changes (and thus skill improvement) that follow learning attempts.

I’ll use motor skills as an example but the same holds true for all types of skills. Let’s say you want to learn tennis. You need to learn to serve the ball. At first, it’s likely that you’ll hit the ball into the net often. Each time you do, it’s an error that you register as objective performance feedback. You adjust your serve accordingly. You may decide “that last serve was too hard, I’ll use less force this time” or “perhaps I am gripping the racket too high on the handle, I’ll hold it lower” or “I’m throwing the ball too high before I swing,” and so on. Even if you have a tennis coach who gives you instructions, you are the only one who has access to the proprioceptive information associated with each serve attempt—by that I mean the awareness of your body’s movements. Your nervous system tracks each and every one of those, and compares it to the performance outcome. Some of that is conscious, and some is unconscious, working below your level of awareness.

Remember back in chapter 3, when we discussed what your nervous system does? As you may recall, whether you are asleep or awake, your nervous system is handling the basic stuff of survival, making sure that your heart keeps beating, your lungs keep expanding, your digestion keeps flowing, and so on. It is also letting you perceive the world around you. And, as we also discussed, your nervous system is also a *prediction machine*. It’s constantly trying to make causal inferences: “If I do A, then B seems to happen immediately afterward… If I don’t do X, then Y happens a few hours later…” When you are awake, your nervous system is running a ceaseless if-then analysis of you and your actions and feelings, thoughts and memories; of others and their actions and feelings, thoughts and memories; of the world around you, and on and on.

Here is the key thing to remember: Any time your nervous system figures out that one of your actions leads to a successful outcome, it starts to shift the pattern of neural firing that occurred from your conscious awareness into your *implicit motor memory*. It works to make the action automatic. The rationale for that is obvious: Thinking and doing and making associations is metabolically demanding. As is rewiring brain circuitry.[^c6-175] The more your brain can make things automatic, the more energy it can devote to other things. This is especially true in the case of skill learning. With maintaining focus, moving into a state of urgency, making errors, and calibrating adjustments, we can all learn to execute new skills. Once we do, we don’t need to think about each step. We simply activate performance of the skill. We serve the ball, play the chord, finish the math problem. Voila!

I acknowledge that your reaction to this point might be: “Duh!” But I said there was a key thing to remember. It will forever change the way you approach learning.

First, your brain doesn’t work alone here. It needs your second brain. No, not your gut. I’m referring to the mini brain tucked right under your occipital lobe. If you touch the top of your neck where it meets the back of your skull, you’re touching the area just above your cerebellum, aka your mini brain. Many people have heard of the cerebellum for its role in balance, but your cerebellum is also crucial for eye movements related to attention, for proprioceptive awareness, for speaking, for estimating time, for your sense of rhythm, and much more. Your cerebellum is also a key site of action for comparing what you are trying to do with what you’re currently doing, and sending the rest of your nervous system the signals it needs to close the gap in performance.

I would love to devote a thousand pages to the function of the cerebellum in learning because it is that cool, but I’ll keep it (relatively) brief. When you make errors in the context of trying to learn a new skill, you activate neurons in your cerebellum. The bigger the error, the larger the response from your cerebellum. Your cerebellum is kind of like that tennis coach in this regard, except unlike a coach that observes you and makes educated guesses as to what you need to do in order to improve, your cerebellum has full access to both your inner and outer workings: the angles of your limbs and joints, the speed and stretch of your muscles; it knows when you blinked relative to your maximum effort, your level of autonomic arousal, et cetera. Thus, your cerebellum is also uniquely suited to be your coach because of both the *specificity* and the *interconnectedness* of its wiring. Different cerebellar neurons respond to the movement of different parts of the body, even your eyes and lips and tongue. It also encodes how movement of one body area changes the movement of all the others. If you consciously adjust the angle of your elbow and it improves your serve, your cerebellum registers the many other changes that accompanied the elbow adjustment and then makes sure they become part of your serve “motor program” going forward. If your elbow angle adjustment makes things worse, your cerebellum registers that too. With repeated effort, your brain eventually stamps down the exact motor program needed to serve the ball properly.

I wish we all learned about the role of the cerebellum in learning when we were kids. Instead, we watched *Star Wars, Harry Potter, X-Men*, and Marvel movies, et cetera, which are all wonderful stories, but sadly also embed the false idea in us that skills are things that just need to be activated, as if by magic. Of course, that’s fiction. The real-life superpower all of us possess from birth is our ability to focus and learn. We can progress from unskilled to skilled, and from skilled to mastery. Your cerebellum, and the larger neural circuit it participates in, is the coach that guides the entire progression. If that were the message, I believe the frustration that comes from errors would take on a whole new meaning. We would (and should) view errors and the agitation that come from genuine attempts to learn as something to seek out, not to avoid. *Errorful learning*, as some researchers call it, appears to be the most efficient approach to acquiring new skills.[^c6-176]

##### The Goldilocks Zone for Errors

You may be asking, “How many errors are needed? And what kind?” In a study published in 2019, researchers set out to determine the optimal level of difficulty—the Goldilocks zone for learning new skills.[^c6-177] They calculated the ideal rate of error using several learning algorithms and found that training progressed much faster when the level of difficulty set was associated with an accuracy rate of about 85 percent (an error rate of 15 percent). A few additional insights emerged from this study. First, when something is too hard such that 50 percent of attempts were unsuccessful, the brain can’t seem to capture the right strategy for neural circuit modification. It was much better, the researchers found, to continually adjust the training level to maintain the approximately 15 percent error rate. This was a quantitative modeling study, meaning the findings are based on a simulation, but it was aligned with studies of visual-perception-based decision-making and motor learning.

It works for cognitive tasks too. For example, students who are allowed to figure out how to solve complex math problems on their own—and therefore can make mistakes—tend to do better than students who are told the right way to do it from the start.[^c6-178] And we seem to know this intuitively. In one study, researchers at Columbia University asked fifty-two people to play a series of computer games.[^c6-179] They were free to choose from a range of games, some of which were easy, some harder, and some impossible to learn. As the task progressed, participants chose increasingly difficult games and preferred to repeat the challenging games rather than repeat the easy ones.

Remember the 15 percent “rule” is an approximate measure. There’s no need to become obsessed with maintaining this exact error rate. To put it in simple terms, you want to work at a level at which you’re getting things right much of the time, but also wrong some of the time.

This insight can be used in education as well. Given the relationship between errors and plasticity, and the pivotal role of the cerebellum in that process, teachers should consider reserving verbal feedback to students in cases where the students thought they got something right but actually didn’t. Otherwise, it’s better to give students the opportunity to register their own errors.

The moment immediately following making a mistake is critical for learning. Negative reactions typically occur within 100 milliseconds,[^c6-180] but the sympathetic arousal lasts longer and provides the milieu for enhanced focus and plasticity as we have discussed many times now. Which means our systems are primed for learning in those immediate post-error moments. This internal state improves the effectiveness of the whole learning bout. Studies of motor learning show that within-trial errors and across-trial errors both provide valuable signals for plasticity and learning.[^c6-181] If you leave a language class or tennis lesson or other learning bout thinking, “Darn, I couldn’t seem to get that right on that one part,” well, congratulations! The learning process set in motion by within-and across-trial errors was triggered. You’ll no doubt come back better next time… but only if you do what’s in the next protocol.

### Learning Protocol 4: Prioritize Sleep the Night After a Learning Bout

#### What to Do

- **Get adequate sleep the night after a learning bout.** That’s when plasticity actually occurs, and why it’s an essential step in the SDAP process.
- **Enhance plasticity by practicing ten to thirty minutes of NSDR at any point after a learning bout.** Done prior, as described in Protocol 1 of this chapter, it will increase your mental and physical vigor.

#### How It Works

During sleep, our brains rapidly replay what we tried to learn during the day, including what errors to avoid in the future. Brain imaging and electrophysiological recordings show that the very same neural firing sequences that occurred during learning bouts occur again at that time.[^c6-182] If the patterns of brain activity in sleep are disrupted, we don’t learn as well. Sleep isn’t just a time for consolidation, it’s also when we build schemas—which are extractions of common themes of movement or ideas that let our brain store information in a more efficient way. They serve as patterns that become part of our foundational understanding of how the world works.

Evidence points to REM sleep in the first night after a learning bout as being the most crucial for the learning consolidation process, a phenomenon known as the *night after learning effect*, but depending on the skill you’re trying to master, deep slow wave sleep may matter more.[^c6-183] I wouldn’t parse things that finely. Rather, do your best to get adequate (for you) sleep every night, but especially in times of striving to master new information and skills. I define adequate sleep in chapter 1, and give you lots of tools to use to achieve it. If you suffer a poor night’s sleep, however, don’t make things worse by fretting about the learning lost from it. Do NSDR the next morning, and get your sleep schedule back on track that night.

### Learning Protocol 5: Incorporate Micro Rests into Your Learning Bouts

#### What to Do

- **Pause now and then between repetitions as you practice a new motor or cognitive skill.** These *waking micro rests* have been shown to accelerate learning by increasing repetition density at the level of neural circuit activation.
  - **Short breaks of five to thirty seconds** during a learning bout in which you do nothing at all (meaning, no checking your phone!) can significantly accelerate motor learning.
  - **Short breaks of five to ten minutes** during a learning bout focused on cognitive learning can do the same. These micro rests induce ten to twenty times accelerated replay of the neural circuit firing pattern related to what you are trying to learn.

#### How It Works

We try to perform a new skill and we fail, and fail again, and get close, but fail again. We get a few nights’ adequate sleep, and when we come back for our next attempt, somehow we’ve improved.

The previous protocol explained how sleep reinforces neural circuit firing patterns that allow our brains to integrate new skills. But recent studies show that a waking micro rest can increase consolidation on fast timescales too—meaning in just seconds to minutes, and even during the learning bout.

The observation that people learn faster if they pause from time to time between repetitions goes back to the late 1800s, when the German psychologist Hermann Ebbinghaus measured his ability to learn new material.[^c6-184] He saw that spaced repetitions led to faster and more stable learning than continuous repetition. That was self-experimentation, but many years later, in a study led by National Institutes of Health physiologist Marlene Bönstrup, twenty-seven participants were asked to practice several keyboard-based motor skills, tasks that were well established in the research of memory and learning.[^c6-185] Participants had to tap out a sequence of five items using their nondominant hand. They were given thirty-six tries to learn the sequence, with each attempt lasting ten seconds followed by ten seconds of rest. Performance was measured according to both speed and accuracy.

At first, Bönstrup and her colleagues examined the learning curve across all thirty-six attempts of a given sequence. They could see the performance improved rapidly, and then petered out at around the eleventh cycle. That’s a familiar pattern. We often get better at a new skill fast and then reach a ceiling when further improvements become harder.

But the researchers noticed something interesting. All along, they had been monitoring the participants’ brain waves. During very brief periods of rest between repetitions—lasting about ten seconds—the patterns of brain activity showed a unique signature. They tended to occur in regions connected to our ability to plan our movements. The researchers hypothesized that some form of additional rehearsal was occurring in their brains during the micro-rest periods, and it might be important for plasticity. That mapped well onto Ebbinghaus’s observation. A second study, carried out in 2020 by Ethan Buch and others, found that micro rests induce rapid plasticity and learning, most likely because the same neural circuits active during the attempt to perform the motor skill get replayed during the micro rest in between repetitions, but at about twenty-fold the speed and forward and backward.[^c6-186] In other words, waking micro rests increase repetition density. This *wakeful consolidation* seems to allow you to integrate the new motor sequence with prior learned sequences. Of course, it’s during sleep when our brains really engrave the circuits carrying newly learned information. Nonetheless micro rests of ten to thirty seconds during motor learning bouts, and five to ten minutes during cognitive learning bouts, have been shown to improve many different types of skills.[^c6-187]

You may be wondering what to do during the micro rests, and how often to take them. For a learning bout focused on motor learning, the key is to simply pause and not do another rep for five to ten seconds. A bit longer, say fifteen or seventeen or twenty seconds is not a problem, so don’t obsess about the exact duration. Just pause for a short time, and then continue. You can draw a bit or just sit there—which sounds boring and might make you feel lazy, but the data say you are learning faster. Yes, you can get up and walk around, use the bathroom, et cetera. Just stay off your phone, web browser, or email…!

Introduce micro rests somewhat at random. How often you do them depends on the complexity and the duration of a repetition. Practicing serving a tennis ball is very different, for instance, from practicing an entire song on the piano. I suggest you start the learning bout by doing continuous repetitions one after the other, and when you start to make errors, introduce a pause every third or fifth trial, then go back to continuous repetitions, and then pause after every error or every other or every third error. If you want, you could set a chime to go off at random intervals. A website that offers that feature for free is <http://www.random.org/clock-times> and there is another great, no-cost website at <http://www.microbreaks.co/timer.html> that lets you set the parameters, including (1) learning bout duration, (2) duration of micro-break, and (3) the tone you want to hear, et cetera. It’s terrific for both cognitive and motor skill learning. (Note: I have no affiliation to it but I use it.)

Waking micro rests are a great tool for accelerating learning and plasticity that are based in behavioral and neuroscience-backed data. I suggest trying them.

### Learning Protocol 6: Increase Retention of New Skills and Information with Mental Rehearsal

#### What to Do

- **Take one to five minutes to reflect on what you read or did during a learning bout at some point after the learning bout concludes.** The key is to test yourself for what you do and do not remember, do or do not comprehend. That’s why it’s the final step of SDAP.
  - **For cognitive skills and new information**, this can be informal, done simply as a mental exercise, or more formal, such as by having a friend or ChatGPT test you for comprehension on the exact same material.
  - **For motor skills**, think about where you were challenged and made errors.

#### How It Works

All of learning is anti-forgetting.

On the one hand, that statement is another giant “DUH!” But through the lens of what we know about how humans learn and remember new information and skills, it’s a very important concept to integrate.

The human brain can’t remember all it senses and perceives. Even though neuromodulators can serve as a sort of highlighter pen for certain experiences, most information is forgotten. Neuroimaging studies have shown that for people who learn to juggle as adults, their brain circuits rewire to reflect the specific skills of juggling but those changes are quickly lost if they don’t practice.[^c6-188] Both memories and new skills extinguish quickly, in days to weeks, unless they are locked in by rehearsal. The exception to this is, of course, the information related to very emotionally charged events, for reasons partially discussed earlier in this chapter. When adrenaline is very high, a second memory pathway involving our amygdala and other limbic-associated structures opens up and we remember more “snapshots” of whatever took place while in the high arousal state.[^c6-189]

Rehearsal in the form of self-testing turns out to be the best way to protect newly acquired skills and information against forgetting. A classic 2006 study from psychologists Henry Roediger and Jeffrey Karpicke compared repeated reading of a passage of text with one-time reading of the text combined with later mental reflection, and found that mental reflection was far superior when it came to both retention and comprehension of the material.[^c6-190] That’s pretty wild if you think about it. People who spend less time with the actual material but attempt to review what they do and don’t remember, and what they do and don’t comprehend, can work with it more flexibly. That tells us that what we remember is not simply a matter of how much time we spend with information or in an experience, but that reflection somehow reinforces and enhances the circuits carrying that information or experience.

This research has vast implications for educational settings, particularly for how best to study. We know that underlining and highlighting information only helps us remember it if we also later write down what was highlighted and underlined. It also means that testing—whether by our teacher or ourselves—is not just a form of evaluation to gauge our level of knowledge, it also represents a valuable “anti-forgetting” tool that helps us remember the information for months or years to come.[^c6-191]

The takeaway is clear: Tests work. If you’re a teacher or coach, yes, this justifies pop and scheduled quizzes. It may help to test on recently learned material in exercises that count toward a grade. And, yes, don’t tell the students that until after the quiz.

For those without a teacher or coach navigating SDAP, reflect on what you learned, and most of all: self test! You can do so informally or formally. AI is a great tool for this. Ask ChatGPT to quiz you on a given set of material as a teacher would. Or simply take a few minutes and test your level of recall or physical skill on your own. Try to find where your ability drops off. It takes only a few minutes and is immensely valuable. You’ll learn faster and retain more of what you learn.

## Chapter 7: Protocols for Personal Growth

![Chapter emblem](images/chapter-emblem.jpeg)

Thus far I’ve focused on protocols, and the science they’re based on, for bolstering key pillars of your health and performance: sleep, exercise, nutrition, stress management, light exposure, as well as focus, motivation, and learning. You’ll notice I did so mostly through the lens of biology, not psychology. Even when talking about mindsets or ways to generate a sense of urgency, the emphasis unabashedly has been on the biological underpinnings of what makes these protocols work. That reflects my training and interests, but as I mentioned in the introduction it’s also an essential part of how these protocols work. They are customizable to your needs. When you know how a machine works—how the parts fit together—you come away knowing which aspects you can modify.

We, however, are *not* machines. We think and feel, and hope and fear, and more. That needs attention too. The quality of our lives is strongly driven by our emotional lives, our relationships to others and to ourselves. After all, what good is it feeling vital and rested, focused and resilient, fit and capable, if we don’t also enjoy our time with others, and with ourselves? We just can’t overlook these aspects of life.

Scores of data now tell us the obvious: that social connection is vital to our health and longevity.[^c7-1] Like all the other Old World primates, we have an immense need to care for and be cared for by others.[^c7-2] Our nervous system evolved to crave and require these types of interactions we consciously or unconsciously register as safety.[^c7-3] Not just safety from harm, but also the sort of safety that makes us feel capable of seeking out challenges: healthy risk-taking in our work, new goals in our hobbies, going on adventures; all things that give us a sense that life, our life, matters.

Equally important but far less discussed is our relationship to ourselves. That’s an admittedly squishy term. What I mean is how we talk to ourselves, and how we think about ourselves—the decisions we make, the paths we choose. In fact, this chapter could have been called “Protocols for Thinking.” My goal here is not to get you to second-guess yourself. Quite the opposite. It’s about clearing the clutter from your mind so you can think better. It’s about moving forward on the right path and not mindlessly slaving away on the wrong one.

What are thoughts anyway?

Marcus Aurelius famously said, “Our life is what our thoughts make it”[^c7-4] and nearly identical statements were made by René Descartes,[^c7-5] the Buddha,[^c7-6] Ralph Waldo Emerson,[^c7-7] William Shakespeare,[^c7-8] and in the Bible.[^c7-9] Most people would agree their thoughts are a crucial feature of their experience of life but few ever stop to ask, “What are thoughts?” Most neuroscience textbooks don’t even attempt to answer that question. They include chapters on sensation, perception, emotions, behaviors, even memories and dreams, but not a single textbook that I am aware of provides a good explanation of what thoughts are. Fortunately, researchers are starting to figure it out.

Jennifer Groh, PhD, neuroscientist at Duke University, researches how our brain maps, or *represents*, to use the neuroscience term, the world around us.[^c7-10] That makes her particularly well suited to answer the question “What are thoughts?” because thoughts are representations too. They are estimates, approximations, best guesses. She explained to me, “When we are thinking, we are running simulations with the sensory and motor infrastructure of our brain.” She gave me the following example, posed as a brief series of questions. If you want, you can answer them now as well.

Think of a cat.

What comes to mind first?

Chances are the partial or complete mental image of a cat, or maybe the sound of a cat. Something cattish.

Now ask yourself: What color is the cat?

What next comes to mind?

For me, it was a gray cat and very soon afterward, the smell of kitty litter, which I intensely dislike. Then a memory of the laundry room in the house where I grew up, which is where my sister’s cat Samantha often slept.

The point is that anything that we focus on—an image seen or imagined, a song, a memory, and so on—causes the sensory areas of our brain to become active. That means our visual areas, auditory areas, the areas involved in processing touch, et cetera, all ramp up their levels of electrical activity. And while each of these areas has a different name and a different job in representing the world around us, they are all extensively interconnected too. They don’t work in isolation. They work as parts of what are called distributed networks. Which sensory area is activated first and which ones follow depends on what “seeds” the thought. In the above example it was the word *cat* but think about the extremely soft fur of a chinchilla. That may set off a thought that activates the touch area of your brain, and you might experience a simulation of touch, what neuroscientists call somatosensation. From there, the patterns of brain activity expand.

Regardless of where it starts, focusing on something—anything—causes your brain to call up memories, as well as any potential motor actions you might take in relation to it. In some, it also conjures up emotions related to that thing. This “simulation” aspect of human brain function is vitally important. Not just as a way to navigate our lives, but for how we eventually come to make sense of our different life experiences. It is among our most valuable mental resources and a key feature of what sets us apart from the other species on earth.

As Groh explained, “Humans don’t hear or see any better than a macaque monkey.
